chapters.summary: Council staff welcome attendees to the joint hearing of the Committee on Oversight and Investigations and the Committee on Education, remind attendees to silence devices, sign in, and not approach the chairs.
chapters.title: Hearing called to order and housekeeping announcements

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Yeah, it's not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Oversight and Investigations, joined with the Committee on Education.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please sign to all cell phone and electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to speak in today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, no one is to approach today's chairs.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We are ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shekar Krishnan, Chair of the Committee on Oversight and Investigations, introduces the hearing topic and thanks co-chair Eric Dinowitz, DOE representatives, students, educators, unions, and council colleagues in attendance.
chapters.title: Chair Krishnan opens hearing on screen time and digital devices in NYC schools

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Shekar Krishnan, Chair of the Committee on Oversight and Investigations, and today we will be looking at screen time and the use of digital devices in our New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'd like to thank my fellow co-chair of this hearing, Councilmember Eric Dinowitz, Chair of the Committee on Education, for co-chairing this hearing with me today.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank the representatives of the Department of Education, students, educators, unions, members of the public, and my council colleagues who have joined us here today, including

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Councilmember Shulman, Councilmember Ong, Councilmember Lewis, Councilmember Rano, Councilmember Lee, Councilmember De La Rosa, Councilmember Carr, and Councilmember Wong.

chapters.summary: Krishnan describes how the 2020 pandemic forced children onto Chromebooks and Zoom, and how digital devices have since proliferated in classrooms and homes, creating ongoing negotiations over screen time at home.
chapters.title: Krishnan recounts pandemic-era screen reliance and proliferation of ed tech

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And we are also honored to have joining us today, too, our public advocate, Jumaane Williams.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We're also joined by many parents and advocates who share the same concern about how much technology our students are relying on to learn in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As parents, we all remember the dark days of 2020, where we sat over breakfast with our young kids in front of their Chromebooks.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We logged on to Zoom and Google Classroom, figured out how to use them after many tech issues logging on, figured out how to mute on Zoom, and then tried to finish up, after all of that, our cup of coffee while our children were learning on the screens.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And our children spent hours of the day, unfortunately, learning on the screen.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: After the pandemic ended, we were all happy and breathed a collective.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: sigh of relief when they went back to school.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Our kids finally got to see their friends and their beloved teachers again.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And we would get to close those Chromebooks.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Or so we thought.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But in the years since 2020, we've seen the proliferation of digital devices and screens in our classrooms and our homes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: They are pervasive now.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: For years after the pandemic, I've watched my children lug the same heavy Chromebooks to school, home, and back and forth every single day.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We've had protracting negotiations at home about screen time, YouTube, and the online apps that they want to play that are on their DOE-issued laptops.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I know every parent in this room knows those negotiations, battles, all too well.

chapters.summary: Krishnan highlights studies showing digital devices disrupt student focus, cites Google admitting YouTube is unsafe and distracting, and criticizes big tech companies profiting from millions in school contracts while accessing student data.
chapters.title: Krishnan cites research on screen harms and big tech profiteering in schools

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Parents, teachers, and advocates are rightly concerned that the use of ed tech products in our schools has become excessive and is distracting students from actual learning and undermining our teachers in the classroom when our students are distracted.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Studies have shown that digital devices disrupt student focus.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In fact, Google, that owns YouTube, has openly admitted that YouTube is, quote, unsafe and distracting.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: End quote.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Not to mention the health effects, disrupted sleep cycles, decrease in social coping skills, and eye strain.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: All while big tech companies profit.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: These massive companies are being awarded millions of dollars.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: of dollars in contracts, gaining access to critical student data while still being vulnerable to security breaches, and creating future customers for themselves.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In one breath, these billion-dollar companies are telling us that our kids will fall behind without their technology and then selling us their latest upgrade.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: All of this at a time when there's an entire national conversation raging about the need for government regulation of AI, around the mental health and addictive harms of social media, not just on adolescents, but on us as adults.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Meanwhile, ed tech is trying to import all of their products into the classroom to addict children early on in their education, from elementary school all the way through high school and beyond.

chapters.summary: Krishnan outlines the DOE's September guidance: no individual devices for pre-K through grade 2, 30-minute limits for grades 3-5, 45 minutes for grades 6-8, no limits for high school, and exemptions for standardized testing. He argues mandates are needed.
chapters.title: Krishnan reviews DOE's new screen time guidance and its limitations

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: These companies are pouring gasoline on this fire, all to generate profits for themselves.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now in September, the Department of Education published new guidance on the use of artificial intelligence and screen time.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The new guidance is an important and necessary first step.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now, most students from preschool through second grade will not be permitted to use individual devices in classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: For students in the third through fifth grade, the policy recommends limiting the use of individual devices to 30 minutes, and for sixth through eighth grade, that limit is 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There are no screen time limits, however, for high school students, and the limits do not apply

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The standardized testing.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether DOE is committed to overhauling technology reliance, auditing tech companies, and protecting students from predatory big tech. He calls for concrete plans and mandates, thanking council staff for their work.
chapters.title: Krishnan poses key questions for DOE and calls for action

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: While this policy is a good and necessary first step, I believe we must do more, and parents, teachers, and advocates have far more unanswered questions.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The reality is this.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The problem of screens in our schools, in our society, is pervasive, and it is simply outpacing current solutions.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: This moment requires more than recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We need mandates across our schools to protect our students and to support our teachers.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Today, we will learn what led the DOE to lay out their specific screen time recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is the DOE committed to overhauling technology reliance in our schools?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Will they audit these technology companies that store our children's data and distract them from learning?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And is the DOE prepared to protect our students from the predatory big technology companies in our schools?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: More than a decade after we've invited screens into our schools, the DOE needs to ensure that they have a concrete plan to address the rapidly rising concerns of screen time use that we as parents and teachers have.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We collectively need to tackle the increased use of big tech programs before it is too late.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now is the time to act to ensure we are giving our future generation the best shot possible.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: to be the generation that finds scientific breakthroughs, writes the next great novels, and becomes the best version of themselves.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so much of that does not happen on a screen or with YouTube or with gamified apps.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It happens off of all of those things.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We will not let the greed of big technology companies get in the way of our children's future or our students'ability to succeed.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Before I conclude, I would like to thank the following council staff for their work on this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Our O&I committee staff, Nicole Cata, Erica Cohen, Alex Yablon, and Owen Katowski, and Oversight Investigation Division staff, Kevin Frick and Ryan Parkin.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Education Committee staff, Alejandro Carvajal, Chloe Rivera, Katie Selena, Andrew Lane Lawless, and Grace Samato.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And of course, my staff, Chanel Martinez, Hunter DeVine-Gracia, Victoria Opperman, and everyone working here to make this hearing run as smoothly as possible.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Eric Dinowitz introduces himself as a former NYC public school student and teacher, now Chair of the Committee on Education, and co-chair of the hearing on screen time and digital devices.
chapters.title: Chair Dinowitz delivers opening remarks as former teacher and Education Chair

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now I'll turn it over to my co-chair of this hearing, Councilmember Eric Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Co-Chair Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's really a pleasure and honor to be here with you, someone who cares so deeply about the future of our city and the children in our school system.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Eric Dinowitz, former New York City public school student, former New York City public school teacher, and now chair of the Committee on Education in our great city.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz recounts teaching through a screen during COVID-19, notes that screens stayed after in-person learning returned, and frames the hearing as addressing whether students should continue facing screens all day.
chapters.title: Dinowitz describes the pandemic pivot to screens and the choice we now face

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm pleased to be here to co-chair the hearing to examine screen time and the use of digital devices in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Six and a half years ago, New York City public schools shut their doors in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I was in a classroom then.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like every other teacher in our system, I started teaching through a screen, almost overnight.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Teachers and students were asked to embrace learning management systems, video conferencing platforms, and educational software because the alternative was nothing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We had no preparation, no warning, no choice.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But today, we have a choice.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And as students and teachers went back into the classroom, the screens stayed.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The pivot to screens was necessary when we were locked away from each other.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: With the return to in-person learning, did students need to continue facing a screen all day instead of each other?

chapters.summary: Dinowitz cites research linking excessive screen time to obesity, sleep disorders, depression, and anxiety. He also acknowledges assistive technology's value for students with disabilities and English language learners, but stresses tools must be vetted and teachers trained.
chapters.title: Dinowitz on health risks of excessive screen time and assistive technology needs

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Research shows that excessive screen time in children is associated with increased risk of obesity, sleep disorders, and mental health conditions,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: including depression and anxiety, not to mention the challenges we as parents face when our children are engaged so much with their screens instead of with each other.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As a special education teacher, I also know what assistive technology can do for students with disabilities and English language learners.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But for some of our most vulnerable students, we must also ensure that these tools are vetted and teachers receive robust training lest these tools become substitutes for learning

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: rather than an accommodation that opens up access to the classroom for our students.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz describes the policy banning individual device use for 2K through grade 2, recommending limits for grades 3-8, and a moratorium on student-facing AI through grade 8. He questions the DOE's assumption that screens are good and necessary.
chapters.title: Dinowitz reviews the new AI and screen time policy and remaining questions

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Earlier this year, after mounting pressure from this committee, along with Chair De La Rosa from the Committee on Technology, along with parents and advocates,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels paused their original AI policy and announced a new AI and screen time policy for New York City schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This policy bans individual device use for children's 2K through second grade.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Recommends limited individual device use for students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Grades three through five, 30 minutes a day, recommended time limits.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Individual device use for students grades 6 through 8, 45 minutes a day.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And of course, these recommended limits exempt screeners and other assessment tools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To some degree, the release of the policy does demonstrate that the DOE is being responsive to the concerns of families and the elected officials, banning screens in the earliest grades and banning AI, a generative student-facing AI, through grade 8.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yet while the new policy provides some guidance around screen time in schools, it leaves many questions unanswered.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Undergirding the guidance from the DOE lies an assumption, an assumption that the DOE has yet to defend with robust evidence, that screens are good and necessary.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The DOE has an obligation to provide evidentiary support for the use of individual screens related to specific tools or products, not just a nebulous 30 minutes or 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Every tool, every product, and what is on those screens.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz notes teachers and administrators are unsure how to apply or circumvent the new limits, and asks what evidence DOE can produce for blanket screen use, what teacher training is offered, how stakeholders are engaged, and whether DOE will lobby for handwritten state assessments.
chapters.title: Dinowitz raises implementation concerns and key questions for DOE

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As a parent, as a teacher, we know, we feel it, like we know that there's a difference between a child alone

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: scrolling for the next video on YouTube or alone on a screen waiting for the next dopamine hit on that gamified learning, and a teacher in front of the room showing a short clip of a documentary and having a class discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Regarding the updated policy itself, for the start of school last week, many teachers and administrators were left wondering how to apply these new limits in their classrooms or in other cases, how to circumvent the new limits.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Superintendents are left to figure out specific guidance for their individual school districts.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For the success and health of our children, for the future of our city, we must get this right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What evidence can the DOE produce to demonstrate that blanket screen use is beneficial to our children?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What training is being offered to our teachers on products and methods that do meet a standard of efficacy?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How is the DOE continuing to engage stakeholders, and who are those stakeholders?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How will the DOE continually evaluate the policies affecting this throughout the year and at the end of the year, or as we say, formative and summative assessments?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And will the DOE join us to lobby New York State to return to handwritten statewide assessments?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So name a tool, name the study behind the tool, identify the professional development the teacher receives before deploying the tools to their classes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We all want the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A world-class education system for our children.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The hard part is how to get there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I look forward to today's hearing to move us all forward in the right direction for our children.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz names council members in attendance, thanks his staff and co-chair Krishnan, and concludes his opening remarks.
chapters.title: Dinowitz thanks council members and staff, turns back to Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I want to thank the members, I think they were all named, who are here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'll name them again.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Council members Joseph, De La Rosa, Wong, Minority Leader Carr, Frank, Council Member Murano, Lee, Ung, of course, Co-Chair Krishnan,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Ashulman, Narcisse, our Speaker, Julie-Menin, and our Public Advocate, Juwani Williams.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank my Chief of Staff, Jenna Klaus, my Legislative and Budget Director, Theo Solter, Education Committee staff, including Legislative Council, Alejandro Carvajal, Senior Legislative Policy Analyst, Chloe Rivera,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Legislative Policy Analyst, Katie Selena, Principal Financial Analyst, Angelina Lawless, and Financial Analyst, Grace Amato, for all of their work on today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And of course, once again, my co-chair, Council Member Krishnan, who I will now turn it back to.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin thanks the chairs and frames the hearing around parents' basic question of how much of the school day children should spend in front of screens, noting technology should support instruction, not replace it.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin delivers opening statement on screen time in schools

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thanks so much, Chair Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And now I'd like to introduce our speaker of the City Council, who has been a staunch advocate on this issue, both as the Speaker of the City Council and also as a mother herself.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And now I'll turn it over to you for your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I really want to thank you and Chair Dinowitz for all of your leadership on this issue and for convening this very important hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I want to thank DOE and other stakeholders who are here to participate in this important discussion.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: As another school year begins, families across New York City are thinking about the quality of the education our children are receiving, as well as the environment in which they are learning.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Increasingly, parents are asking a basic question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How much of the school day should children be spending in front of a screen?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Technology clearly has an important role in education.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It can support visual learners, provide translation, and give students with disabilities access to essential assistive technology.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But technology should support instruction, not replace it.

chapters.summary: Menin references screen time restrictions in at least six states and Los Angeles's limits, and highlights that more than half of American teenagers use AI chatbots for schoolwork, with research showing AI may harm independent performance.
chapters.title: Menin cites other states' and cities' screen time laws and AI concerns

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New York City is not alone in confronting this issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: At least six states, including Alabama, Iowa, Maine, Tennessee, Virginia, and Utah, have also addressed this issue by putting in place laws that are restricting, limiting class screen time.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And at least 10 other states have also enacted similar types of legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Los Angeles has also adopted some limits, including a total of six hours per week of screen time for middle school students and 10 hours per week of screen time for high school students, and that includes homework as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Artificial intelligence also raises very significant issues and questions as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: More than half of American teenagers report using AI chat box for their schoolwork, and one in 10 say that AI is

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: with all or most of their schoolwork.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And research suggests that while unrestricted AI may help students perform better on a particular task,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: they perform significantly worse when they're asked to complete the exact same type of work independently without any AI assistance.

chapters.summary: Menin notes reading scores dropped six percentage points for grades 3-8 and third-grade proficiency sank nearly 14%. She calls for guardrails ensuring every device, platform, and screen minute serves a clear educational purpose.
chapters.title: Menin cites declining reading scores and calls for guardrails on technology

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So then what are we teaching these young people?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This year, the overall reading scores for students between third and eighth grade dropped six percentage points compared to last year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And third grade proficiency alone sank by nearly 14%.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These numbers are truly alarming.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We need to make sure that our schools are helping students develop much needed reading, writing, reasoning, and problem solving skills.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: DEWE's guidance significantly restricts individual device use for younger students, recommends limits of 30 minutes per day for grades 3 through 5, and 45 minutes for grades 6 through 8, and establishes a one-year moratorium on most student-facing

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: generative AI through 8th grade, affecting nearly 600,000 students.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But we really need to know whether the screen time recommendations will actually be followed, whether teachers have the books, instructional materials, and training they need to provide meaningful screen-free instruction,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and whether every technology product purchased with taxpayer dollars is supported by evidence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: so that it actually improves learning.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This hearing is about putting in place guardrails to ensure the responsible use of technology in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Every single device, every platform, and every minute a student spends on a screen should serve a clear educational purpose.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our goal should be classrooms where technology is a useful tool, but never a substitute for teachers'books, critical thinking, creativity, and interaction with classmates.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams thanks the chairs and acknowledges the administration's new AI and screen time policy as a response to widespread advocacy and research on negative effects of excessive screen time for young children.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams delivers opening statement on AI and screen time

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now it's our honor to call up for an opening statement our public advocate, who also cares deeply about this issue, Public Advocate Jumaane Williams.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair Krishnan and Chair Dynowitz, for this hearing and, of course, the speaker, all for your leadership and giving me the opportunity to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As mentioned, my name is Jumaane Williams, public advocate for the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Following widespread support and countless advocacy by concerned educators and parent groups calling for an AI moratorium, I was heartened to see the administration acknowledge that they missed the mark with the initial preliminary guidance released in March.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The new AI and screen time policy are not only an acknowledgement of the moment we find ourselves in, another turning point in the evolution of technology, but also a natural conclusion to the decades of data and research that highlights the negative effects of extending screen time for our youngest kids.

chapters.summary: Williams references State Senator Gounardes's FOCUS Act and Norway's ban on generative AI for elementary students, and calls for schools to recommit to teaching basics amid declining reading and math scores.
chapters.title: Williams highlights state and international momentum on AI limits

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These policies reflect a growing momentum at the state level.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: and even abroad.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Earlier this year, State Senator Andrew Granatis introduced the Fostering Optimal Classroom Use of Screens Act, aiming to strictly limit student exposures to screens and artificial intelligence in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Across the Atlantic, Norway made headlines this summer with a new ministerial directive banning the use of generative AI tools for elementary school students and limiting use for older students.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: At a time when reading and math scores continue to decline year after year, it is important that our schools recommit to teaching the basics and do not allow machines to co-opt our children's ability to learn and think critically.

chapters.summary: Williams discusses his office's new report calling for responsible AI use, ongoing public engagement, and AI-specific procurement standards to prevent problematic contracts like digital bathroom passes and voice recognition apps for young children.
chapters.title: Williams discusses new AI report and procurement oversight concerns

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In relation to this, my office released a new report yesterday calling for responsible use of AI with one of the foremost recommendations being ongoing engagement with the public on the topic of artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I also call for greater oversight of the kinds of contracts the city signs with vendors by creating AI-specific standards for procurement.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We believe greater scrutiny on this front will prevent concerning and potentially problematic contracts like this that have caused alarm in recent weeks, including the use of digital bathroom passes in schools and voice recognition application for our youngest kids.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The New Technology in Schools Coalition composed of elected officials, parent leaders, educators, and other experts will serve a critical role in examining the impact of those new screen time and artificial intelligence policies.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And expanding on this existing foundation of dialogue.

chapters.summary: Williams shares quotes from a community forum on AI, urges using current knowledge to change course before more harm occurs, and warns that the house is already on fire regarding technology's impact on children.
chapters.title: Williams shares community feedback on AI and urges action before it's too late

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In this spirit of open dialogue, when we rolled out our report, we took the opportunity to host a community forum with New Yorkers who have seen many waves of new technology in their lifetimes.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Here are just a few pieces of feedback we heard.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: AI needs to be nonpolitical.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The system is designed where you find out about these things after the fact.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We are skeptical about everything.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Please support AI guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These quotes convey how ordinary, everyday New Yorkers are thinking about AI and its impact on their daily lives.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I look forward to being a partner in these discussions and helping craft and shape future legislations as it pertains to the impact of technology on our youngest children.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As I said outside, I think many of us are impacted.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I know many of us may have stayed up way too long, doom scrolling, and realized it's 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Many folks can't even go to the bathroom without their phones.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But all of us learned in a way that allows us to critically think.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We are now talking about young children who have not yet got that ability to critically think.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And what would happen if we can go back with this knowledge before the social media harmed our kids, before we allowed cell phones in schools?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We'd probably do things differently.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I'm hoping that we can use this knowledge and change now.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The house is already on fire.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's about how long are we going to allow it to burn?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Are we going to let it burn it down, or are we going to stop it?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And, of course, your president said we don't have anything to worry about as long as we have a president that has a high IQ, which means we're all in a lot of trouble.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But even if there wasn't a president with high IQ, it cannot be left to just one person, whether it's climate change or tech.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We need to have folks who are not just focused on money, but trying to make sure we have a world.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: leave my young daughter.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So thank you for this hearing and hopefully we can take this information and do better for our youngest kids.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Krishnan recognizes Councilmembers Brewer and Farias on Zoom, and explains that before DOE testifies, a panel of educators, organizers, parents, and activists will speak first about their experiences with screens in schools.
chapters.title: Krishnan recognizes additional council members and introduces first public panel

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Public Advocate.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We appreciate your leadership and testimony and advocacy on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Before going any further, we just want to recognize that we've also been joined by Councilmember Brewer and Councilmember Farias on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now, before turning it over to the Department of Education for their testimony, both Chair Dinowitz and I feel it's very important that,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: on all issues, frankly, but especially on an issue like this, that we understand from those most directly affected and impacted by the issues how they are perceiving the problem of screens in our schools, how they are working on them,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and how they feel about perhaps even their own children being exposed to all of these different big tech products.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So with that in mind, before we hear from the DOE, we're going to call up a panel of educators, organizers, parents, and activists to testify first.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up now for their testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Khalid Salas from CEC4, Aracelis Lucero from MASA, Naveed Hassan from Panel Education Policy, and David Monahan from Fair Play.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I'd like to, on behalf of both Chair Dinowitz and myself, thank the Department of Education and the administration for their willingness to have this testimony first before turning it over to the DOE for their testimony.

chapters.summary: Dr. Salas-Ramirez, a neuroscientist and parent, testifies about the impact of ed tech and screen time on children's cognitive load, emotional engagement, and mental health, calling for an audit of ed tech platforms and a moratorium on AI and ed tech.
chapters.title: Dr. Kaleri Salas-Ramirez testifies on ed tech's impact on children's cognition and mental health

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Dinowitz and Chair Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: My name is Kaleri Salas Ramirez, pronoun she, her, ella.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: I should also say Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: Salas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: The Department of Education has heard me multiple times, but in this moment, I want to speak not just as a parent of a 10th grader and a second grader, but also as a neuroscientist and a fellow educator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: We are seeing that our children have been deeply impacted, not just by the use of ed tech, but also by mandated curriculum that has ed tech embedded, as well as screen time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: Since the pandemic, not only are we seeing a decrease in test scores, but we're also seeing an increase in diagnoses of children with autism,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: with children with ADHD, in addition to mental health concerns of depression and anxiety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: The American Psychological Association and the Association of American Pediatrics have all listed

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: recommendations in terms of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: of screen time use in our schools, but also the direct correlation between these mental health conditions and neurodivergence related to trauma and their experiences in schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: I think it's absolutely critical to take a look at not just how we are, if we are effectively using technology in our classrooms,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: but also the connection between the assessments and the experiences of our children in the classroom and what we know are evidence-driven practices that our teachers are fully aware.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: So I will say there are some really amazing things happening in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: So I am not, this is not a knock.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: On what our teachers and educators are doing in our classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: This is about improving our practices now that we have evidence that what we are doing in our classrooms has been directly impairing cognitive load, emotional engagement, and has increasing racial bias in our classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: So we're asking for an audit of all of these ed tech platforms and that we should have a full moratorium on AI and ed tech until we understand what this technology is being used for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kaleri Salas-Ramirez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aracelis Lucero, executive director of MASA, describes how AI, screen time, and digital curricula exacerbate inequities for immigrant families, sharing a personal story about her son's declining literacy and writing skills due to screen-based learning.
chapters.title: Aracelis Lucero of MASA testifies on ed tech inequities for immigrant families

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Hello, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: My name is Araceli Sucero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I am the executive director of MASA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: We are a community-based organization that partners with Latino immigrant and indigenous families to develop strong learners and leaders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I am also the parent of two public school students.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Araceli, if you can bring the mic a little bit closer.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I am also the parent of two public school students in kindergarten and fourth grade, and I'm also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: The proud product of immigrant parents and the New York City public school system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: As an immigrant and education advocate, I've witnessed over and over how black, brown, immigrant, and indigenous communities have been failed by our public school education,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: as displayed by the educational outcomes that we see across race, class, and subgroups like English language learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: The over-reliance and use of AI, screen time, and curriculums that rely on them, like HMH and iReady, have only exacerbated these inequities for immigrant community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Immigrant parents already face language access issue in our public school system, leaving them feeling unwelcome and in the dark about what is happening in the school and in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: The use of technology, especially when all communities are not being brought along responsibly and equitably, has only widened the quote-unquote achievement gap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: For example, many of our families...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Cannot afford internet and students are expected to practice online at home or complete assignments online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: At MASA, many families ask to either use our internet or our devices for their children to complete their assignments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Furthermore, all parent communication about schooling has moved to online platforms, which not only

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: which not all parents can access, leaving a key part of a student's educational trajectory out of the picture, the parent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: At Masses After School program, we have also witnessed how teachers are less able to provide meaningful feedback and strategies, both to parents and to us, about how to support the students in our program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: My own experience with my son, who is a fourth grader,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: has illuminated the issue for me and helped me understand how education has changed and why students and teachers are more disconnected than ever, contributing to the results we see today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: When he entered kindergarten, he was advanced in reading by two grade levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I have seen how my son over the years has started to struggle in literacy and now

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: reading at grade level, but has fallen behind in writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, this is upsetting to me.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Simply because he doesn't have the stamina to write since it's not a critical focus in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Students are put in front of screens to learn content and different subjects are not being properly monitored to ensure they are even completing the designated task

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: and rely on unit assessments evaluated by a computer to gauge where they are without providing the opportunity for relationships to be built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: For teachers to really get to know how students learn and why they are struggling to master certain concepts and to adapt their lessons to address those gaps and teach to the different learners and styles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: In March of last year, I noticed that my son's headphones were missing in his classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: When I asked him where they were, he said that he hadn't seen them since January and that he had told his teacher about it when it happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: When I asked the teacher about it, she said she didn't know he was missing his headphones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I responded by saying, you mean to tell me that my son has been sitting in front of a screen for three months now without being able to engage in key instructional lessons and content because no one noticed his headphones were missing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: And I was met with a blank stare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: At the end of the year, I reached out to his teacher to ask for feedback.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: only to be met with very general feedback.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: When I forwarded what another private tutor from the Hunter College Literacy Center had provided me with strategies, then

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: She was able to offer me more feedback, literally verbatim with what his tutor had given me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I'll fast forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: As a parent with a lot of privilege, including a master's degree from a top university who works for an education nonprofit, I always feel like a fast one is being pulled over my head.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I can only imagine how day in and day out families and students are made to feel left out and their full potential left untapped, especially when we have bias in the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I believe many teachers are doing the best they can with what they have, but AI, screen time, the current ELA and math curriculums we use, the digital tools we rely on to teach and engage our children are doing a disservice to our children, including my own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: I fully support the elimination of screen time and AI in the classroom, especially during the critical years of learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: There are other ways to address ensuring there is a technology gap, like a technology class that doesn't have to sacrifice the core subjects, our need for genuine human interaction, and developing the skills our children are expected to learn so that they can thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: David Monahan, campaign director at Fair Play, testifies about correlations between screen time and mental health declines, the addictive design of YouTube and gamified learning tools, and urges DOE to put mandates in place.
chapters.title: David Monahan of Fair Play testifies on harms of ed tech and addictive design

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: I'm David Monahan, campaign director at Fair Play.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: We're a national nonprofit organization that works to enhance children's well-being by eliminating the exploitative and harmful practices of marketers and big tech.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: We're an independent voice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: We do not accept funding from tech companies or any other corporation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: I submit this testimony on behalf of the thousands of our supporters who reside in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: I live in Massachusetts, but I'm a native of Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn, a proud product of the New York City school system, including Abraham Lincoln High School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Stinowitz and Krishnan for holding this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: You know, in our work nationwide, we have been inspired by a wave of passionate advocates who have succeeded in changing the narrative on screens and ed tech in schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: Parents, educators, and advocates here in New York have supercharged that movement and are showing every day that we can and will put the well-being of children and teens ahead of the profits of corporations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: with the help of leaders like the members of this body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: They played an important role in advocating for bell-to-bell phone-free schools across New York State, which is removing the distraction of smartphones from classrooms and lunchrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: The AIM Coalition played a pivotal role in demanding protections from the encroachment of generative AI into education, and in part they were armed with a letter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: led by Fair Play and signed by experts from across North America saying we needed a moratorium until we learn better about the impacts of AI in education and kids' well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: The result last week, the mayor announced that city students will be protected by a broad moratorium, and we've discussed today that we also need to go and take

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: further steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: Parents and advocates are here today to say there is more work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: Studies have shown correlations between increased time spent on digital devices and declines in children's mental health, including anxiety, depression, isolation, attention deficits, and addiction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: One-to-one devices in classrooms have been associated with weaker learning outcomes and are exposing students to manipulative sites which monopolize their attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: The verdict in the KGM case in California this spring established Google intentionally designed YouTube with addictive engagement mechanics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: How can we possibly allow students to stare at YouTube in school or on school-issued devices?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: And unproven gamified learning tools are designed to make kids stare at the screen for hours and then nag their parents to purchase upgrades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: But they're not designed to educate or pique a student's curiosity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: We urge the DOE to put mandates in place to take the next important step in making New York City schools effective and safe learning environments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Monahan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Navid Hassan, a PEP member and parent, testifies about the need for sovereign municipal tech infrastructure, criticizes DOE's reliance on outside vendors, and highlights privacy law violations by ed tech products using YouTube loopholes.
chapters.title: Navid Hassan of PEP testifies on need for municipal tech infrastructure and vendor oversight

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: My name is Navid Hassan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: I'm a parent elected to the panel for educational policy, which is the New York City School Board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Here's my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: New York City must take a bolder policy stance with regards to technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: New Yorkers should benefit from the size of our budget with tech services that are designed for public benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: We need to move away from school purchasing choices based on hype and marketing and develop sovereign municipal tech infrastructure within which we engage with outside vendors in a more private, secure, and sustainable way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Protecting our children from harm and exploitation by big tech can only start if we lay the proper foundation for this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Our school system has been enmeshed in a decades-long process of privatization of core responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Letting outside vendors do the thinking when we should be cultivating our highly trained in-house professionals, including educators with graduate degrees, to develop the pedagogical stack of how to best teach New York City students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: This includes responsive curriculum, appropriate modalities of delivering it, hopefully whole chapter book reading, which I don't know what happened to that, and properly supported safety and privacy preserving technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Needs and wants will also differ from borough to borough, neighborhood to neighborhood, and school to school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: So top-down dictates lead to one-size-fits-no-one solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: With an academic and professional background in computer science and AI, and a board of ed graduate,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: a DOE parent of two students in public schools uptown Manhattan, and an elected member of the PEP for five terms, it is my experience that the DOE unfortunately does not have the will or appetite to do this foundational work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: It's not clear what it means to ask vendors to remove AI from software already in schools and districts when that product is just a thin code wrapper on ChatDPT or Claude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Even when tech vendors themselves, for example, Google with YouTube, have told government customers that their product cannot comply with laws around student data privacy, years later, consumer YouTube is still a big part of many ed tech services in DOE classrooms,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: using loopholes and workarounds that are in violation of the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: A lot of these ed tech products are provided for free before local smaller dollar purchasing agreements bypass any PEP oversight on the propriety of these tools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: There is a significant amount the city can do by refusing to buy products or services from companies behind the attempt to privatize intelligence,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: sell it as a utility, and wantonly disrupt society, undermine democracy, all for their concentration of wealth and power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Let's make sure that this is not our children's future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Navid Hassan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Krishnan thanks the first panel and calls up DOE representatives for their testimony, noting questions for the first panel will be deferred until after DOE testifies.
chapters.title: Krishnan thanks first panel and calls up DOE representatives

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know there may be questions for this panel, but in the interest of time as well, we'll return to this panel for questions after the Department of Education testifies.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you all very much.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And now we'll call up the representatives from DOE for their testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I'll turn it over to our committee counsel to administer the oath.

chapters.summary: Committee counsel introduces the DOE panel—Danielle Giunta, Scott Strickland, and Laura Lai—and administers the affirmation to tell the truth before the committee.
chapters.title: Committee counsel administers affirmation to DOE panelists

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We will now hear testimony from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: The panel will consist of Daniela Junta, Scott Strickland, and Laura Lai.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And present to answer questions include Suzanne Sanchez, Mark Ramper Sant, Erica Smith, Kyle McDonald, Dennis Doyle, Tunisia Mitchell,

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And Randy Asher.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Panelists and those answering questions, please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aracelis Lucero
utterances.text: You may begin when ready.

chapters.summary: Danielle Giunta, First Deputy Chancellor, introduces herself and her team, states DOE's guiding ethos that students learn best through connection with teachers and peers, and references the successful cell phone ban policy.
chapters.title: DOE First Deputy Chancellor Giunta begins testimony on learning philosophy and cell phone policy

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: All right, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Dinowitz, Chair Krishnan, and members of the Committees on Education and Oversight and Investigations.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: My name is Danielle Junta, and I'm the first Deputy Chancellor of New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Overseeing superintendents and key offices including academics and instruction, district planning, enrollment, new school development and design, policy and evaluation, and our Office of Student Pathways.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'm joined today by Scott Strickland, our Deputy Chief Information Officer, and Laura Lai, a Senior Policy Advisor, as well as other New York City Public School colleagues who you just listed.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for your continued advocacy and engagement on this important topic.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We've met with many of you through this process and I've appreciated your feedback and commitment to New York City students.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: As educators, we want all of our children to learn.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We know that our children learn best when they connect with their teachers,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: and their peers, and when they experience productive struggle.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In other words, we agree, our students need to learn how to learn, and that is the guiding ethos in all we do.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Last year, that same ethos, along with Governor Hochul's leadership on this issue, led us to our cell phone and electronic device policy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Which is a full ban on personal

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: internet-enabled devices in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: A personal internet-enabled device includes any electronic device not issued by a school or a New York City public school program that can connect to the internet, allowing the user to access content online.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We saw firsthand the success of this policy in shaping productive, engaged classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Students were no longer distracted and could connect with each other in class and at lunch.

chapters.summary: Giunta outlines the updated screen time policy: no individual screen use for 2K through grade 2, recommended 30-minute limits for grades 3-5, 45 minutes for grades 6-8, and course-dictated use for high school, emphasizing technology should be used sparingly with clear instructional purposes.
chapters.title: Giunta presents new screen time policy for grades 2K through 8

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And while we're grateful to Governor Hochul for enacting this law statewide, we know cell phones are not the only screen students interact with in their day-to-day lives.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: When it comes to our classrooms, we believe technology best supports student learning when it is used sparingly, with clear instructional purposes, and for younger students, only under the direct supervision of their teacher.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: All of our students, but our youngest in particular,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: need hands-on learning, social interaction, play, and teacher-guided instruction.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And routine individual screen use can crowd out those experiences.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Technology should not be the primary means of instruction or as a go-to tool for keeping students busy,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: entertained or quiet.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Building on the shared understanding on September 2nd of this year, this administration announced an updated policy on

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: AI and screen time for the 26-27 school year to establish more robust guardrails beyond the initial guidance released in March 2026.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This updated policy is designed to further protect our students from the negative impacts of excessive screens and artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: On screen time specifically, we know that unfettered, unstructured time in front of screens can diminish the interpersonal interactions necessary for growth in areas like language development and cognitive functioning.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It can also negatively impact emotional development and behavior, especially in our young children.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: As such, for the 26-27 school year, students in grades 2K through 2 will have no individual screen use, and students in grades 3 through 5

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: will be limited to a recommended 30 minutes maximum of screen time per day.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And for students in grades 6 through 8, the recommendation is no more than 45 minutes per day.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: For our high school students, device use will be dictated by the course.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are communicating with schools that as in the lower grades, use of screens must be for specific instructional purpose, used sparingly, and that unstructured device use is not acceptable.

chapters.summary: Giunta details exceptions to the screen time limits: assistive technology for students with disabilities and multilingual learners, digital assessments and diagnostics, out-of-school learning, and centrally approved instructional programs like e-books and coding classes.
chapters.title: Giunta explains exceptions to screen time policy

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: To ensure this policy serves students equitably and effectively, there are a few important exceptions to the restrictions outlined above.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The first is for students with disabilities and multilingual learners who require the use of assistive technologies.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Assistive technology is preserved across all grades under the screen time policy as well as our AI policy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In fact, we are legally required to utilize technologies mandated by an individualized education plan or 504 plan.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: These are specific tools for specific students determined by the student's IEP team, which includes students'parents.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Other exceptions to the screen time policy include assessments and diagnostics.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Digital assessments are exempt from screen time limits because they provide information educators need to improve student learning.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Digital universal screeners and diagnostic assessments allow schools to quickly identify students who may need additional support,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: pinpoint specific skill gaps, and track growth over time, enabling educators to determine whether interventions are having the desired impact.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The exemption also reflects the reality that many assessments our students encounter, including the state exams, the SAT, driver permit tests, are all administered digitally.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The screen time limits also do not apply to out-of-school learning, such as remote instruction days and virtual learning programs.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Finally, certain centrally approved instructional programs will be granted exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: These may include e-books and classes such as robotics and coding where the subject matter requires screen use.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The purpose of these exceptions is not to expand a student's weekly screen time without purpose, but to appropriately allow for academic experiences that may require access to a computer.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We will encourage schools to reduce screen time use in other subjects when schools or when students have a period such as computer lab during the day.

chapters.summary: Giunta explains the AI policy: a full moratorium on student-facing generative AI for 2K through grade 8, and for high school, AI restricted to five vetted pilots, career readiness programs, and required AI literacy coursework.
chapters.title: Giunta presents AI policy: moratorium for 2K-8, restricted high school use

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: To briefly review our policy on student-facing generative AI, our new policy represents a cautious, developmentally appropriate approach that strictly limits access to student-facing generative artificial intelligence during the school day,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: especially for our youngest learners, for whom direct interaction and foundational skills are most important.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This aligns with what we know about child development and the limited body of independent causal research on these AI tools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: To that end, we have instituted a full moratorium on AI use in the classroom for students in 2K through 8 for the 26-27 school year.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our policy for high schoolers is different.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: High school students need guided preparation for a world economy increasingly driven by AI and new technologies, paired with instruction on how AI works, its biases and risks, and how to evaluate its outputs.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So in grades 9 through 12, student-facing AI will be restricted to three specific uses.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The first is five limited, carefully controlled high school pilots that involve vetted and approved AI programs.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Students can also use AI under teacher supervision if participating in career readiness programs, such as our career and technical education programs.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And finally, all students, all high school students will complete AI literacy coursework to understand how AI works and how to navigate the technology safely.

chapters.summary: Giunta summarizes that NYC's policy has some of the broadest restrictions on AI and screen use in the country, is a one-year policy, and will be evaluated through a Technology in Schools Coalition to map future technology use.
chapters.title: Giunta summarizes policy as among broadest restrictions in country, outlines coalition work

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Across all grades, the only exception to the AI policy is assistive technologies for students with disabilities and our English language learners.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In summary, New York City Public Schools has announced a policy with some of the broadest restrictions on AI and screen use in the country.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It is a one-year policy that will help us work with a new technology and schools coalition

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: to evaluate ongoing research, our high school pilots, and feedback on this year's policies to map the future of technology use in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We look forward to partnering with all of you in the coming year to ensure our policies reflect the needs of all students and families.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you, and I look forward to the opportunity to answer some questions today.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks why DOE issued recommendations rather than mandates, expressing concern about inconsistent implementation across schools. Giunta responds that the limits are non-negotiable despite the word 'recommended,' and that schools need flexibility for implementation.
chapters.title: Krishnan questions DOE on recommendations vs. mandates rationale

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, First Deputy Chancellor, for your testimony, for DOE's engagement on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I've had conversations with the Chancellor about it as well, and so we appreciate your commitment to addressing it with us and working together.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I've got a few questions to jump on a few different topics, and I'll turn it over to Chair Dinowitz and then open it up to our members to ask questions as well and then come back to myself.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Just to start with some, you know, jumping around to some different topics.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So just at the outset.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
