utterances.text: One of the things that concerned us when I saw the policy was recognizing how ubiquitous the problem is now and how it's getting worse.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What was DOE's rationale to issue a series of recommendations as opposed to mandates?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And what are you hearing so far about how that's playing out?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because my concern is different school districts, different schools will implement these recommendations in different ways.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: They're not all on a level playing field.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so why did DOE approach this from an advisory standpoint as opposed to a standpoint of issuing mandates?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to clarify as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we arrived at this policy based on a year's worth of feedback, listening towards CEC meetings, PEP meetings.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so we appreciate the acknowledgement of the council and our community of how we evolved this based on feedback and research.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: As we got to the word recommended, I want to assure everybody.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: in this room, everybody watching, and has been shared with our superintendents.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Under the division of the first deputy chancellor, which is I, we have our supervising superintendents, our superintendents, principals, teachers, all of our school personnel, and we have made one thing clear.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So this policy, while we don't want it to be punitive,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: while we're implementing, and we know that there will be an implementation, like, kind of gross period, that it is clear that these policies, these recommended, the 30, the 45, the no use, they are required.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They are non-negotiable.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony, we talked, somebody mentioned, I'm sorry, I don't remember who, around the percentage of time our kids are spending on devices in schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we looked very closely at these time limits to make sure that this is not exceeding 10 to 15% of the school day.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And what we're really talking about as well is like this unfettered, unstructured use of technology.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We don't want any of our students participating in that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we also know that our schools are built very differently.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The number of staff, the number of class, the number of students, the way schools are programmed, the curriculum they're using, the instructional tools that they have chosen to use.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we need to leave space for our schools to be able to make those decisions around how it's going to work in their schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Similarly to our cell phone policy, we set up a very clear, we are not using cell phones in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: schools and then schools found pathways into how that was going to work in their given facility and based on the staff that they have.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we know that our schools, you know, I trust our schools, but more than just trusting our schools is like these critical feedback loops that we have between myself, the supervising superintendents,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: their principles about how it's going, how implementation is going, and making sure everyone knows that our stance on the zero for 2K to 2, 30 for 3 to 5, and 45 for 6 to 8 really is a non-negotiable.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But we don't want schools to, you know, this is the fourth day of school.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want schools to feel comfortable to figure this out, to have time to collaborate and make really

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: very intentional decisions on if we're going to use technology in our classrooms, when will that be and for how long, and have a landscape across the student's day of how that lands for the student.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how DOE defines the 30-45 minutes of screen time. Giunta clarifies it should be intentional, active instructional use, not passive or routine use, and that routine device use is not acceptable.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks how DOE defines screen time; Giunta clarifies active instructional use

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I want to come back to that issue in a second.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Just a couple clarifying questions.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So when we say 30 minutes of screen time or 45 minutes of screen time, how are you all defining screen time?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is it active instructional use for an educational benefit?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is it passive use where the students are messing around on the computers?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What defines that 30 to 40 minutes of screen time?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because that wasn't clear in the policy, but I obviously think those two are very different uses of screens.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want active.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: If we're going to be using digital devices, technology in our classrooms, it needs to be intentional, active, not passive.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We don't want to see kids on a one-to-one device isolated for all the reasons that everybody's opening statement spoke to today.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want it to be very intentional around this tool is critical to the need of this learning target or this instructional moment that we're having in the class.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that is how we are defining the 30 minutes of use.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And also, we're clear to say, like, the routine use.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We don't want anything to be a routine use of a digital device in the school.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So the permitted screen time, whatever the allowable amount is, should be active instructional screen time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Krishnan raises concerns about K-2 students bringing Chromebooks home, opening up screen time negotiations at home. Giunta acknowledges limited need for daily device use at home but notes remote learning days require device readiness.
chapters.title: Krishnan questions Chromebooks going home with K-2 students

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now, I know there's a difference between K through 2 and 3 to 5.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Focusing on K through 2 for a minute, no one-to-one devices are allowed.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The policy was silent, though, on are students permitted to bring their Chromebooks home with them, which raises a number of issues.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: One, just they're very little, carrying those laptops back and forth every day.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But also, once that's introduced at home, it opens a new door and a new set of negotiations over whether to use those laptops, whether to play on them, under the guise of...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: eyes of learning, which our creative kindergartners through second graders are always citing as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So what is the DOE's policy for K through 2?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: If there's no one-to-one learning, are Chromebooks permitted to come home with students?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We would imagine that, of course, children should not need their computers on a daily, their individual Chromebooks on a daily basis at all.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We also want our kids to know, like, we will have a remote day.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We might have a pivots remote, whether it's weather or some other event.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We're also planning for a remote day on election day.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we do want to leverage opportunities for students to be able to understand how to access their Google Classrooms, how to access homework that might be posted digitally.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we also know that in our schools, there might be an opportunity not for one-to-one device, but, you know,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: we have our digital library where kids might be pulling up, a teacher might pull up a book and a kid can read along with the story.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But I think we'll see limited back and forth of our littlest carrying our laptops every day.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks what drove the different policy for grades 3-5, wondering if standardized testing starting in grade 3 was the reason. Giunta and Laura Lai explain the policy was based on developmental research, not solely testing.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks why screen time policy differs for grade 3 and above

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That's something that, you know, of the different things that we wanted to explore with you all, too, was just, you know, the necessity of kids bringing home their laptops K through 5.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know the line right now is K through 2, but the reality is, you know, and I'm sure you all are aware of it, too, but once we start opening that door, especially with home use, too, it opens up a whole number of doors on top of that, and it becomes yet another.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: distraction in the home as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, you know, I do wonder about the utility of Google Classroom for a kindergartner, for example, or a first grader.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So I would want to urge you all to really think about the necessity and how we ensure that if we have no one-to-one devices, we're not, you know, allowing these devices to come home to and opening up another.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As we as parents struggle with how to limit tech and screens at home, we're not kind of opening up a back door to allow it in because the kids will absolutely see it and will absolutely take advantage of it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: On that note, for three to five,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What was the reasoning for having a different policy for third grade on?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I've read some things about there's this larger issue of, which we can talk more about later, online standardized testing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That starts in third grade.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But was that the reason driving the policy, or why was there a different policy for third through fifth grade?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm going to introduce Lara Lai into the conversation in a moment.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I would say the sole determinant was not about preparing our kids to take digital assessments.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We were looking at research.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We were looking at sort of like the limits that were being set around

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: recommended in the research, how it was going in other school districts that were implementing our recommendation from even some of our labor partners, all the work that was coming out over the last year and the feedback that we were getting in our listening tours.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But Lara and I will talk a little bit more about

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: some of the specific research and thought processing.

chapters.summary: Laura Lai explains DOE took a developmentally based approach, noting stronger research on screen time impacts in early years for language acquisition and psychological development, and that some limited examples show benefits under teacher supervision for older students.
chapters.title: Laura Lai explains developmental research basis for screen time limits

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Thank you, First Deputy Chancellor, and thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We really took a very developmentally based approach to both our screen time and our AI policies.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We spent a good amount of time looking at the research, both with regard to child development and also with regard to outcomes with these types of tools.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: I'll say first of all that the child development research has a much stronger foundation in terms of looking at the types of impacts that screen time can have on behavior, language acquisition,

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: psychological development, attention span, and all of those concerns that so many people have about screens.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And that a lot of the most foundational aspects of child development are taking place in those earlier years and are most highly impacted by screens.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Our policy is not trying to say that there's no impact later on.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We thought that the most impactful period of time

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: were those early years when children are acquiring language and basically learning how to learn for the first time, learning how to read and do all of those things.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: As children, the research as children get older, what we found was that there are examples, although limited, and I do want to emphasize that in looking at the research on specific tools,

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: as I'm sure you're probably aware, a lot of that research comes from vendors.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And so it's very difficult to find peer-reviewed, independent academic studies on specific tools, for example.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: But there are some examples that show that under teacher supervision, for example, tutoring programs can be impactful when combined with teacher instruction.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And to your question about what is screen time, is that just kids sitting on a computer, or is that actually active, engaged, teacher-directed learning?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: When combined with those types of conditions, teacher-based, short periods of time, instructionally directed, there can be benefits.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And so we wanted to find opportunities as students progress through elementary school and then into middle school to have opportunities to engage in those types of experiences on a very limited basis.

chapters.summary: Krishnan raises concerns about students accessing YouTube on school devices, getting around filters, and asks if DOE will mandate blocking student YouTube access. Giunta agrees and Scott Strickland explains YouTube has been filtered out of all student devices as of that week.
chapters.title: Krishnan questions DOE on student access to YouTube in classrooms

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Just a few more questions for me, and I'm going to turn it over to Chair Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: First, I want to recognize that we've also been joined by Councilmember Zhuang and also State Senator Andrew Ganardis, who is a

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: been leading this effort on the state level and been a great partner in the work as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: A few more questions from my end.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: One is going back to the issue of mandates versus recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You know, I understand there are conversations to be had about these different, you know, issues and how to address them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But one thing I would hope that we could all agree on and address is

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: the issue of student-led access to YouTube in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There are a lot, children have virtually either unfettered access to YouTube or they're able to figure out ways to get around the filters in the classroom to use YouTube.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now I want to distinguish the use of YouTube for instructional purpose, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: When teachers are using it as an educational aid to show videos, that's one thing, that's a separate conversation.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What I'm talking about is when students have such access and dependence on screens, their ability to go on and watch different

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: programs on YouTube, get around the filters, watch things they shouldn't, and the number of parents that I've heard from around the city hearing their kids talk about

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: things they've watched on YouTube in the classroom on their own, or talking to their peers about, and parents have overheard it, about things that they've watched, clearly that happened in school in the classroom, or how they got around these different filters, it raises a really serious question.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: of putting aside the educational use of YouTube, has the DOE explored and considered the importance of instituting a mandate on student access to YouTube, which is a policy that the LA Unified School District has as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And at least maybe that's a starting place where we could institute a mandate, because I fail to see the educational value of allowing students that kind of access to YouTube for their own passive screen time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We couldn't agree more, actually, and so thank you for raising that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to Scott Strickland to explain some of the working behind it, but we have, in fact,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: turned off the access to the unfederated version of YouTube and kept sacred just a very limited educational purpose, as you just described, but I'm going to ask Scott to jump in.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Scott Strickland, I'm a deputy CIO at New York City Department of Education, Division of Information and Instructional Technology.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Been with the department for eight years in a senior leadership role, so I appreciate the early discussion about the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: I recall when I joined, it was interesting to me that

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: No DOE student had a device at home, or a DOE device at home.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: All devices that the DOE purchased had to stay in school all the time.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: So when the pandemic hit, we had a problem.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: There were no devices at home that were DOE-oriented, no internet for a lot of our students.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Went through the whole process of unwinding a no-device policy to a full-device policy, as you both summarized.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: In terms of where we are now, the devices are there, the internet is there, the students have learned to use these devices,

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: and I think we have come to a point where it's time to manage this better than has been done in the past.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: So, for YouTube, we heard everyone loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: As of Wednesday night, 5 p.m., we've filtered YouTube out of all student devices.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether filters are strong enough to prevent students from circumventing YouTube blocks. Strickland describes using Google Admin Console for Chromebooks and agents on iPads to block access both at school and at home.
chapters.title: Krishnan presses on filter strength; Strickland describes blocking measures

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: So they shouldn't be able to access it either in a Chromebook or a iPad at school or even at home because the filtering has an agent on the device that notices they're trying to get to that URL and will block it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm very glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So is it your testimony today that no student will be able to access on their own laptop or on a school computer YouTube on their own volition in the school day?

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And the filters in place, have we looked at those?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because students are smart these days.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I've heard stories of them chatting over Google Docs.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: They figured out things in ways that I have not thought of before.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So are we sure the filters are strong enough where they're able to not get around them and game the system, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Yeah, as best we had Google and the Google Chromebook, which is the Google and Alphabet-owned YouTube, is the thing we can most tightly...

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: because there's something called the Google Admin Console.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: And from that, we can easily block things that are on a Google device.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Took a little bit of extra work to do it on an iPad that comes through our filtering, what happens both at the network level and an agent that's actually installed in every device that allows it to happen both at home and at school.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: So I think we've got it covered.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: If we find reports or start hearing about workarounds, we're going to go after that strongly because we agree that this is a good time to stop that.

chapters.summary: Krishnan questions how student data is shared with vendors and third parties, citing Amira as an example that records student voices, and asks about parental consent and disclosure requirements.
chapters.title: Krishnan raises data privacy concerns with ed tech vendors like Amira

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm encouraged, very encouraged to hear that, and I look forward to continuing to work together to monitor that issue as well, and I'm sure we'll hear about it from kids and parents if there are any gaps in the coverage there, but I'm very glad to hear it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The other thing I would just encourage you all to is, as we think about laptops at home, without the guardrails in place, before it was YouTube, now it's going to be other programs.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There is real need to think about the importance of having those guardrails in place, too, around laptop and at-home laptop policy as well.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: We appreciate that, especially since they are city-issued devices.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: We've kind of made them come into the home.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: We need to help our parents and our students manage them effectively.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And then my final question is on a separate topic altogether, but very, very related.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Right now, there are a lot of programs, whether it's some of the gamified apps that we can talk more about that kind of still register.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: those same dopamine hits as we see in social media later, that are a concern, there's a real question of how data is being used by the vendors

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: of these programs, the third parties that they contract with, and how far children's data travels

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: with all of these different programs, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: For example, there's Amira, which you all know is a reading tool online.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now, I strongly believe that, you know, reading with a good old-fashioned book, as we talked about, is important.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But Amira records student voices.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now, I know you all are keeping, you know, recording it but saying it's stored locally, but...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You know, or turning off the AI component.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But what I've heard is that AI is such a central part of Amira, there's no way to turn off the AI component and keep Amira functioning as is.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So with programs like these, one, are parents aware of

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: how far their data is traveling.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In other words, is there any disclosure?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm not aware of them, but is there any disclosure or any consent required, or is it sort of a blanket consent when you go to school?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Their data is being captured, it's being shared.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And two, with programs like Amir and things like that that store this information,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Doesn't that heighten the need for parents to be aware that their children's voices are being recorded or data is being captured?

chapters.summary: Dennis Doyle, DOE Chief Privacy Officer, explains the IRMA data privacy compliance process, data processing agreements with vendors, and that no parental consent is collected because DOE relies on the FERPA school officials exception for sharing student data with third-party contractors.
chapters.title: DOE privacy officer explains data sharing under FERPA school officials exception

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How are we handling the issue of parental consent when it comes to the sharing of data?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I am going to ask Dennis Doyle to come up while I speak.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So, you know, we...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The idea of parental consent and the use of tools and tools that schools have selected for an instructional purpose, we have not had a consent process in place for.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that was a lot of the feedback, too.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: My kid is engaging with generative AI, and I don't want it.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Can I opt out of it?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that was some of the feedback that we took into consideration and even led us to the moratorium of it, especially for our youngest.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: As it relates to the safety guardrails around student privacy and communicating that, I'm going to turn it over to Dennis to share some of our processes.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: Thank you, First Deputy Chancellor, and thank you everyone for the question and for inviting us to be here today.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: My name is Dennis Doyle.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: I'm the Chief Privacy Officer for New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: Obviously, protecting student data privacy is of our utmost priority, particularly from my office.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: And whenever we have any third-party vendor that we use in a way that they're going to be accessing student information, we make sure that they go through a very rigorous data privacy and compliance process.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: We call it IRMA by shorthand.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: But basically what that process means is that those third-party vendors have to enter into a data processing agreement that requires them to keep data confidential, secure, that they only use it for the required purpose, data minimization,

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: And then there's also a data security review that our DIT team conducts, and also a separate review conducted by the New York City Office of Technology and Innovation.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: With respect to consent, there's no consent collected from parents or students in order to share that data with those third-party contractors.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: We rely on a specific exception under FERPA, which is known as the school officials exception, which permits schools to share student data with third-party contractors, provided that we're

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: We have direct control over the use and maintenance of that information, and we do that by having strong contractual agreements in place with all these vendors to make sure that our data is being kept confidential and secure.

chapters.summary: Krishnan expresses shock at the FERPA exception, urges DOE to adopt a consent or notification policy for student data sharing, and argues NYC should hold itself to a higher standard given its advanced screen time and AI policies.
chapters.title: Krishnan urges DOE to adopt affirmative consent policy beyond FERPA exception

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I would just conclude by saying I know that exception under FERPA.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And when I read about it, I was very shocked just because the way in which tech, big tech, data, AI has exploded.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I mean, FERPA, you know, the landscape is changing so fast every single day.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We're reading a conversation right now nationally about AI, the lack of regulation.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I strongly feel that we as New York City must do more to protect our children's, minors'data.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so I'd urge you all to consider a consent policy or notification.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I don't think we should be relying on the exception.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know a lot of school districts across the country rely on that FERPA exception to not get parental consent.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But I want to hold us to a higher standard.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We are passing some of the most advanced policies around screen time and AI in the country.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: This is an area where we shouldn't be sort of backing into consent, but we have to affirmatively, I think, seek consent.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I urge you all to think about that.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks whether DOE's data privacy policies extend to subcontractors of ed tech vendors. Doyle confirms contractual requirements extend to subcontractors, but DOE does not collect those contracts directly. Dinowitz presses on how many audits have been conducted and demands answers during the hearing.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions DOE on subcontractor data privacy and audit records

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'll now turn it over to Chair Dinwitz.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you wait?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you stay?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I just, I figured while you're here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Might as well say, I just want to clarify, since we were talking about data confidentiality, that we have programs like Amira that I believe contract with Claude.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: for their programming, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: I'm not familiar off the top of my head of who Amir contracts with for their subcontractors.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, let's pretend it's Anthropic, or let's pretend any of these companies then contract with another company, let's say like a ChatGPT or a Google.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to confirm your data

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: policy extends to the company like a mirror that you're contracting with does it then extend to the company that they are then contracting with

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: yes absolutely thank you very important question and it's not just a policy it's the actual contractual agreement the data processing agreements that we have with these vendors

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: There's terms in that agreement that require those third-party contracts that we contract with,

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: that they require the same data privacy and security terms that we require of them, that they implement those same strict requirements on any sub-processor that they would use to provide the service.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And you are privy to those contracts?

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: The contracts between the data, our contractor and their sub-processors?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: I mean, we could, as a matter of course, no, we do not collect all of the contracts between our third-party contractors and the sub-processors.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How do you, I mean, how do you verify?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That the student data isn't being misused by the other company that you don't directly contract with.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: We do have continuous monitoring that we conduct of our vendors.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: We have terms in our data processing agreements that permits us to conduct audits, to collect different reports like SOC 2 type 2 reports for vendors to make sure that they're adhering to those standards.

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: And we have ability under our data processing agreement to collect that information at any time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many audits have you conducted in the 26 to 27, 25, 26 school year?

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: I don't have that information offhand.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Have you conducted any audits in the 2025-26 school year regarding data privacy?

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: I would have to go back and look at our records on that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, can we find that out during today's hearing?

utterances.speaker: Dennis Doyle
utterances.text: I don't know if we'll be able to do that today, but I'm sure we could find that information and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please find that out today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's very pertinent to the topic we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I would appreciate that very much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks Laura Lai to share the research supporting the specific 30 and 45-minute limits. Lai says she doesn't have citations on hand but offers to send them, and Dinowitz requests all cited research be posted publicly.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions DOE on research behind 30 and 45-minute screen time limits

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to go back to the research, Lorelai.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You were talking about the research that was done to support the use of 30 minutes or recommended 30 minutes from 3 to 5, 45 minutes, 6 through 8.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you share with the committee what that research was?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: I don't have the research sitting in front of me, Chair, but I'd be happy to send you a list of citations with all of the research that we used.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You put on your Screen Time and AI Policy website two documents, the Brookings Institute and the American Association of Pediatrics, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Those, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Would you also, or will the DOE put all of the research that they cited on that website as well?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We'd be happy to look at doing that, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: A number of those citations, though, the two that you mentioned from Brookings and American Academy of Pediatrics, especially the Brookings, has within that document quite a number of those citations as well.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: So we can take a look at the ones that perhaps are not covered by Brookings, which was a meta review of all of that research and see what we can provide.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, they were much less in favor of screen time than I think the TUE's policy, if I read that document correctly.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz contrasts DOE's process with LA Unified's public process that consulted pediatricians and collected feedback from 19,000 community members, asking what DOE's equivalent process was and who was consulted.
chapters.title: Dinowitz compares DOE's process to LA Unified's public consultation on screen time

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But like the Los Angeles Unified School District screen time limits were developed through a public process.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The Enabling Resolution Incorporated American Academy of Pediatrics finding was consulted on by a pediatrician who co-authored the AAP's policy on children and digital media.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It was analyzed by the district's office of research and program evaluation and drew feedback.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: From nearly 19,000 community members collected before the policy was adopted.

chapters.summary: Giunta describes DOE's internal conversations with pedagogical and computer science teams, feedback from advocates and council members, and plans to use the Technology in Schools Coalition for more formalized stakeholder engagement going forward.
chapters.title: Giunta describes DOE's internal and community feedback process for policy development

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think in your testimony you spoke broadly about the community feedback, but what was the DOE's equivalent process for coming up with these 30 and 45 minute recommendations?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Who specifically was consulted?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We started our conversations internally with our pedagogical teams, with our folks leading our computer science teams, our digital learning teams.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We took feedback as we met with different advocates, inclusive of some of the recommendations from this council when we met with you and certainly Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa's work.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, not in complete alignment, but, you know, that feedback served how we arrived at our minutes.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we will be using our technology and schools coalition in a very strategic way.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So as we get ready to see, like, the impact of this policy and where this policy evolves to for the following year, that will be more of a formalized structure with very localized representation from the state.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz raises concern that tech companies may have been consulted in prior policy iterations and asks DOE to share who was consulted and the specific research used. Giunta says the coalition work is being finalized and will be shared publicly.
chapters.title: Dinowitz presses on who was consulted and whether tech companies were involved

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There was concern, I think, two iterations ago that the people consulted were the tech companies.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Will the DOE share with the committee and the public who they consulted and the

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: specific research that was done to arrive at this policy?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are finalizing our technology and schools coalition work and we will be sharing more with the council and publicly shortly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The Technology in Schools Coalition is that group that will meet monthly?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And at the end of that, there will be a report?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is our intention.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks why vendors are approved without research on specific tools and whether there is third-party verification of product effectiveness. Giunta acknowledges this is an important next step and discusses plans for stronger vendor accountability.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions DOE on vendor efficacy evidence and third-party verification

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And is the intention to then continue that coalition, knowing that AI and screen time is a constantly evolving technology, constantly evolving field?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or is the...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Intention to have a summative one and done report?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think we are very truly and authentically open to see where that process with that coalition leads us in terms of where the policy goes and the continuation of the coalition, the need for it or not, or any shifts.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are entering into that coalition

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: very authentically in partnership.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we want to study how this policy landed.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What did we get right?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What did we get wrong?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Where can we adjust?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And share that publicly.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we hope to do that certainly in partnership with some of our council members serving on the coalition, but also here in these spaces for feedback.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I look forward to that work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Again, you know, as I said in my opening, there's disagreements or a lot of questions, but it's very clear that changes were made and that it demonstrates a responsiveness that I want to commend the DOE for and thank them for.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You testified that you've done the research for the broad 30-minute, 45-minute, but individual vendors are approved without research on specific tools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm just wondering why vendors who put tools in front of our children in a classroom, that even the reports that you cite

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: reference real harms they could cause, why it is not incumbent upon them to provide any evidence or research to back up their claims that it will improve student learning.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And some of the vendors that we partner with provide robust data around student usage, time limits.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They are able to flag too much time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They are able to show growth in their product.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They work with us to kind of cross-reference different data sets sometimes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can I pause you for a sec?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You've just mentioned, in broad terms, very reasonable things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, what is too much?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What does growth look like?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Why is that not a standard for every vendor?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yeah, you're right.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that is the next step for us, that every tool that is in our schools has a very concrete instructional purpose, supports the school's

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: instructional vision, is captured in their comprehensive education plan, is determined in partnership with their school leadership.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: teams, and then centrally as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The products that we're looking to bring into the system, you know, making sure that they're able to deliver on these exact items that you're citing and that we're expecting in this next phase of where we take New York City public schools

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: in any technology use.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Who provides that data?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That their products are effective.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The company that, well, of course, the company is going to tell us their products effective.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'm talking about the evidence, the research.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So, for example, you might, you know, you're looking for a specific thing.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Schools are looking for, do you want to jump in on it?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Or no, you're looking for Randy?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: No, but schools will look, you know, what do I need?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, I don't want to get too drilled into a specific product, but like if it's at the school level or central level, we, you know, we meet with vendors all the time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They have their sales pitch, but our questions back to them are, you know, what is the evidence of impact?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And now we are making sure, even as we are entering into partnerships with anyone, that they are informing us.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, they're part of the data privacy guarantees that Dennis just talked about.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: If they've added anything to their platform that wasn't there when we entered into a partnership, the onus is on the company to make sure that we are aware of any changes, such as adding any kind of...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: AI to the product or taking it out if that's what they did and having more of that up close personal pulse on the product.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks if there is a timeline for holding companies accountable and canceling ineffective contracts. Giunta agrees it's an important next step, and Laura Lai describes the five high school AI pilots as a first step toward independent assessment.
chapters.title: Dinowitz presses on timeline for holding ed tech vendors accountable

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is in addition to data provided by the company itself, of course they're going to say their products are good.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is there third party verification?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right, or any research or even internal research by the DOE that demonstrates the growth, the effectiveness of it, or lack thereof, and that you'll cancel the contract and take away their vendor license.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think that is an important next step for us to be stronger in.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that part of your...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: goal, is there a timeline for actually holding the companies accountable and honestly holding all of us accountable to what we're putting in the classrooms?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Laura, did you want to jump in?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Yeah, I just wanted to uplift the five pilots that we're doing in high school.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: That is exactly the purpose of those pilots.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: It's our first step towards

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: This question that you, that parents, that many advocates have, that is, where's the data?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Show us the data.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And we want to be responsive to that, and we want to better understand not just what the vendor believes these tools are capable of or what their research in Oklahoma shows, but

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: how are these products working in New York City public schools?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: How can we take a first?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: our step towards measuring that ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: That's why we're doing the five pilots in high school.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We have basically three classes of tools that are going to be part of those pilots, very low dose.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: You know, I'm talking about like 15 minutes of interaction with the tool at a time.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Five different kinds of pilots.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Five pilots, three different kinds of tools.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: One's a project-based learning tool.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: One's a tool that teachers use to design customized solutions for their students.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And one is a writing supplement, and one is a math tool that we made sure don't have any gamification properties that allow students to do their own thinking.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And we want to take a look in a structured way at how students use these tools and what impact they have on student learning.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And that's going to be happening over the course of this year, that we implement those pilots to help begin that question of how can we independently assess whether

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: educational technology tools work in our classrooms.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz shares parent and teacher anxiety about AI tools being described as 'vetted' without evidence of efficacy or safety, noting no rubric has been shared, modules haven't been seen, and teachers haven't received professional development on AI implementation.
chapters.title: Dinowitz expresses anxiety about AI pilot vetting and lack of rubric

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I have to share with you the anxiety that so many teachers and parents feel.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Especially after hearing testimony and hearing the description, and I really want you to tell me where I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It would give me no greater joy than to hear where I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In the testimony, it was testified that these AI tools

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: vetted and approved.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: When I hear the word vetted, I think that it is vetted for the quality, for what it brings to my students, not just for IRMA, which you acknowledge needs to be updated, needs to include algorithmic bias.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I hear vetted,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And then I hear that my child or parents'children are actually going to be the test subjects for something that isn't vetted for efficacy and safety.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm hearing you're going to look at things, but we have not seen a rubric for what is actually being looked at, what is actually being investigated.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We haven't seen what these modules, what the educational modules actually look like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the teachers have not received professional development on how to implement AI broadly or these particular tools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So that's a lot of the questions and anxieties that parents are feeling.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just want you to tell me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Which where I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I can go through it as questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Does vetting...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You don't need to.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, no, it's...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, in our last testimony, we talked about the development of a tool selection rubric that is under design.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It's advancing.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have in our procurement and contracting, we have a...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: A way that we're working with our vendors to assess like levels of AI in their programs and making sure that they can be, you know, enter into our schools and stay within this policy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have very limited...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm sorry, not to interrupt, but I want to be like...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right now, you're talking about the policies that are in place, the vendor process that I think, when it comes to a lot of these technologies, is lacking in many cases.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You're talking about the IRMA process, which we know has places lacking, and you're talking about...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: 15 to 45 minute time limits, but it doesn't really speak to what is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It doesn't really speak to what data you're actually looking for and what it means for our children and our family.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just want to highlight that and then please continue.

chapters.summary: Laura Lai explains the pilot selection process: IRMA compliance, existing tool use in high schools, no gamification properties, no cognitive offloading, three categories of tools, application process for schools, and a target launch around November with a framework to be shared publicly.
chapters.title: Laura Lai details high school AI pilot selection criteria and rollout timeline

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Do you want to jump?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We hear you, and I'm going to ask one of our colleagues to come up and talk about the modules if you want some elucidation on that.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: But I'll just talk about, I think we hear you on the frustration.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And we are working very hard right now on putting together the framework for those pilots that we are going to be more than happy to share.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: The timeline right now, hopefully, to have something like that is over the next month.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And we're looking to be able to share that with you.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And have that ready to go soon.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Have you chosen the pilot schools yet?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, have the modules been rolled out?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, will the rubric and will exactly what you're looking for in this technology be rolled out before you start putting AI or more screens in front of our students?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Can we talk a little bit about the process for the criteria that was used around the five pilots so that you can kind of, that might help answer the question in case you would like to take us through?

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Yeah, so,

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We looked at many of the tools that are being used in

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: in high schools.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And again, I want to make it clear that broad-based use of artificial intelligence, student-facing generative artificial intelligence in high schools will no longer be allowed.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: There are only three ways in which a New York City public school's high school student

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: could possibly engage with student-facing generative AI going forward.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: One is for the AI literacy modules, which you referenced.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: One is for the pilots, and the last one are for technology-based career readiness programs like CTE or other professional certification programs,

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: some of which may have a requirement for a student to use a tool with AI to receive that certification.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Those are the only three.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Sanctioned ways in which high school students going forward can engage with generative AI in classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: With regard to the pilots, we went through a selection process to really identify the tools that would be involved in the pilots.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: First, we wanted to make sure the tools were IRMA compliant.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Second, we looked at tool use across our high schools.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We wanted to engage with tools that at least several high schools had already used so that we would know that we had

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: A base of high schools that would be interested in doing a pilot.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Third, we looked at the tools to make sure that they did not have game-based properties, so we did not want any tools that had those features to them.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We also only wanted tools that allowed students to retain ownership of their thinking and work, so no cognitive offloading, no giving students answers to questions,

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: only tools that at most would prompt students to do more, to write more, to think more.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: As I mentioned, there were three sort of buckets of tools we were looking for.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: A tool that supported student writing, a tool that supported math, tools that helped teachers design customized solutions for

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: different learners in their classrooms, and the last was a project-based learning tool.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We used all of these criteria to identify the five AI tools that we're going to be piloting.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We're going to be rolling out shortly an application every high school.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: I mentioned that a number of these tools are already in use in high schools, but we're going to offer the opportunity to be involved in a pilot to any high school.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We're going to...

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: look at, make sure we have good representation in terms of

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: geography and demographics, that we also have a commitment from these schools to do the work that's going to be involved in a pilot.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: This is not going to be just like signing up for your subscription and turning it on.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: This is going to be

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Number one, partnering with us on data collection.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Number two, we didn't get into the specifics on this, but every high school student

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: who is actually involved in using AI at school is going to be required to take a long-form AI literacy class.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: So every high school student is going to be required to take the short-form AI literacy class that we can go into a little bit more detail about.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: But every high school that does a pilot is going to have to offer their students this 12- to 15-hour AI literacy course.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And then there's going to be some professional development involved as well for their teachers.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: So this is a real commitment that schools are going to have to make to be involved in the pilot program.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And again, I just want to make it clear we're working on the high school application that we hope to roll out soon.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: We're going to take some time to evaluate those applications to make sure that the schools have that commitment and that they meet the needs of the overall pilot.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: process and then we're hopefully going to be able to launch those pilots sometime in the November-ish timeframe.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: That's the goal that we have right now.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: And as I said before, as soon as we get that framework for the pilot up and going, we're committed to sharing that.

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Both with you and with the public to make sure that everyone understands the metrics that we're going to be using.

chapters.summary: Krishnan expects the rubric and metrics to be public before pilots launch and asks if AI companies are paying DOE for the pilots. Dinowitz asks if pilot schools and modules have been chosen yet—DOE confirms they have not.
chapters.title: Krishnan and Dinowitz press on rubric transparency and pilot data collection

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Yes, I would expect that rubric, those metrics, just like we give rubrics to our students, so they know what to expect.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I would expect those rubrics and evaluative tools to come out before you launch the pilot.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And for all the data you collect to be public, I would also hope these AI tools, given that they are collecting, would be collecting an immense amount of data and research from our children, that at least you get it for free.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I would sure hope you're, you know, they're paying you to put this in our classrooms.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks what equivalent document justifies technology use for multilingual learners compared to IEPs for students with disabilities, and how DOE ensures screens don't disadvantage ELLs. Kyle McDonald explains federal and state policy grounding for ELL technology access.
chapters.title: Krishnan questions DOE on screen time exceptions for students with disabilities and ELLs

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I have one other question going back to screens, and then I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Shulman and other members for member questions.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In the policy, in the screen time policy, it states the exceptions, one of those exceptions is for students with disabilities and English language learners or multi-language learners, and they're sort of in the same category.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Students with disabilities have an IEP, an Individualized Education Plan, where it may specify a specific adaptive device.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What is the equivalent document or tool that is used to justify using technology for L's and multilingual learners?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I will ask Suzanne Sanchez from the Division of Inclusive and Accessible Learning to join us, and also Kyle, who oversees our Office of Multilingual Learners.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This exception is...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Both steeped in law, a child's IEP, but also deeply around access and removing potential barriers.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so as it relates to our multilingual learners, ensuring where there's an opportunity to give them access that they have it.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So Kyle, can you share a couple of those examples?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And Suzanne, thanks for joining.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Can I have your counsel?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because of timing, okay?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I just want to make sure you know what I'm not asking.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm not asking what are some great tools that we can give to L's.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm asking compare the justification for students with disabilities that it's written in a legal document compared to L's where...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Where if you could explain what the equivalent document would be, how it's researched and justified,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and how it wouldn't turn into just, well, let's just give RLs translation tools and screens and put them more at a disadvantage by some of the detrimental effects of screen time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Chair and Committee.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: I'm Kyle McDonald, Executive Director of Policy and Data for the Office of Multilingual Learners within the New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: And I appreciate the advocacy on behalf of our multilingual students and our English language learners.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: The general grounding of policy is in both federal and state policy that English language learners must be provided equitable access to content that is appropriate in grade level.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: And that includes language scaffolds.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: There are technology tools that enable our English language learners then to access content regardless of their home language background.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: It also helps us have those students be more integrated within their classrooms so they can participate meaningfully and then provide appropriate home language scaffolds when possible.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: And so it's the grounding within our state and federal policies that ensure that we want to uphold those same rights for all English language learners.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether DOE has considered what screen use looks like for ELLs beyond just allowing it, and whether ENL teachers receive specific professional development on technology use. McDonald describes curricular scaffolds and PD within NYC READS curriculum.
chapters.title: Krishnan presses on ELL technology use policy and teacher professional development

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay, well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There is a fear and a concern, and I think it's rooted in reality, the reality we see around screens where it's the solution to a problem rather than a tool to enhance learning.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And in your policy, have you considered not just that we're allowed to give screens to multilingual learners, but what that looks like?

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: So again, grounded in the rest of the policy around that we do not have any unstructured, unfeathered, unsupervised time with our students using the devices.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: And so that same requirement that when English language learners are using instructional technology devices, that it's something that is directly tied, it is intentionally connected to the content that the student would be learning,

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: and then is equitable to the grade level that the students will be participating in.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And lastly, as part of your policy, are ENL teachers being specifically provided with professional development related to technology use for English language learners?

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: As a part of the New York City READS curriculum, we're working on a variety of curricular bases.

utterances.speaker: Kyle McDonald
utterances.text: And some of these include scaffolds for English language learners as well as some home language curriculum that do have some technological elements that teachers are receiving professional development in if they're participating in those curricula.

chapters.summary: Council Member Schulman asks when DOE will issue a clear list of exemptions, reports parents seeing no change in device use due to policy caveats, and raises concerns about 3K children being shown movies on teacher cell phones during nap time.
chapters.title: Council Member Schulman questions DOE on screen time exemptions and 3K device use

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay, we'll talk more about that probably at a later date, but I want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I want to turn it over to Councilmember Shulman and to start our member questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Dinowitz and Krishna, and appreciate this really important hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: First, I want to acknowledge I have a constituent here, Kate Mulvaney, who represents a number of parents in my district, and I want to thank her for being here for her advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I have a couple of questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: One, parents are reporting that their schools have not changed any device use because of the many caveats in the new AI and screen time rules.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When is the DOE going to issue a clear list of what is and is not exempt from the screen time regulations, and how is the DOE vetting this list?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, today's day four of schools, and our, you know, so we know that the policy dropped, you know, right before our schools came back, and we saw immediately our superintendents, their teams, and our principals jump into action.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: There are ways that they're leading.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: With what they know, they're leading through what they're waiting for.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so we've been keeping a pulse on some of those.
