utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We know there are some like, can you tell me specifically, can I use this or not?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are working through some of that for them.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We're working with our vendors to also confirm if there is generative AI or not in the product.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And if not, then it would just be subject

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: to the screen time limits rather than the moratorium.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so we are pulling through all of that and getting those

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: answers out into the field as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so we're working through that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In the meantime, I've met with a teacher, a principal, a superintendent, and even in their, I'm not sure, so how are you leading through this?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: How are you teaching through this?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Well, where I'm not sure, I'm just not using it right now.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And they have been talking and sharing stories about going back, you know, with their full arms around the print-based materials to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Parents with children in 3K have reported that their children have been given teacher cell phones and are being shown movies to occupy them during nap time when they are not napping.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What is the DOE doing to ensure 3K programs are providing appropriate activities for children?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In the first four days of school?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Well, these are what parents intend.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So that's important feedback.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is not the vision for time that we would want, especially our littlest, to be spending during precious school time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so if, you know, that would be a great opportunity to provide clarity on the early childhood guidance, which has always been in place.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Early childhood has had a restriction on device use before our policy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our policy mostly complements it and doubles down on their own policy within the Division of Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So that's an important story, and we'll work with the Division of Early Childhood and our schools to make sure.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: that that is not happening.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how many assessments DOE requires annually, whether schools must use screen-based assessments or if paper options exist, and whether parents can opt out of screen-based assessments. Giunta explains the assessment structure and says there is no opt-out option.
chapters.title: Schulman questions DOE on assessment requirements and paper alternatives

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How many assessments are required by DOE each year?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So in the New York City public schools, outside of the New York State assessments, we ask our schools to administer a screener assessment three times a year.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Pretty much, I would say,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: October, January, May, so, you know, beginning, middle, end of the year.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our schools have opted into, and typically by district, they're using one of two academic screeners in both ELA and math.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: There is a...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: A citywide screener for literacy in K-2 that all schools are using.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that is what we are looking at centrally.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And then schools take the curricular choices that they have and they decide which assessments that are within the curricular programs or otherwise that they find valuable.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And at the school level, that could look different.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But at the central level, those are our assessments.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are schools required to use screen-based assessments or are paper options available?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: For the screeners, our screeners are online and they are part of the exemption in our policy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have some of our core curriculum that has digital assessments.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are asked.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: asking our schools to transition away from digital assessments to the paper versions of these tests.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But some of the current, like the end of a module assessment, might be digital only right now.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so that is part of that grace that we're giving in the implementation of this policy and where we might need to make adjustments going forward.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do parents, caregivers have the right to opt out of screen-based assessments?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we do not have an opt-out policy for what our valued assessments and core curriculum choices are in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is the core part of the instructional program.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So at this time, there is no option to opt out of those tests, those assessments.

chapters.summary: Council Member Morano picks up on Schulman's line of questioning, asking if an hour of digital assessments doesn't count toward screen time limits and why all screen time isn't counted the same given children's eyes and brains don't distinguish.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano questions DOE on assessment screen time exemptions

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chairs, and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thanks so much, Councilman McShulman.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I think that last question is a very important one, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think, you know, there's a standardized test, but there's also the everyday assessments, math and everything else that are happening digitally.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I do think it's worth the O.E.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Considering other ways to opt out of that to take these assessments.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I want to recognize that Councilmember Maloney is here.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And now we're going to turn it over to Councilmember Morano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: First of all, I'm aware of the irony of me reading questions off of a laptop that I just typed.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I think it goes to show there's an appropriate place for technology.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You're a lost cause.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Clearly.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I want to give the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: credit for recognizing that technology should be used sparingly and shouldn't crowd out teachers' books, hands-on learning, and interaction with other kids.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to focus, I want to pick up where my colleague, Councilmember Schulman, left off, the one exception in your policy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You say that digital assessments and diagnostics don't count towards screen time limits.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So if an elementary school student has 30 minutes of instructional screen time and then spends another hour taking digital assessments, that additional hour doesn't count as screen time under the current policy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But we would also ask our schools to be very mindful that if this is your day that you're administering a screener, that on this day you are also balancing that out by minimizing or not using at all

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: screen time that would otherwise be part of the curricular day.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But here's what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The child's eyes and brains don't know DOE has classified that hour as an assessment.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If we're concerned about the effects of screen exposure on children, why wouldn't all screen time count as screen time?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We just, it is part, that is a great question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And I think for us, our current ability to keep a pulse on our students are our screener assessments.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They are digital.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that is why we were asking our schools that on these days, in order to get this data to understand how kids are performing, what interventions or accelerations they might need, that we are able to maintain those screeners.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And if we need to continue to revisit as we look at this policy over the next year, the kinds of screeners that we have and where that...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Plays in digital, we will make those adjustments.

chapters.summary: Morano asks if DOE would support a paper and pencil testing option as UFT has called for, and asks whether DOE believes the COVID emergency response became too much of a permanent educational model. Giunta agrees the moment requires reevaluation.
chapters.title: Morano asks about UFT's paper testing proposal and DOE's COVID screen time hindsight

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But for this year, that's where it lives.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And again, we want to empower our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want to ask our schools, too, to just be mindful that there is that balance, that today is not the day.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Even in my testimony when I shared, if we're going to the computer lab today,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: that it's outside of the instructional day, but it does become part of the student's experience that day, and we want to truly limit technology.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know the UFT is calling for a paper and pencil testing option for every student.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Would DOE support giving students and parents that option?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We will continue to work with our labor partners on some options that might be available to us going forward.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I also want to ask you to look backwards for a moment.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, they say hindsight's 20-20.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to use the prism of hindsight.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your own testimony says routine individual screen use can crowd out hands-on learning, social interaction.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: action, play, and teacher-guided instructions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Those things were true three years ago, too.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So looking back, without blaming anybody, does DOE believe we allowed an emergency response to COVID to become too much of a permanent...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Educational model?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think this current administration, from our mayor to our chancellor to myself to this council, I think we would agree to that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And I think that was very beautifully said in Councilmember Krishnan's testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We thought we were sending our kids back and the laptops were going to close.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And I do think that the moment that we're in, in this national conversation, emerging research, the feedback we're getting from

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: community stakeholders has allowed us to say it is...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We do need to look at this.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We do need to look at this.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We need to slow it down.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We need to study it better.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that is why we're in a one-year, this is a seismic shift, to your point, for our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are so entangled in so much of the digital use in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we wanted to offer a very developmental, research-based, and like what does year one of this look like that our schools can continue to thrive in?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so I would agree with you, and I think that is why we're exactly at this policy.

chapters.summary: Morano asks what parents should do when homework is on Chromebooks and whether DOE would consider giving parents the right to request paper alternatives. Giunta says the policy doesn't address homework but teachers can support paper options.
chapters.title: Morano questions DOE on homework screen time and paper alternatives for parents

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Finally, your screen time limits don't apply to out-of-school learning.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What's a parent who's trying to limit screens at home supposed to do when their fourth grader comes home and says, my homework is on the Chromebook?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Would DOE consider giving parents a right to request a reasonable paper alternative when the assignment doesn't inherently require a computer?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes, so our policy doesn't speak to homework.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We know some of our teachers will maybe post homework in the Google Classroom.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are happy to continue our teachers, you know, supporting paper, pencil, homework options.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We also know that at home in their devices, we need to get our kids ready for remote learning days, which while we have one planned for Election Day this year,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: often our remote, our pivot to remote days are under some kind of weather or other emergency, God forbid.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so we do need our kids ready to do that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we also know that outside of school, we also have our after-school programs as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so we partnered with, I had a great meeting with our DYCD commissioner to share our policies, to make sure that during the school day, our partners during the instructional day were aware of our policy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so that they could be inspired to think thoughtfully about how they are using technology in after school as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Restler asks how DOE tracks students' screen time at home and how much homework is assigned on computers. Giunta clarifies the policy doesn't cover out-of-school time or homework limits.
chapters.title: Council Member Restler questions DOE on tracking home screen time and homework

utterances.speaker: Laura Lai
utterances.text: Councilman LeBlanc?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm reading over here that you have this limit on screen time, the maximum of screen time for grades three to five will be limited to a recommended 30 minutes,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: and the screen time, and then grade six to eight recommendation is no more than 45 minutes per day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My question is how do you track

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: students screen time when they get home.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Like, because people, yes, you have Chromebooks as issued by schools, but students may use their own computers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So how do you track that?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our policy does not speak to out of school time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is either my answer.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Can I ask you to elaborate on your question?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah, so...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So, for example?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For example, if they do the homework, you know,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So extending on the Chromebooks.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we're asking kids to do.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So how are we monitoring how much time our teachers are giving for homework on computers?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay, yes, that will be.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: All right, that is a great example.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have not put a limit on homework at this time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is something we are going to be listening in the field for.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But what I would say to you is that our system now knows that our policies are very, you know, very strictly enforced during our instruction.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: time with children, we don't want to then say, therefore, you could have four hours of homework.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are not looking to go to any kinds of extremes.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We're just trying to find that balance, but we did not roll up homework into this policy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Did you want to jump in or?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I don't know if there's any other.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That's probably enough.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Restler asks how DOE tracks screen time for kids who don't have Chromebooks at home and how parents can restrict screen time. Giunta and Randy Asher describe device distribution, LTE connectivity, and parent resources for managing screen time.
chapters.title: Restler asks about Chromebook access and tracking for students without devices

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My follow-up question is that what about kids that don't have Chromebooks?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How do you track their screen time?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Like to bring home, like I know kids who bring Chromebooks home.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And my question is how do you track screen time for kids who do not have their own Chromebooks?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we have made available that all of our children have access to devices, especially for our remote instruction days.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Some schools have one-to-one devices available in school and a second set for home.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Other schools, children are traveling back and forth with their Chromebook.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But if a child doesn't have a Chromebook and would need it for instruction, our schools will work with that child and family to make sure that they have a device at home.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But if that is not a belief of a school, because some of our schools are not, they're only using that for a remote day.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They are not using laptops outside of the school day.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So then a child wouldn't be expected to use it for homework or count as minutes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My follow-up question is, how would parents effectively restrict the screen time for kids at home?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Because I myself know I can configure a router and say, oh, turn on the internet only from 7 to 9, but what do you have a general advice to parents how to restrict screen time for the kids once they get home?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I believe that if at home you have a screen limit for your child and you as parent want to take that device away, I know that that is not going to be easy as Council Member Krishnan shared.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But in the home, we would rely on your amazing parenting to decide if the device needs to be pulled away from the child or not.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And if you feel at the school level the homework is requiring more device use than you want to personally allow in the house, that is a wonderful conversation for you to have with the school.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah, and I also want to, to the ordinary parent, they do not know how to configure their routers or their devices, so the internet gets turned off.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But it seemed to me this is clearly a necessity, because when parents see kids using the computers at home, oh, they're doing their homework.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or they tell the parents that, oh, I'm doing my homework.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They're not.

chapters.summary: Restler notes ordinary parents don't know how to configure routers and asks what general advice DOE provides. Asher describes digital literacy outreach through parent coordinators, Common Sense Media partnerships, and resources on parental controls and appropriate use.
chapters.title: Restler presses on parent resources for restricting home screen time

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So I'm understanding your question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: How are we supporting parents?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What are the tools and strategies that we're giving them?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have some wonderful resources available.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have Randy Asher with us that oversees our digital literacy curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We've made that public for families as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And I know, even as a former superintendent, some of the work that we led at the district level around, you know,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: supporting families at home with using technology, screen limits.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We used to have, I'm not sure if they're still doing it, I think they are, a wonderful screening of a movie called Screenagers

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: and a panel discussion after that that allowed the community to have a conversation around what are the decisions we want to make, what are the impacts of this on our children, what are the decisions we want to make as a family.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so I saw

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think those are important tools and strategies and information that our families get.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Randy, would you like to talk about any of our public-facing resources available to families as well?

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member Wong, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: My name is Randy Asher.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Chief Information Officer for Educational Technology.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: We partner on our digital literacy outreach with parent coordinators, with school leaders, and with parents.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: We provide a curriculum set of options available.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: Two lessons are mandated each year for all students.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: Around the use of digital tools.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: And we also inform parents through our partnership with different companies like Common Sense Media and several others about how they can help govern and work with their children at home on the use of digital technology and appropriate use

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: of technology.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: So some of this is about helping to educate our parents.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: We don't expect parents to reconfigure routers or other technical solutions, but it's about how to have conversations about appropriate use, what are reasonable screen time limitations.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: Screen time is not only a laptop or a Chromebook, but we also have students that when they get home are on gaming devices, they're watching television.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: There's lots of different types of screens that kids utilize, and it's about finding appropriate tasks and hobbies and interests that will engage the students where not everything is in a digital format.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: So we provide a lot of instruction around that and resources to help parents know how to control some of the applications, know how to install parental.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: controls on some of these devices because sometimes the device use is not necessarily the only concern, but it's about what they're doing on the device.

utterances.speaker: Randy Asher
utterances.text: So we work with parents to be able to do that and we turn key it through our parent coordinators and other groups to help get that out into the community.

chapters.summary: Council Member Narcisse, drawing on her healthcare background, asks what health department or school health services contributed to setting the 30-45 minute limits and whether they were based on clinical evidence. Giunta references the research Laura Lai shared.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse questions DOE on health evidence for screen time limits

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Cheers.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now, Council Member Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, cheers, both of you, and thank you, Madam Deputy, and say thank you to the Chancellor for meeting us and helping us the best way that we can help our community.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I know the conversation will continue with all your leaderships.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I have spent my time, my career in healthcare.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And how, and I know what hours of screen time can do to our children's eyes, sleeping pattern,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: ability to focus, and we can say how engage with one another and critical thinking and analysis, I can go on and on.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Setting daily limits was the right thing to do, the right call.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But a limit, only limit, only to mean something if someone is actually counting.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: the minutes and the families can see the result.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So what did the health department or school health services contribute to setting the time from 30 to 45 minutes as the numbers?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we're

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: those based on clinical evidence, because we know everything is evidence finding.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Well, for your specific question, that would speak back to the research that Lorelei was sharing.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We reviewed as we arrived at our 0, 30, and 45-minute screen limits.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks who is responsible for ensuring schools stay under the limits and what happens if they don't. Giunta reiterates the limits are non-negotiable despite being called recommendations, and describes feedback loops with superintendents and school visits.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks who enforces recommended screen time limits and what happens if schools don't comply

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The caps for grade three through eight.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are described as recommended.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Who is responsible for making sure a school stays under them?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And what happens if a school does not?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This is back to the conversation earlier around the use of the word recommended versus mandate.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want to make sure that

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, I know words matter, so we can argue that mandate would have mattered as much as recommended.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We also know that sometimes mandate leads to a punitive result.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We did not want to make this.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: first year of this massive shift in our system, feel punitive or anyone to feel under pressure.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want to really support our schools in scaling down and paring back how much screen time they're using and how much access to AI, generative AI, that they're using in their schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, as the first deputy chancellor, underneath me again are our superintendents and all of our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We're working in lockstep.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have incredible feedback loops.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Some of them are formal, where we get on calls with our superintendents to check the pulse.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think you know the chancellor and I love to be in schools, and so do our superintendents.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we'll be using our school visits to gauge how this is going and course correcting, you know, in...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In ways that might be necessary if we come across something.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We learned so much through the cell phone policy that we have implementation of that because these were some of the questions that came up as we launched the cell phone policy as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And our schools blew it out of the park with their ability to implement this cell phone policy with fidelity.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And when issues came up, you know, we followed, like, for our students who were really insisting they needed their phone, access to the phone, or finding those great workarounds that are brilliant.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: children know how to do, that we're using a more progressive discipline approach than going straight to.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we want to take the same concept as we implement this this year.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: If for some reason we get word of a school, we'll support them through stronger implementation.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And if we get to the point where we really are like, okay, we've done recommended enough, let's like we need to double down on the word mandate going forward, like that is a place that we are willing to evolve and grow.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And again, it was so much community feedback that led us to this policy, and we are not done listening to the community.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks if policy information is available in different languages and whether DOE will sign the Microsoft agreement that AFT and UFT have. Giunta confirms the website translates into many languages and says she needs to speak with VP Vaccaro about the agreement.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about multilingual policy materials and Microsoft agreement

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm so appreciative.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's structure and guardrails we have to put for our children.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I heard about the guidance, I mean, how we're distributing the information and all.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It is available in different languages, the information that we're giving?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our policy?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our policy is on our school website, and our website translates into many languages.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Confirm for me our number.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I have one.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Do you want to know how many languages, or you're good?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The languages, as long as you have it in all languages, especially in the different schools that are located from Spanish, Haitian, Creoles, and all.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are you going to sign on the Microsoft agreement that AFT and UFT have?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you hear that?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Oh, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I do need to speak with Vice President Vaccaro about that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We haven't had a chance to connect on it.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Does that come up for us?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because we talk about safeguards and God well and structure.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks if DOE has provided schools with a list of which approved programs contain AI components, noting teachers can't comply with the moratorium if they can't identify AI tools. Scott Strickland describes ongoing work to research and list AI-containing products.
chapters.title: Narcisse questions DOE on teachers' ability to identify AI-containing software

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: There's one question that I need to ask you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Committee staff have heard that teachers cannot readily identify which one of the software programs they use contain AI components.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Has DOE provided schools with a list of which approved programs included in the AI features?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And if not, how are the teachers expected to comply with the moratorium?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are working to make this a more easily accessible answer for our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Strickland, you can take it away.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: We have a list of hundreds of software products that have been used in our schools in the recent past.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Each one of them we're researching whether it says or we know that it has an AI component to it, and we'll be working with those vendors.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: To see if that AI component can be turned off, especially if it's student-facing generative AI.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: In the meantime, we're going to provide a list to the school saying, right now, it looks like this product is in this state, and therefore it's either good or it's not.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilor.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: First, I have to mention I got good news.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: VP Vaccaro is here.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So you all stick around.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Stick around after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Before I go to...

chapters.summary: Krishnan notes UFT VP Vaccaro is present, asks DOE if they have the number of data privacy audits conducted, and notes that for a $40 billion budget they should be able to find that number.
chapters.title: Krishnan notes VP Vaccaro's arrival and asks about audit numbers

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney, quick update.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Do we have those audits?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The number of audits?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: For almost $40 billion, I feel like you could find the number of audits you've done.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Just me?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Council Member Maloney asks how DOE is rethinking in-person instruction vs. at-home assignments to mitigate AI risks, and asks about the digital divide and how many students depend on schools for device access.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney questions DOE on homework, AI tools, and digital divide

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'm glad to see that the report, that was quick.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: All right, thank you for your questions.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: That you recognize how tech and AI can be used to enhance education, but it really cannot be used to replace any human interaction.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And that these tools are changing how students are learning, including testing and homework when you're tempted to turn to chatty instead of going through the mental efforts to get to the answer yourself.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So to the homework question, how are you rethinking in-person instruction and testing versus at-home assignments to mitigate some of the risks that come with these tools that students are going to have access to?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: At home?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think what this moment is offering us now is exactly that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What does homework look like when our students leave?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: How are we asking them to demonstrate their thinking so that we know this is their work?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What are ways that we can have them

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: show their work as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So it's, you know, we can really get into how they're processing.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: and understanding content.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I don't have a clear pulse on how much digital homework versus paper pen homework takes place.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our policy does not speak to homework per se, but this is an important place for us to dig into.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Even written homework, you can still have those digital tools.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The second thing I wanted to dig into is the digital divide issue.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How many of these students are dependent on their schools for getting access to these devices, or do they have access on their own?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Scott, can you talk?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Just to say this is, it is a valuable tool in some cases, and how often are parents or students relying on

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: public schools for that access.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes, so I'm going to bring in Scott to just talk a little bit about our device distribution and what is available to our students.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Sure, as I mentioned early on, at the pandemic, we got a device to every student, took us six months, and that policy has continued through several other administrations.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Rule is a school should provide a personal device, DUE laptop, Chromebook, iPad, to every student in the school.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Off and on, there's been access to LTE services, internet services connected to that device.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: So if the home base doesn't have

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: Broadband internet, they still have a connectivity.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: And recently that was ended, but each school can purchase LTE connectivity for individual students that need it.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: And some schools have taken advantage of that.

utterances.speaker: Scott Strickland
utterances.text: So as of right now, every student should have a device that's been issued to them and has a way to get over the divide through either their home-based internet or getting it through the school.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So DOE is very involved in ensuring no student is left behind.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how DOE evaluates exceptions for assistive technology, AI literacy, and workforce development, and how DOE will have the capacity to continuously evaluate the evolving ecosystem. Suzanne Sanchez and Tanisha Mitchell describe assistive technology vetting and AI literacy modules.
chapters.title: Maloney questions DOE on exceptions for useful technology and evaluation capacity

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The second question I want to ask is about exceptions for useful technology.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So I come to this conversation as a former product manager with full visibility in tech of the things that can go wrong and also

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: benefits that come with technology like assistive technology, one of the exceptions you called out, multilingual learners, making sure our students don't fall behind with SAT prep and testing,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: AI literacy, because we all know our students are going to encounter tech in the wild, and then workforce development like coding, robotics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So how is DOE evaluating these exceptions, and whether it's a use case where technology is appropriate or a specific software that you want to approve, and how are you going to staff this exceptions list?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Can you just, the last part, how are we going to...

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Have the capacity.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Have the capacity.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned this is a seismic shift in how people learn.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The use cases and tools that are being created are numerous.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One is what's the criteria to determine what is appropriate for students?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then two, how will you have the capacity to continuously evaluate this ever-evolving ecosystem?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: All right, I will have Suzanne, who jumped up from Dial, talk a little bit about that for our students with disabilities and multilingual learners, which live under the Division of Inclusive and Accessible Learning.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Laura Lai shared a little bit of, or actually a very comprehensive outline of how the five pilots came in.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we also are joined today by Tanisha Mitchell, who has helped design and pilot some of the AI literacy modules that our schools will be going.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And to your point about monitoring, before I turn it over for a little bit more nuance in those conversations,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: is we're really going to be relying on our technology and schools coalition to help us with that and with subcommittees that are studying different aspects of this policy as it implements across the year.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But Suzanne, you look like you are ready to say something.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: Suzanne Sanchez, Chief of Special Education for New York City Public Schools, and I want to

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: Just acknowledge and thank you and the council for your thought for our students with disabilities throughout this entire process.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: And in terms of efficacy of device and support and how do we know this tool works for this student, when it comes to students with disabilities, the

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: exceptions that are in place for them are student-specific and specific to a specific device or tool.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: We employ a team of experts.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: It's our Center for Assistive Technology.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: And this group of, they are experts in assistive technology.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: They vet and try and test any tool that is before it is recommended on a student's IEP.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: And so they are trying it out, making sure that it's going, if it's a speech-to-text tool, if it's a word vocabulary tool, if it's an eye gaze that's giving a child full access who doesn't have mobility,

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: they are testing these tools in-house before we recommend them on a student's IEP.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: And also checking in throughout the school year.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: How is the device or the program supporting that student's access to learning?

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: What are the outcomes we're seeing?

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: And it is an iterative and fluid process for which we make adaptations and changes to along the way.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: And one thing I would also call out is that we also drive some assistive technology innovation by this process by saying to certain vendors, hey, we see our students need X, your product is providing Y.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: Let's look at how you can shift and change that so that our students are getting the actual assistive technology supports that they need, and that is following that review process.

utterances.speaker: Suzanne Sanchez
utterances.text: And so that's how we navigate, monitor, track, and revise for students with disabilities around anything related to assistive technology.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: It would be helpful if I turned this on when I did.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: My name is Tanisha Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: I am the Executive Director of Computer Science Education for New York City Public Schools, and I am grateful to be here with you all today.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: Council member, you had asked some questions in terms of how we are understanding and assessing what is happening with our students.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: I can speak more towards the AI literacy that is part of the exceptions that we have listed as part of our AI guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: So as you all know, this is a new effort

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: to ensure that broadly across New York City public schools, there is guidance and understanding what AI literacy is in a way that we can norm upon across New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: As part of the AI guidelines, we have developed a two 45 minutes

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: offering for high school students to ensure that high school students have a broad understanding and a foundation of what

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: AI literacy is.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: So what is AI?

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: What is it not?

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: Understanding data privacy and appropriate uses when it comes to school.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: That is meant to support students in getting a strong foundation.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: We are planning to pilot it later this year.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: And so for us, the way we are going to track that is having a mixture of formative assessments, as Chair Dinnowitz has shared earlier.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: There will be a range of surveys to understand what is happening when it comes to that learning progression.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: And also,

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: this will be administered through Central itself.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: And so we are taking a deeper stance in understanding what is coming in front of our students.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: I will also share, along with AI Literacy, Laura Lai has given some information about this earlier.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: There will be a 12 to 15 hour AI Literacy course that will be offered to students who are within a career readiness pathway.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: So what that means is if they are in a CTE school, a career technical education school, or if they are participating in pathways when it comes to work-based learning and thinking about future radio at NYC,

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: any student that will be participating in one of those career readiness pathways or will be participating in one of the approved pilots that Laura Lai discussed earlier will also go under

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: AI literacy course.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: This will be monitored through Central as well to support an understanding of students and what they are learning.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: And we will also provide those reportings across for their schools.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how DOE monitors whether apps and programs remain useful over time, whether DOE consults with teachers, and how it measures when programs need to be phased out. Giunta says gamified apps with AI fall under the moratorium and describes the purchasing review process.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about ongoing monitoring of ed tech program usefulness

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Chair?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I had a few questions left.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then I'm good to go.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Sorry, one minute.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So one of the questions to start out with was, you know, we talked a lot about gamified apps and, you know, data protections and the utility of these educational programs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So how is DOE on an ongoing basis monitoring the usefulness of these programs?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Are you consulting with teachers?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And are you looking at student performance and progress?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What way are you measuring that apps and programs that may have once been useful are not useful anymore and need to be phased out?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, a lot of our gamified apps, by the nature of including AI in them, are now part of our moratorium.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are looking, even we are looking closer at all of the software that is in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And as part of the purchasing process, we have a team

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: at Central that is reviewing the requests to make sure that any software that's brought into our schools is at a minimum in alignment with our policy.

chapters.summary: Maloney summarizes key concerns: mandates vs. recommendations, laptops coming home for K-5, homework on computers, opt-out policies for online testing, and affirmative consent for data sharing, urging bolder action to address problems outpacing current solutions.
chapters.title: Maloney summarizes concerns about mandates, home device policies, testing, and consent

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I will, I'll end my questions here.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I just wanted to, you know, there are a few points that I think, you know, we should continue a conversation around and work together closely, right?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One, I think, is the point that we mentioned, which is the point that we mentioned, which is

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: is even with the, one, mandates versus recommendations, and I think with those things, even as recommendations, there are a lot, I think what we're seeing today, the theme of the hearing is there are a lot of

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: areas, loopholes or workarounds or other things that are unaddressed that we need more specific solutions around, right?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If you think about when laptops come home,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What are the restrictions there?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I mean, frankly, I don't think they should be coming home for K-5, but, you know, what is DOE doing to restrict and monitor?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Because I think putting the burden entirely on parents is too difficult of a burden for them, and frankly not fair to parents to have to figure out how to monitor yet another device at home and what kind of access you have there.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So I think there is a real question of what comes home, when, how often, is there storage for laptops in the classroom to the extent that students are using them from 3 to 5.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: On top of that, you know, there's...

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Really a question of when is it required to do homework, really required to do homework on the computer, and when it's not.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Are there policies in place for parents to opt out of online testing?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I know there's a larger issue, and NICE has been big on this, about

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: the standardized tests, but even the assessments going forward, can parents opt out of that to take pencil and paper tests, which I think are so important too.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And, you know, I think those are, I think cover the main areas.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Oh, then the last one, I think, was around consent when it comes to data sharing.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I think we've got to really revisit and look at, as the landscape changes both legally, as the problems with AI and digital tech explodes,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: rather than relying on that exception in that federal statute, are there more affirmative consent policies that we have to have in place regarding the sharing of student data?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And so I bring those all up just to say.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: With the when big tech is allowed in the classroom, even when there are policies put in place, there are many other doors that are opened that create their own issues and their own problems.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And so we all need to be a lot bolder in how we address a problem that's really outpacing our ability to keep up in the current moment.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And so these are just a few areas that I think going forward we really need to be paying attention to and working together on.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I look forward to continued conversation around that.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I'll turn it over to Chair Dinowitz, unless there's anything else you want to add.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I just wanted to thank you for that statement.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I want to thank you for, I know we're not done yet, but the opportunity for us to go a little deeper into the policy and also to receive your questions and your final statement as some feedback for us to keep guiding us forward.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I appreciate it very much, too, and your willingness to partner together to really address these issues in an effective way.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks if DOE will commit to banning gamified apps the way it blocked YouTube, noting these apps existed before AI and may not be caught by the AI moratorium. Giunta says gamified apps are not what DOE envisions but takes it under advisement.
chapters.title: Krishnan questions DOE on banning gamified apps beyond AI policy

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, you know, and I think a number of the things we heard today, it sounds.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: like you've been thoughtful about, and making it public, putting it on the website, I think would make a lot of students and teachers and families feel more at ease.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I want to go back to the gamified apps for a second.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: This is, these are really damaging to our kids, much in the same way that social media could be.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You're always looking for the next dopamine hit, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And they take so much of the learning out of these gamified apps.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You've committed to banning YouTube for the younger students, blocking it from their student accounts.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is that same commitment going to be made for these gamified apps?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We will take it under advisement, but a lot of these are going to end up being subject to either our AI moratorium or perhaps not, you know,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'm not sure which ones we're talking about, you know, specifically, but I do think we're going to see a very limited use.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I don't, you know, gamified apps is not something that we really want to see in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is not really the intentional instructional use of technology that we're envisioning.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Yeah, I will note that before the advent of AI, these sorts of apps existed, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So beyond the AI policy, beyond it happening, it happens to be caught up in your AI policy, maybe, and it may not be.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so it's important to take a look at that and make sure, as I've been saying, what's going in front of our children is actually beneficial to our kids and supported by research.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks if DOE has curriculum modules to teach digital health and safety before children are given screens, similar to D.A.R.E. programs. DOE staff describe existing digital literacy curriculum and computer science education that includes unplugged activities for young students.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about digital health and literacy curriculum for youngest grades

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You spoke about for AI, the long-form modules and also the shorter modules for students who don't have AI in front of them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But digital literacy and digital health, right, is really important.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In general, and it's important to start teaching that long before a kid sees a computer.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is there, as part of the curriculum, or are there modules to teach digital health?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and well-being before you even give a kid an iPad or a computer?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes, we have a digital literacy curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Randy Asher spoke to it a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to ask additional questions or if he wants to come up, I'll defer to you on how much deeper you want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think for us now, we are focusing these modules on our high schoolers because we have in our policy them having some access to the ability to use these tools and we did not apply a screen limit for 9 to 12.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So for this year and in this moment, our focus is on our 9 to 12s.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But Tanisha's team and Randy's team have some digital literacy and the AI modules in development for some of our younger grades as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we know that even what I've learned from meeting with Ms.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Vaccaro and Ms.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Weingarten in part of our feedback process is that they too have some great resources to lean into.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And additionally, we met with Senator Gonzalez and Councilmember De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Like, there's a lot that we can pull together for our younger students, but for right now in the launch of this policy, that's why we're speaking specifically to 9 to 12.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We'd be happy to answer any specific questions, but we do have a digital literacy program that spans the grade levels.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It gives kids experience and exposure to concepts that they just need to be familiar with when interacting in a digital environment.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Some of the very things we're concerned about, like bias, inappropriate content, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Is part of that process is explaining to students how to be in a safe environment, how to avoid or respond to cyberbullying, on why you should not put personally identifiable information into open programs.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So it's about informing students on how to use tools appropriately.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: When to use those tools, under what supervision they should or could use those tools, and it's about general information on practices that are expanding throughout everything they do, touch, and see.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And as the students get older, it becomes more and more important as they're interacting with higher levels and more sophisticated levels of digital technology, whether in their career tech pathway or other.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Yeah, and it's true, you don't need to reinvent the wheel.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: U of T, AFT, and other nonprofits have great resources.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is this a requirement even in our youngest grades, kindergarten, first, second grade, before they even touch a screen?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is this being implemented?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, it's kind of hard to do without the screen, but it is a requirement.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Remember D.A.R.E.?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Remember that?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Or like, you know, I didn't have to do drugs to like learn about drugs.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: could learn about it, but to actually see, touch, and experience some of the simulations, it becomes an important component.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm saying you don't need to.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What I'm asking is, can you teach these skills?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yes, and we do, but as the kids get older, it gets more complex.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And I think one of the things that's important to know is...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And as they get older, they have screen time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so what I'm suggesting and asking is in the youngest...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: No, they're not our schools to do this.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Right, in the youngest grades, right, those kindergarten, first, second grade.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Do we have curriculum?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, of course, as always, supports for the teachers to teach the safety and the literacy they need long before they get an iPad thrown in front of them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Does that exist?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We have some of that that was done before this screen restriction that now will be modified based on new policy.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we wouldn't teach it in a digital environment now.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And will that be mandated or recommended?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's mandated that we do this for part of our Children's Internet Protection Act compliance.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's part of the entire...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Understanding of how to interact in an academic setting.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Including for the youngest grades?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We do some exposure to it in the youngest grades, but it's very surface level because they're just not old enough to engage at the deeper level of content.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I think that this involves a much deeper conversation because I think the point is kids are interacting with screens much younger, perhaps,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: than third grade, which is when there's, according to your policy, supposed to be starting.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But they need to learn.

chapters.summary: Krishnan presses on whether digital literacy education is required for all schools or just those that choose to participate. Tanisha Mitchell clarifies there is no strict requirement for all students, but state standards exist for schools doing computer science.
chapters.title: Krishnan presses on whether digital literacy is mandated for all schools

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: the safety and the literacy long before it's introduced in a classroom or even while they're doing it at home.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Even in our computer science for all curriculum, it's guided by state standards.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It also, in our early grades, and Tanisha, correct me if I'm wrong, the vast majority of some of that learning is unplugged.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And programming that has nothing to do with a screen.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So in those spaces, it's not necessarily the literacy of it all, but it's getting ready, you know, it's part of the readiness of, you know, the programming aspect and making, and, you know, all the work that's involved in.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Yeah, or being even aware of what a screen

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: does to you, being aware of what social media does to you before that kid has an Instagram account or TikTok account, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Do you want to add more?

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: Okay, I'm just making sure I was on this time.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: You're doing great.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: I really appreciate our first deputy chancellor and bringing me in for this topic.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: When it comes to our computer science programming, not all of it involves screens.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: Not all of it involves the usage of tools.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: Actually, in elementary school, some of the biggest components of computer science education is understanding

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: technologies, the effects of that in society, ethics, decision making, how you're communicating, and in the earliest grades, to your point, Chair Denowitz, for our kindergarteners.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: It's first graders, second graders.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: It's also understanding the differences of what humans do, what technologies do, different types of technologies, and how to interact with it, and what are some of the good uses of interacting with technologies.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay, and again, at what age does it start?

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: So computer science programming, we had that across K to 12.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
