utterances.text: Okay, so it does include that, and is that every student has access to that, or that's just in the schools that engage with those programs, or the teachers who happen to teach it?

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: So we provide offerings and programs throughout the year to support K-12 schools in receiving that.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: And in accordance with the state, New York State Computer Science and Digital Fluency Standards were passed off across K-12 with the expectation for schools to implement them.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: So we provide resources year-round to support any school, K-12, to be able to provide that type of programming.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to get through the language I'm hearing, be able to or support them in their...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Are they required to do it?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Do all schools have to do this?

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: In New York City public schools, we don't have a strict requirement for all students in doing computer science.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But your expectation is that they...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You said the expectation.

utterances.speaker: Tanisha Mitchell
utterances.text: There are standards that have been produced by the state where if schools are doing computer science, the expectation is to use those standards so it can hit a certain type of rigor across K-12.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: To 12, yes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I mean, I want to make sure our kids are safe and literate before they touch a screen.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm hearing mumblings, it sounds like it's not.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's the distinction between recommendations and mandates, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I posit that in this age, our youngest kids, before they have a one-to-one screen, need to know exactly what you spoke about, the safety and the dangers and the way it can impact them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You know, without that education, they're going to suddenly be presented with a screen and do the things that we're scared of.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You know, whether it's the cognitive offloading or it's the addiction to the screen, they need that education.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And it shouldn't be, well, if the school...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Engages in computer science.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It really should be something that all of our kids are getting.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how many of DOE's 73 technology contracts involve instructional software or hardware. DOE staff report $105 million was spent on educational software in fiscal year 2026, and discuss the process of reviewing contracts for compliance with new policies.
chapters.title: Krishnan questions DOE on technology contracts and spending

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I want to lastly ask about the contracts.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: At the fiscal 2027 preliminary budget hearing for the Education Committee, DOE stated that there were 73 technology contracts in the DOE's budget.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How many of these contracts involve instructional

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: or classroom software or hardware?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: For our procurement team, it's not with us today, but we have some information.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I have the answer with me today on that specific question.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You guys got homework, the audits, the contracts.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We don't mind homework.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Nor should you if you're the education department.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Do you want me to share the information?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yeah, what we have.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So with regard to software specifically,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: In fiscal year 26, which is the last full year that we have spending information,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: for, and just to be clear, this is both school-based and central software spending.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: $105 million was spent on educational software for that fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Wow, I'm in the wrong business.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And how many of those contracts needed to be amended based on the screen time and AI policy?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's something that we're working through right now for sure.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're working with our vendors to figure out the whole turn off, turn on AI situation and all of that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And we can get back to you on that once we've worked through that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And are there any specific contracts?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That the DOE is contracted for a service that is now no longer necessary and no longer required, you no longer require given the new screen time and AI policies?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, again, that's something we have to work through.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Is your product still usable under screen time policies?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Can it still work without AI?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Is it a tool that's used in both high school as well as in middle school?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So there's still some use.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So for every tool, we're going to have to really take a closer look at that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And of course, at some point saying, is your tool effective?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Utilizing our DOE rubric, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks about the 38 programs DOE announced it would discontinue or disable AI components for, requesting the full list, and asks about projected costs for implementing the AI and screen time policy. DOE says it will share the list and doesn't have cost figures yet.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about 38 discontinued AI programs and policy implementation costs

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: On this.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Second, two weeks ago, DOE announced it would discontinue or disable the AI components of 38 previously allowed programs.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As of today, the DOE has not released the list of those programs.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Will the DOE provide the committees with the full list of all 38 programs, indicating which are being discontinued entirely and which are having AI features disabled?

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: Yes, to Lara's point, the 38 is part of we're checking with vendors to make sure and giving them the opportunity to also connect with us on what it has, what it doesn't have, and if it can still apply for use inside of our schools.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But those will be shared with the committees?

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: I believe that is the intention.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: What is the DOE's projected cost to implement the AI and screen time policy for fiscal 2027,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: including things like staffing, the expanded contract review, the technology and school coalition, and the AI literacy modules, which again, my opinion,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: is that the company should be paying for it, given that we're piloting it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But please, what's the projected cost?

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: I think I'm going to have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: I don't think we have that number with us.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: One second.

chapters.summary: Krishnan adds the assessment screen time loophole to the follow-up list. Dinowitz summarizes remaining concerns about teacher PD, research rubrics, data privacy audits, and calls for the best policy in the country rooted in research and transparency. Chancellor Samuels thanks the committees.
chapters.title: Krishnan and Dinowitz close DOE questioning with follow-up items and concerns

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I just wanted to just add one thing to the list we said before of things to follow up on.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I think Fiancema Murano had said a really good question, too, about for now, I think this is an immediate step you all could take, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How do you balance out in the screen time policy you all have in place, 30 or 45 minutes allowed?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Online assessments are exempted from that, but obviously that's also a loophole that could be a huge carve out if they're online assessments and they're screen time.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so I would ask that you all look at ways to issue instructions to the school too, that that loophole shouldn't become something in addition to the screen time allowance right now too.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I also, I know, Chair Krishna, I want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mean, there's significantly more to discuss, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think it's clear that both there have been changes to policy made, that you're listening, but that there's also a lot more to do.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Families remain concerned.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Teachers remain concerned with the amount of screens in the school.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I still remain concerned about the PD.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That teachers are going to get, like what the policy actually looks like.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I still remain concerned about the research, the rubric that you're using for each of these technology companies, what that actually looks like.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I remain concerned about the data privacy audits, whether any have been done, and with that being shared with the public.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so it's clear that the ideas for moving forward and keeping our kids safer there, and what we're really eager to do is make sure that we have

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: the best policy in the country, rooted in research, rooted in transparency,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: rooted in evidence, and that we are all holding each other accountable to make sure our kids are getting the best education possible, that our kids are protected as they use these screens,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: and if necessary, go back.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And determine, you know what, let's figure out a way to ban the gamified apps.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, let's work together to switch back to get this.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: to switch us back to handwritten state assessments.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And that'll open up an entire world of better education, get rid of the excuse so many teachers feel they need to put screens in our kids'hands.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But again, I wanna, we will follow up with a number of the elements that we didn't get answers to today, but I do wanna thank you for coming, for answering the questions, and I look forward to a continued conversation because this is by no means

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: over and I encourage you to stay to hear some of the students testify and some of the community members testify as well.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: Thank you so much again.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: You know, it's hard to believe we announced the policy 13 days ago.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: We're in the fourth instructional day of school.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: We have much to learn.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: I want to thank you so much for the opportunity today to have this conversation so publicly.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: I know that a lot of the conversation today helped clarify some of the policy and raised really great feedback that we look forward to exploring with you throughout the school year.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: And we can't wait to collect more stories about how implementation is going and bring those back to you.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: So thank you today for the time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Krishnan transitions to public testimony, calling up State Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Joanne Simon to testify on their work on screen time and AI legislation.
chapters.title: Krishnan calls up state legislators for testimony

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay, thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We are now going to move to public testimony and start with two state legislators who have been doing great work on this issue and been very vocal about it as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We're going to call up State Senator Andrew Ganardis and Assemblymember Joanne Simon.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Go for it, Senator.

chapters.summary: State Senator Andrew Gounardes credits the administration's new policy, then details his FOCUS Act legislation setting age-appropriate screen limits with force of statute, creating a right to analog learning, regulating vendors, and requiring school-issued devices to be free of social media and AI platforms.
chapters.title: Senator Gounardes testifies on FOCUS Act and ed tech oversight

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Well, is it on now?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Thank you to Chairs Krishnan and Chair Dinowitz and members of both committees for holding this hearing and for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I am State Senator Andrew Gernardis, representing the 26th Senate District in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I have spent much of my time in the legislature working on the question that this hearing asks.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: What obligations do we owe children in a world built by companies that profit from their attention?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I want to start by giving credit to where credit is due to Mayor Ramdani and Chancellor Samuels.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Two weeks ago, they did announce a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for students through eighth grade, restrictions on individual screen times for our youngest learners, and daily screen time limits for elementary school students.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: This policy will reach roughly 600,000 children.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: It is one of, but not the largest, action that any district in the country has taken, and it came about because parents, educators, community education councils, and members of this council pushed hard for it.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: That pressure worked, and the administration listened.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I'm not going to spend my time here today telling you that New York City got this wrong, but I do want to stress that what New York has built so far is a policy and that policies can be rewritten, policies can be quietly revised, policies can have glaring loopholes.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And that left unforced can slowly erode.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: What families deserve and what our students deserve is a floor that does not move.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Let's talk about how we arrived here.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Last year, New York became the largest state in the nation to adopt bell-to-bell cell phone restrictions, smartphone restrictions in K-12 schools.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: The results of this first year were not ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Teachers reported better classroom behavior, stronger engagement, and students talking to each other again.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Lunchrooms got loud.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Bullying incidents fell.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I was proud to support that law and prouder still of the educators who made it work.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: But that law only reaches the phone in a student's pocket.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: It says nothing about the laptop or the screen that schools hand that same student at the start of the year.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Nearly nine in 10 American public schools now run a one-to-one program issuing every student a device.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And the evidence connecting more classroom screen exposure to better learning outcomes is thin to non-existent.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I think there's a reason why we heard earlier that there aren't a lot of independent reviewed studies justifying the use of these platforms and these schools because there is a lack of them.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: An OECD study spanning 31 countries found that students who use computers more often in schools scored lower on reading and math tests than students who use them less.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Sweden, once amongst the most aggressive adopters of classroom tablets, has spent tens of millions of dollars buying back paper textbooks after their reading scores declined.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Earlier this year, we learned that reading scores on the third grade state exam plummeted in New York City by nearly 14 points.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Surely the fact that eight-year-olds were mandated to take the exam on a computer and not with paper and pencil, as is appropriate for their age and cognitive development, contributed to this drop.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: A study spanning 50 countries found that the use of artificial intelligence in education can undermine children's foundational development.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: The researchers pointed to a specific mechanism.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Students who offload their thinking onto AI tools skip the cognitive struggle that produces real learning, so the skill never gets built in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: We told kids to put their phones away and then in too many classrooms, handed them a screen and called it instruction.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Many of us grew up with the mantra that learning should be fun, and it should be.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: But making learning fun by creatively creating the friction necessary for cognitive growth and making learning like playing a video game are two different things.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: One works and the other clearly does not.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: That is the gap of legislation that I've introduced over the summer.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: The Fostering Optimal Classroom Use of Screens Act is meant to close.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And I would ask this council to consider several things that state law can do and that city guidance cannot.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: This is not meant to be a ban on tech, but guardrails on the intentional use of technology in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: First, the FOCUS Act sets age-appropriate limits with the force of statute.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Students in pre-K through fifth grade would learn primarily face-to-face.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: and on paper.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Sixth through eighth graders would access devices through a shared cart or lab model, and high schoolers would have cart access or one-to-one access with a parent's opt-in.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: These are limits, not recommendations, and they don't expire after a year.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Second, the bill creates a right to analog learning, including, yes, Chair Dinowitz, the right to take your exams using paper and pencil.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Schools would be required to assign work that can be completed without a screen whenever it is feasible, and families could opt out of digital assignments where a reasonable alternative exists.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I have heard from parents across the state who tried to opt their children out and were treated as a nuisance rather than the decision makers of their children's education that they are.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: A right that a principal can decline to honor is not a right.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Third, this bill regulates the vendors, not just the classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Ed tech companies would have to register with the Attorney General before selling to a school district, demonstrate compliance with federal and state student privacy laws,

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: show that their products do not contain distracting features unrelated to learning, and point to at least one independent study showing their product annually improves academic performance.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Products that cannot clear this bar cannot be installed and should not be installed on school-issued devices.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And this is the piece I want to underline for this council because it speaks directly to your oversight authority and to some of the questions that were asked earlier.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: The state comptroller produced an audit earlier this year finding that New York City public schools do not consistently follow the laws governing student data.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: and identified real weaknesses in transparency and technical safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: A district managing millions of student records across dozens of outside vendors needs more than a purchasing process.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: It needs a standard of proof.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Lastly, the bill requires that school-issued devices be free of social media, gaming, and direct messaging apps, chatbots, and generative AI platforms and cameras.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And it requires the state education department to update our digital fluency standards that have not been touched since 2020, before the advent of ChatGPT and Claude and other types of AI tools.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: So that students can actually learn about the effects of excessive screen use and how to navigate these platforms safely.

chapters.summary: Gounardes asks the Council to codify screen time policy in local law, require a complete ed tech product inventory, require independent evaluation before contract renewal, guarantee families' right to non-digital alternatives, and support his FOCUS Act in Albany.
chapters.title: Gounardes urges Council to codify policy, require ed tech inventory, and support FOCUS Act

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: None of this work is meant to displace the council's role, and there is work here that only you can do, and I would respectfully suggest four places to start.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Codify an appropriate screen time and AI policy in local law so that it survives this administration or any administration.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Require the department to publish a complete inventory of every ed tech product in use in city schools, what it costs, and what evidence there is to support using it.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Require independent evaluation before any significant contract is renewed.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And guarantee in writing that families are notified of their right to a non-digital alternative, with particular care that students with disabilities keep every piece of assistive technology that they need to rely on.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Nothing in this effort should ever come at the expense of a child who needs a device to access the curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And I want to be unambiguous about that point.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I would also welcome the Council's formal support for the FOCUS Act as the Legislature reconvenes to do its work up in Albany this January.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I have spent several years engaged in this work.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: The Safe for Kids Act now has final rules from the Attorney General and takes effect in January of next year.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: The Child Data Protection Act that I authored is already law.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: We've passed laws requiring social media warning labels, Stop Online Predators Act, and one of the strongest AI safety laws in the country.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Every one of those fights that I've taken on has followed the same pattern.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: An industry insisted that it could police itself, families who said otherwise, and the law eventually catching up.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: We are at this same point with ed tech.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Schools should be places where children read, write, argue, and struggle with a problem.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And learn from an adult who knows them, not an AI robot teacher.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Technology has a real role in preparing students for the world they will inherit, and I'm not asking anyone to pretend otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I'm just suggesting and I'm just asking that we stop letting the companies decide the terms.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Thank you again to both chairs and the members of these committees and the council for taking on this work, and I'm eager to work with you as partners in government to get this work done.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you, Senator.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's very clear you went to a good college.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: Hunter.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It was Hunter.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It was Hunter.

utterances.speaker: Chancellor Samuels
utterances.text: Hunter.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I just want to reference, before we go into the assembly moment, reference one point.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I didn't get to ask this, but I do want to share it on the record that as part of the state law for banning phones in school, which is great,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It says no later than September 1st, 2026, New York City Public School must publish a report on its website detailing enforcement of the cell phone and electronic device policy, including

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: non-identifiable demographic data of students who have faced disciplinary action for noncompliance and analysis of any demographic disparities in enforcement of this policy.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's a report that's important, but one that we are unable to find.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But did want to highlight that as we do still have members of the DOE here, members of the public, and it's referencing the law that you referenced in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So thank you, fellow Hunter grad.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Senator Gornardis, for your work on this, for the FOCUS Act, and all our partnership.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to keep pushing on this issue, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Senator Simon?

chapters.summary: Assemblymember Joanne Simon discusses assistive technology's importance for students with disabilities, the need for better AT evaluations at IEP meetings, attention and executive functioning issues, and the value of programs like Amira and CUNY Reading Fellows when used appropriately.
chapters.title: Assemblymember Simon testifies on assistive technology, attention, and nuanced tech use

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I did not go to Hunter.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I did not go to a CUNY school or a SUNY school, so I'm really like, you know, out there.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So I'm going to take a slightly different approach and kind of talk around some of the issues that I think are important that we look at and some of the things I have learned over the years about how to suss through some of these things.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Because as you know, from just listening to the testimony and your own work, there's no easy answers here.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And it's very nuanced.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And that whole endeavor of educating our young people is much more nuanced than I think a lot of people realize.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So let me just say that, you know, as a matter of background, I have my master's in teaching preschool deaf children.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So for me, zero to three are very big, important issues, as is language development, which is

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: something that is, I think, critical to what it is we are in some cases using assistive technology for.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I moved to New York to get my doctorate in clinical psychology.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I did not finish that degree.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I know enough to be dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: But really what I know is what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I have a very healthy appreciation.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: for that.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And it's stood me well in representing people with disabilities for 30-some years and in my role as chair of the Assembly Mental Health Committee.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So one of the things I learned by trying a case that was a seminal case on

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: who has a disability under the law, which was a case representing a woman with dyslexia who was denied accommodations repeatedly on the bar exam, my favorite people, the bar examiners.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It was a lot about tests and measurement and about assessing what works and for whom.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So a couple of things that I wanted to just mention.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Number one, I think we need to keep talking about assistive technology in a way that is constructive.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Assistive technology opens the door for so many of our students.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And, of course, we're talking about screen time here, but assistive technology is not exclusively about screens.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And so I want to make sure that we don't inadvertently kind of just not focus on other aspects of assistive technology because they're not related to screens.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: One thing is, for example, at IEP meetings, they're supposed to ask about assistive technology, but most parents don't know to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And so many fewer students get an IT evaluation than should.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And if they had an appropriate assistive technology evaluation,

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Right off the bat, we would have an IEP that better provides for the...

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: services for that student.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And we could make a huge difference in children's lives if we did more of that.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: But we need to be doing more training of teachers, related services professionals, and administrators on using that to help achieve IEP goals and make our students succeed.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Tech can also be a large part of the accommodations package, right?

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And so that is true at all levels.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I did a lot with younger kids, but also a lot with higher ed and testing.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: But I think it's very important that technology is also about not just reading on screens, but on text-to-voice and voice-to-text.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And we know that when children are reading with their ears, for example, that they are learning just as much.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: For years, we've been told that reading comprehension correlates very highly with IQ.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It does, unless you have a reading disability, then it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: But we do know that listening comprehension correlates just as highly, if not more so, with intellectual ability.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And so for our students who have difficulty with reading, really better utilizing the assistive technology that provides that information through listening comprehension is critical.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: But also building that listening comprehension and developing that with tech and without tech is critically important.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Attention is a huge issue.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: We know that technology can be distracting.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: can lead to distraction, can affect attention.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Really, the battle for attention is often on our screens.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Chris Hayes wrote a whole book about that.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It is a real issue, but it's also about executive functioning, and our kids really need to learn more about executive functioning, and I think that our teachers and our support personnel need to understand better what executive functioning is,

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: because it's very easy to miss that piece of it.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So it's not just attention.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It's about marshalling your resources and being able to organize and plan and follow steps, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: The CUNY Reading Fellows Program does an excellent job.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It is partially in person.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It is also partially remote.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: But I think it's important to mention that it's not AI.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It is just a remote tutoring with an adult on the other side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I want to make sure we don't lose sight of some of those kinds of programs that are working very well and are, in fact, helping our students with learning to read and guiding that.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: They hold cognitive issues around attention and...

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Executive functioning and learning.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: The other issue about devices is that they can be communication devices.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And for many of our students who have difficulty communicating, whether they're on the spectrum, for example, or they have neuromuscular disorders, there's a whole host of communication devices they may

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: They have a screen, they may not, but it's how they communicate with other people.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And so the devices can actually connect you in many ways, although we also know that obviously there can be a downside to that,

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: where it helps a child learn to focus, where it gives them confidence that they can control the craziness in their world, for example, that they can develop relationships with others through assistive technology.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: We need to make sure that we cabin that so that they are not not learning how to communicate with others.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And for some students, that may be the only way they can communicate with other people.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So I think it's very important that we focus on that.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I don't know how much of that is AI-driven at this point.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I think most of it is not, but I think it's very important to look at how we weigh those various factors.

chapters.summary: Simon warns about students forming relationships with chatbots leading to self-harm, stresses digital literacy for parents and students, and recommends Maryanne Wolf's book 'Reader, Come Home' on how screens change reading brains.
chapters.title: Simon discusses mental health risks of chatbots and recommends book on reading brains

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I do want to say a word about AMERA, which I know has been mentioned a couple of times, that it was at the press conference we did releasing the AI policy.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It actually is a very good program, but it's a supportive program.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It's not an intervention program.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And I think that's something we need to recognize as well.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I'm a little concerned that people have been using it for instruction or it may not have been used appropriately.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It really is because you need redundancy.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: You need repetition for kids who have reading disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It does work very well.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I looked at it when it first came out, for example.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I had an expert that I've worked with.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: of my expert witnesses who looked at it.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It's a really good program.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So I want to make sure we don't lose what's good about AMERA for those kids who really need it.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: The other thing I want to mention, just some notes I have.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: As we're adding reading interventions, I know we have these wind, you know, what I need periods.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It's important that kids who really have Tier 2 and Tier 3 instructional needs are not just sitting there doing iReady with the same screens as everybody else.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I think in some classrooms we're finding that that's been happening.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I think school personnel need guidance on how to address this issue.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Another point that I want to make is that we use this technology for the purposes for which they're designed.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: You know, certain off-label work can work for certain students, but the dangers of overuse for these purposes for which they're not validated is an issue.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And if you remember, we did the teacher evaluation thing probably about 10, 12 years ago, and they were using the tests to evaluate teachers and using the math scores to evaluate the art teachers.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: That's a classic example.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: They were never meant for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Those tests were never meant for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: The Davidson Protocol was never meant for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And we put it into law.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: They undid it a year later because it made no sense at all.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: But that's a classic example.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And if I have to quote Martha Stewart, I will.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: The right tool for the right job, right?

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: You use the right tool for the job.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And we don't do that enough.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Mental health, the committee's report addresses a few things.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I think one thing that we have to recognize is that, again, for mental health purposes, for some neuroatypical kids, the screens and devices can make a big difference for them.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: What we need to do is get a better rubric and a better sense of how we can evaluate when they are becoming dangerous, right?

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: We have kids who have formed relationships with chatbots, and they have self-harm.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Some of them have, in fact, taken their own lives because it's almost somewhat Rogerian the way the chatbots work.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: They make you feel better about what you're thinking.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Well, if you feel that way, go right ahead.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: This is not a helpful thing.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So I know that we're not doing that with our young kids, but our teenagers, if they're going home and using that.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So I think it goes to this issue about digital literacy, how to protect yourself, have parents understand how to protect their children, and to learn more about what their kids are using so that they're not in the dark.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Because what happens, you find our parents had no idea that this child had a relationship with a chatbot until it was too late.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And we want to keep that from happening.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And then one other thing I want to just...

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Suggest is a book called Reader Come Home, which was written by Mary Ann Wolfe, who was at Tufts for many years.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: She's now at UCLA.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: She wrote Proust and the Squid, The Science of the Reading Brain, about 10, 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: She just did a book, Style.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: as sort of letters to readers about various aspects of brain functioning and screens

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: and the development of language, how language actually changes how you think and feel and relate and how you understand yourself but also others and how you connect with literature.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And there are real differences that we're seeing in brains from the use of reading on screens.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And she talked about how she's changing how her brain is functioning by using screens.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And so it's an easy book to read.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: I listened to it on the way up to Albany for a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: It's really pretty short.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: But I really do recommend it because it's a very different eye-opening introduction to what's going on in our brains.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: When we're using screens.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: So thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: No, you're good.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: No, I was going to say thank you so much, Senator.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I think there's really important points to keep in mind, and I appreciate you highlighting these nuances, too, and considerations for us all to think about as we work on this together.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, I want to thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I understand from growing up the assembly is the hardest working legislative body in the state.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: The Senate does nothing.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's what I was brought up to.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Belief.

utterances.speaker: Joanne Simon
utterances.text: And they have better food in the lounge.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, they have all these perks and they don't do anything.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, the ice cream and the cookies.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I've had them before.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But, by the way, when you mentioned the testing and the gym teacher getting the, you know, being judged on, like, what the math.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Teacher, I think I was chapter leader when we were dealing with all that, and so thank you for the PTSD.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But I do want to thank you, first and foremost, for the work you've done over the years, particularly for the disability community.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Those are my students, so I want to thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and also for your testimony, which recognizes, I think, some of the points that Chair Krishna and I are calling for, which is an evidence-based approach, which is when you have a tool that works, it's the same in the FOCUS Act for Senator Granardis.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's, you know, what's the evidence there to support the implementation of this product?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Aligned with the training for the teacher to make sure that if it is a good product, it's being used properly and not to offload

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: work or not to rely on it, but as some sort of supplement or whatever the product's designed for with the teacher training.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so I appreciate the both of you for the work that you've done, the work that you're doing, and the continued partnership to make sure we are getting this right for our kids.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, I want to, if I can, give you an example like of Zoom, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, when COVID happened, we all learned how to Zoom, and we learned how to do various things on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But now you find that we're using Zoom as a way, you know, just in community meetings, for example, to not have anybody ask questions.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You disable the chat.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You don't allow people to unmute.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then there's no interaction.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so I think it's an example of one of those things that really can work great.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It brought more people into the fold.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It allowed us to communicate in a way that we weren't able to communicate.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: During certain times, it makes it much more convenient for people to participate in meetings.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's great in many ways, but we have to be careful that we don't kind of go off the...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: the edge and have it become the thing that does bring us together but starts dividing us.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's amazing though, six and a half years later and so many people still can't find that mute button.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Not a public meeting, it's amazing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Councillor Wong, you had a question I think, right?

chapters.summary: Council Member Wong asks whether limiting screen time could alleviate school violence. Simon discusses social-emotional development and problem-solving, while Gounardes connects the replacement of childhood play with phone play to reduced ability to navigate conflict.
chapters.title: Council Member Wong asks senators about screen time and school violence connection

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes, a question for both senators.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What I noticed is that school violence has been

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: uptaking is happening more and more and the students involved are getting younger and younger either with guns or knives.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This morning we have a mother bringing the kids to school and he was stabbed.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Well my question is do you agree that limiting or reducing screen time would

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: would relieve or would alleviate this problem?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or can you want to talk about the connection between screen time and violence, school violence in kids?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mean, there were studies early on that people talked about whether kids exposed to violent movies, for example, made them more violent.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I don't think they really found a connection there.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The reality is, however, that it goes to that social-emotional issue, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Kids who can't communicate or who are frustrated and angry because they don't have relationships, and they don't know they don't have relationships, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: They're not very good monitors of their own social-emotional development necessarily, and may be more likely to do that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The other thing, especially with young people,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: is it's a way to have bragging rights in some cases, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You would see kids who carry a knife to school because it made them cool.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You see girls who feel more safe because their boyfriend has a gun, when in fact we know they are much less safe, that it's five times more likely they will be shot by the boyfriend they think is going to protect them, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so part of that is also...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Teaching kids how to resolve issues like alternate dispute resolution for problem solving in schools so that they don't pick up a knife, they don't pick up a gun, they don't take that out.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we really need to do a lot of work on social-emotional development and problem solving with kids.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And I think it's less likely that that will happen.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Now, to the extent that they get over-focused on screens and are having relationships with chatbots or with these chat groups and what have you, that can certainly lead to social isolation.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And a lack of effective problem-solving skills.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Oh, you wanted to add to it?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: No, I would just say I think that this is really what a lot of, like Professor Haidt at NYU has talked about, that we've replaced childhood play with phone play.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And as a result, students and young people don't learn how to navigate conflict and tension and how to form interpersonal relationships and how to see that the joke that the council member made about Hunter was a joke and was not an insult.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: But if he had posted it online, maybe the assembly member would have seen it and said, oh, that was an insult to me.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: When students, when young people are only

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: spending their social development through a device, and they're building social relationships through a device, and they're not developing that ability to navigate the playground and to navigate real-life tension and real-life awkwardness and real-life social engagement.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: It's very easy to see how small slights online can become very big problems in real life that result in some of the violence we're seeing or the violent actions we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: It's not the only contributing factor, but it certainly is a factor.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And I think that's one of the reasons why over the last couple of years I have focused so much of my legislative work around the harms that social media has had on young kids'mental development, what the role of these algorithms has had

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: on their cognitive development, on their social and emotional growth.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And the impact that big tech has had on these young kids'lives.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And then you're seeing this play out and manifest itself in real life.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Senators.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Cheers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: One thing I might also add about screen stuff is that, you know, tone of voice is important and matters in communications.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But, you know, the other thing that I think is happening here is social media.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We know if kids are using social media and they're on screens more, they are greater likely to developing anxiety and depression.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And also that they're not learning how to communicate with each other.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so it's this issue of focusing on the screens and not developing friends.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we go back to zero to three.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And if you remember in administration or two or three ago, there was a real focus on trying to teach kids to read in 4K, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: They weren't even in K yet at that point.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And in fact, there are some kids who are very precocious that can learn to read at four.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But really, zero to three, it's really social-emotional development.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Kids need to learn to play.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And if you're reading the literature, there is more attention now to what children learn.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: They learn by playing, and they're learning a lot of things, including ordering their world, but also their relationships with others.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And how to play and how to follow rules and all of those things are really the kinds of things we need to be focusing on with young children, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And not exposing them necessarily to try and put pressure on them to read.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Senators.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

chapters.summary: Krishnan transitions to general public testimony, reminding attendees of the two-minute time limit, decorum rules, and procedures for submitting written testimony.
chapters.title: Krishnan opens public testimony portion of hearing

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you both so much for your testimony, for your work on this issue, and look forward to our continued partnership.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: All right, now we're going to turn to public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Further members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: When you will, you will have two minutes to speak on today's oversight hearing topic, examining screen time and the use of digital devices in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony at testimony at council on yc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: For in-person panelists, please come to the table once your name has been called.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I would just add, I know it's been a long day and we have a lot of testimony too, so I just ask everyone to stick to the two-minute time limit so we can get through to everyone in an efficient manner.

chapters.summary: Mary Vaccaro, UFT Vice President for Education, expresses support for aspects of the new policy, describes UFT's role in creating the AFT's National Academy for AI Instruction, and urges DOE to sign the Microsoft agreement for privacy, transparency, and security safeguards.
chapters.title: Mary Vaccaro of UFT testifies on AI safeguards and Microsoft agreement

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now I'll call up our first panel.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We have a student, Alma Adi.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Ariana Ahmed Misha, and Sika Agbokov, and Mary Vaccaro.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay, so we'll come back to you all if they're here.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Let us know when they're here.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So we'll go to Mary Vaccaro, Jennifer Weber, Doug Spring, and Julie Samuels.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: In the meantime, could we ask Mama to redo her witness?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And we also ask Alma Adi to please redo her witness slip and speak to the sergeant at arms about that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: May I begin?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You're ready.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Mary, you want to go first?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: My name is Mary Vaccaro and I'm the Vice President of Education for the United Federation of Teachers.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: On behalf of the union's 200,000 members, I want to thank Chairperson Krishnan and on the Committee of Oversight and Investigations for holding today's hearing on screen time and the use of digital devices in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: I also want to thank Chairperson Dinowitz and the Committee on Education for their attention to this pressing issue that students, parents, and school staff grapple with daily.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: As educators, we strive to provide students with the best education and learning experience possible.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: Screens, digital devices, and artificial intelligence enhance our ability to do this, but only when they are appropriately used as tools to support learning, not as replacement for interpersonal relationships and hands-on experiences.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: Despite the prevalence of AI in our schools, there has been little regulation and guidance from federal, state, and until very recently from the New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: Earlier this month, New York City Public Schools released guidance on AI and screen time.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: There are many aspects of the plan that we support.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: Banning individual screen use in 2K through second grade makes sense, as does limiting

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: individual screen time for grades three through eight, and reviewing what's appropriate for nine through 12 based on individual courses.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: The New York City Public Schools screen policy also gives schools flexibility for special education students and students with English language learning.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: These educational programs require a device or for when the system or the school needs to go remote.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: New York City Public Schools AI policy leaves many questions unanswered, particularly how the department will be more aggressive in demanding that the products it purchases have AI safeguards built in.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: To fill in these gaps, the UFT has played a pivotal role in creating and running the AFT's National Academy for AI Instruction based here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: The Academy is training hub designed and overseen by educators grounded in trust, safety, and people-first technology built directly on the AFT's common sense guardrails.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: In less than a year, we have provided 2,000 educators in-person training and 11,000 educators year-round.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: And I kind of, we have a ton, but you have it.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: We really want to focus on our agreement with Microsoft that New York City public schools can easily agree to

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: in order to do more safeguards and really talk about what those safeguards are there for privacy, transparency, and security in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Mary Vaccaro
utterances.text: So you can see the rest of our testimony there.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thanks so much, Mary, and thanks to all that you have.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: FT does as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We look forward to continuing to work on this.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Julie Samuels.

chapters.summary: Julie Samuels, CEO of TechNYC, supports AI literacy education with safeguards, expresses concern that high school AI limits are too restrictive for future workforce preparation, and emphasizes data privacy must be central with real enforcement resources.
chapters.title: Julie Samuels of TechNYC testifies on AI literacy and concerns about high school limits

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Krishna and Nandinewitz, Council Members.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: I'm very happy to be here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: I'm Julie Samuels.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: I'm the CEO of TechNYC, an organization that represents hundreds of tech companies and investors here in the city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We really spend our time thinking about the future of our economy in the city and ensuring that New Yorkers are part of that future.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: This year, CBRE ranked New York as the largest tech talent market in North America for the first time beating the Bay Area.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We're very excited about that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We rank second in the United States for AI talent, and our students in New York need to be ready for the modern workplace and for higher education,

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: which we mean believes that AI literacy has to be a genuine part of their education, particularly at the older ages.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: And of course with appropriate safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We agree with a lot of what Mary said.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: I've spoken with some of you about that as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We fundamentally believe students should never be treated as guinea pigs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: AI must be introduced in a supervised way.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We care about building critical thinking.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We don't want to replace it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: But I feel very strongly, we feel very strongly, we don't want to repeat the mistakes we made with social media.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: When new technologies were ignored, when parents and teachers often kind of put their heads under the sand and young people

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: People navigated them unsupervised before regulations and guidance were put in place.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: AI is still in its early stages, but that doesn't mean that it shouldn't be part of a conversation we're having with students and adults together, learning together.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We do have some concerns about the mayor's new guidance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We actually are worried that the limits in high school are too limiting.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We worry that it is an insufficient amount of time for students to develop essential skills for their futures and for the economy of the future.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: Any policy, especially, we're grateful and we're glad it's a year and we're glad that we're going to be working on it on an ongoing basis.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: Any permanent policy should allocate time for AI instruction equal to other subjects.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We fundamentally believe I'm almost done.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: Data privacy must be central.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We support New York City Public Schools IRMA process.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: It's a policy only as strong as its enforcement, and the public schools need to be given real resources to monitor, evaluate, and enforce.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: We fundamentally believe this will only work if, as Mary said, we're focused on privacy, transparency, and security.

utterances.speaker: Julie Samuels
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Doug Spring of the Salvadori Center describes their hands-on STEAM education programs using cardboard, rulers, and glue rather than screens, and shares NYU research findings that project-based learning maintains student interest in math better than screen-based curricula.
chapters.title: Doug Spring of Salvadori Center testifies on hands-on STEAM as screen alternative

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Council members, Krishna and Dinowitz and Wong and General Counsel.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: My name is Doug Spring.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: I'm the Chief Operating Officer at the Salvadori Center.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: At Salvadori, we provide STEAM education services, that is STEM plus the A for arts and architecture, to schools, after-school sites, and NYCHA community centers across the five boroughs, focusing on the built environment.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: For context, last year, Salvadori taught over 12,000 students in 178 sites.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: Our goal is to make STEAM come alive for students through the built environment and to foster the soft skills of collaboration, creativity, and problem solving, just like real-life architects, designers, and engineers.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: At Salvadori, we have seen firsthand the impact of investing in this hands-on approach to STEAM education for young people, and we're grateful for your support through the CASA initiatives and digital inclusion and literacy funding that we receive from the council.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: Our residencies explore and have students create 3D models to reflect their values of their peers.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: These models before me represent a model skyscraper and a model community center produced by students at South Beach UAU Cornerstone on Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: I've included pictures of two recent 3D models prepared as part of Salvadori's STEAM Innovators summer programs at Ravenswood Cornerstone in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: And East Chester Gardens Community Center in the Bronx at the bottom of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: for your review.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: You'll see these models are made without technology, cardboard, rulers, glue, and clay.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: Just to name a few, our STEAM educators rely on hands-on instruction throughout the cohort to demonstrate all facets of the design process with common school supplies.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: Salvadori and NYU are concluding a study this year to present finding that children who received this community-focused project-based curriculum offered by Salvadori maintain their interest and self-efficacy in math

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: compared to declines among children exposed to a particular curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: Particular curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: While Salvadori supports the curated and carefully monitored use of screen time when they meaningfully enhance and support individual goals,

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
utterances.text: for example CAD, which helps architects provide their floor plans, we believe our model of hands-on project-based learning offers top-tier alternatives to screen time in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Doug Spring
