utterances.text: We thank you for the opportunity today and we're grateful for the partnership with the City Council and our partners in the room.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, you all, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We'll call up the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We have Charlotte Pope, Lainey Hemison, Alyssa East,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And Sophia Addison.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm going to, just given the interest of time, too, I'm going to give you all a 15-second warning before it's two minutes and really would ask you all to wrap up at two minutes so we can keep moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You want to start, Lainey?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Go ahead.

chapters.summary: Lainey Hemison criticizes DOE's oversight of ed tech vendors, noting more than 700 programs access student data, questioning the IRMA process's adequacy, and raising concerns about YouTube workarounds through Google Classroom embedding that may still violate privacy laws.
chapters.title: Lainey Hemison testifies on DOE's weak vendor oversight and YouTube workarounds

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Oh, you can turn the mic on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: Thank you for holding the hearings today, Chairs Dinowitz and Shekar Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: My testimony, written testimony, is very detailed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: I'm just going to make some points after listening to the DOE testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: I think they said only 78 software programs they use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: By law, they have to post the software programs that have access to personal student data, and there are more than 700, and we know that that's a minimum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: I'm very skeptical that just asking vendors whether they use AI is sufficient with no verification techniques.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: In general, we've seen very shoddy and weak oversight from the Department of Education when it comes to making sure that these products comply with state law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: And it came out today that their invented IRMA process doesn't even ask the vendors which AI programs they use and what data they collect and how it's used.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: It is illegal under state law to use data mine personal student data for product improvement, and yet we've seen that in the privacy policies of many of these vendors and their sub-processors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: Thank you for your advocacy around YouTube.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: For nearly two years, the DOE allowed YouTube to be assigned to students, even though they were told by both Google, the owner,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: and by the state education department that Google had announced that YouTube would no longer comply with the state law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: Now they say they're going to use a workaround by allowing teachers to embed YouTube into Google Classroom, which will not provide the same privacy violations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: And yet I've asked several tech experts who say that that still may not work

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: in terms of being allowed to look at the IP address and then monitor the students'use of YouTube that way and still be able to use that for marketing purposes and targeted ads.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: I have several recommendations for the bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: I just wanted to, it's in my testimony, the bills that have been introduced, but I really want to urge you to introduce a new one, which would require

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: the reporting of screen time in schools by grade and which specific uses and apps and programs are exempt from those requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: We've seen very contradictory testimony today about whether it's required or just advised those limits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: We even know in the early grades it's only advised, and then there's still so many exemptions in terms of diagnostics assessments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: And basically what principals are telling teachers that all the apps that are being used, even in those earliest grades, can be exempt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: as long as they're calling them assessments, diagnostics, and screeners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lainey Hemison
utterances.text: Thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Alyssa East, parent and co-leader of Distraction-Free Schools NY, criticizes the blanket exception for students with disabilities in DOE's screen time guidance, arguing ed tech is not assistive technology and excessive screen time exacerbates attentional issues for neurodivergent children.
chapters.title: Alyssa East testifies on ed tech exemptions for students with disabilities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: Thank you for convening this hearing and the opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: My name is Alyssa East.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: I'm a parent of a Carter case child, a member of the AIM Coalition, and co-leader of Distraction-Free Schools New York, the state chapter of a national grassroots education policy program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: seeking to restore learning by realigning school approaches to technology with child development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: Senator Gunardi's FOCUS Act was drafted from our model bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: So it's been pretty well established here today that children are uniquely vulnerable to persuasive technologies, excessive screen exposure, manipulative design features, and artificial intelligence systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: Their cognitive, emotional, and social capacities are still developing, making them more susceptible to distraction, dependency, and behavioral impacts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: Schools have adopted these technologies without consistent standards for safety, educational effectiveness, developmental appropriateness, privacy protection, or procurement integrity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: This gap leaves children exposed to risks that research has repeatedly documented as problematic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: These exposures are particularly challenging for families of children with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: The public-facing language around the DOE guidelines calls for a generic exception for students with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: disabilities, implying that AI and screen limit guidelines are for gen ed kids alone, not for students with disabilities or English language learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: As Assemblymember Simon testified, the world of students with disabilities is wide and deeply nuanced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: Guidance around students with disabilities should reflect the beauty and diversity of this community and its varying needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: EdTech is not sped tech.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: EdTech is also not assistive technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: But many students with disabilities are given excessive amounts of ed tech, either in the classroom or assigned as homework for remediation purposes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's about 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: One in five children have ADHD, and many more have ADHD-like symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: Why is the DOE creating a blanket exception, given that we know that screen time exacerbates attentional issues for all children and is especially harmful with regard to one of the most common forms of neurodivergence?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alyssa East
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thanks so much.

chapters.summary: Charlotte Pope of the NYCLU describes AI vendors shifting language to evade city policy, vendors celebrating pilot announcements, and concerns about student monitoring and inability to opt out of pilot classrooms.
chapters.title: Charlotte Pope of NYCLU testifies on AI vendor evasiveness and pilot concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Charlotte Pope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: I'm with the New York Civil Liberties Union.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: Since the June oversight, we've seen a lot of scary shifts, like AI ed tech vendors providing coaching to school leaders to help them rebrand AI and sell screen time to families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: Educators tell us that their DOE inboxes are full of vendors assuring them that their AI products comply with city policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: The chancellor said publicly that DOE shouldn't be responsible for combing through every product, but right now that burden falls on teachers, students, and families to scour vendor materials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: But these products are slippery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: After policy prohibited AI grading, vendors that once sold AI grading systems now instead call it AI feedback or AI insights or AI scoring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: An electronic hall pass vendor recently changed their branding from, quote, AI powered to, quote, a rules-based algorithm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: AI vendors are simply shifting their language to squeeze into really imprecise city policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: When the mayor endorsed five pilot products for high schools, those vendors instantly celebrated through press releases, emphasizing how safe their products are and saying these pilots are for collecting evidence about AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: We're concerned about how students will be monitored to collect this evidence on top of their inability to opt out of these classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for talking about the issue of consent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: Thank you also for calling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: Alling students in these pilots test subjects, DOE's answers about data collection are worrying and we'll watch for this so-called pilot framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: The great progress we've made makes AI governance even more important and thank you for the continued close oversight and we appreciate your partnership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: We have a lot more in our submitted testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Pope
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sophia Addison of the Child Mind Institute describes their work in NYC schools, supports precautionary safeguards on technology, and calls for mental health literacy curricula teaching healthy technology relationships alongside no-device policies.
chapters.title: Sophia Addison of Child Mind Institute testifies on mental health and digital wellness

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Hope you can turn your mic on, yep.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: My name is Sophia Addison.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: I'm the Vice President for School and Community Programs at the Child Mind Institute.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: Nationally, the Child Mind Institute has reached more than 2 million children.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: And here in New York City, we've actually reached over 375 children in New York City public schools, as well as caregivers and parents.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: Our team has built and delivered New York City workshops on mental health and social media, strategies for promoting healthy digital engagement, and early childhood screen time and regulation, along with conducting studies to survey how teens are experiencing

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: belonging both online and in person.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: At the Child Mind Institute, our work with schools equips educators and school communities with evidence-based tools and resources that support students'emotional well-being and relationships.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: As a leading voice in youth mental health, we are committed to advancing rigorous research that informs evidence-based policy and practice.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: We support precautionary safeguards on technology that are justified

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: by current evidence, including age-appropriate design standards for users under 18, platform transparency backed by independent audits, and mental health impact assessments for new features that reach younger users,

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: alongside technology literacy initiatives that make clear what a given tool is and is not, so families and educators can make informed decisions.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: On AI specifically, our own next generation digital therapeutics frameworks builds fit for purpose, responsible by design digital tools for youth mental health.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: We believe any AI used with students should meet the same bar, developmentally appropriate, safety tested, and always paired with a path to human.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: New York City has already adopted a no-device policy during the school day, and we support that approach, especially during instructional periods.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: A no-device policy on its own doesn't teach students how to regulate their own digital behavior.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: What's still needed is a clear look at how it's working in practice so it's implemented fairly and benefits all students alongside mental health literacy curricula that teaches healthy technology relationships.

utterances.speaker: Sophia Addison
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thanks so much.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony and look forward to our continued work together on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Our next panel is Shannon Ritchie, Naomi Sachs, and Amy Turchiano.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And as they're coming up, I know the other panel just left, but I want to thank Lainey because in her testimony, she referenced Intro 959 and 960.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Those are two of my pieces of legislation that we're looking forward to to get more better reporting, more transparency around the dealing and the use of these devices, including AI.

chapters.summary: Shannon Ritchie, a parent, describes discovering her third grader had access to violent and sexualized games on school Chromebooks after finishing state test prep, and being denied access to her son's internet history while Google has all the data.
chapters.title: Shannon Ritchie testifies about inappropriate games on school Chromebooks

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Shannon Ritchie.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: I'm a parent of a fourth grader in Greenpoint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: I'm also an SLT member and Hunter grad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: I'm here today to speak out against the overuse of ed tech and screens in our public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: I don't want to fight with the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: I'm a staunch advocate for public education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: But it feels more and more that the DOE is not there to support our public school students, but is instead an opportunity for people to scoop up lucrative contracts in an effort to eventually be hired by these very same ed tech companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: We heard the DOE today say that they instruct schools to only use screens for specific learning purposes, but that is not the reality we are seeing every day in our schools with our kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: I live in District 14, where kids are required to use one-to-one devices for iReady screeners and for state test prep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: And I just want to quickly share a story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: Last spring, my son came home and told me his class had been playing freaky games at school on their Chromebooks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: He explained that his teacher had sent them to a website when they were finished with their state practice tests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: He used this site for days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: I checked it out myself and I was horrified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: I saw a game called School Fury, where you use various weapons to destroy classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: There was a disgusting surgery simulator with graphic blood and gore content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: There were cam girl games, sexualized games.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shannon Ritchie
utterances.text: The amount of horror, gore, violence, and just garbage on this website was shocking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: I cannot believe that my third grader had full access to this during class time for days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: I immediately emailed the school and asked how this got through the filters, and they did not know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: We cannot blame teachers for this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: I used to teach, and I assure you, there is no safe way to have 30 kids on one-to-one devices, all wearing headphones, especially knowing there are few, if any, guardrails on what they can access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: I asked for my son's internet history, and I was denied access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: But Google, however, has all of this information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: In fact, we pay them to take our kids'data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: Parents have no way of knowing what their children are doing on their Chromebooks at school, and that is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: I have more, but I'll submit it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Turchiano
utterances.text: Oh, please turn on your mic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: There we go.

chapters.summary: A school psychologist testifies that NYC public schools have become data collection centers, devices disrupt natural development of young children, and teachers are not allowed to teach creatively due to Google-based curriculum mandates.
chapters.title: School psychologist testifies on device addiction and need for creative teaching

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm a school psychologist, and I'm here as a collective voice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: You're my assemblyman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I have two minutes to say that New York City public schools, once considered the showcase of education across America, it's become a data collection center rather than an educational institution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And the DOE is exacerbating the students'visual addiction to devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And I have two minutes to say that the ever-changing curricula do not tap into the developing brain of children, especially those in the early grades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And especially with very young children, giving them devices really disrupts the natural development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So, also, I don't have to talk about the money part because we all know where the money is going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: But I should also not have to point out why Google should not be replacing actual teaching.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: You know, things are kind of worse than what we discussed, and I'm kind of going off of my testimony after listening to everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: The situation is a lot grander, you know, because we're talking about little pieces of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: But we should not be discussing how to use technology in the schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We should be discussing creative teaching methods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And the people actually in the schools,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: where nobody is happy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Teachers are also having symptoms from being on devices for too long with their eyes or getting headaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: The teachers are not being allowed to teach creatively and actually teaching based on what their students'needs are because they have to do everything according to what is on Google.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: You know, I run, for the sake of equity, I run an after-school fencing program for my students.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Okay, and pulling them away from the devices when I go to collect them is like, it's mind-boggling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And we feel there should be no technology at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Except AT.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Naomi Sachs, a recent public school graduate, expresses concern about AI exemptions for students with disabilities and English language learners, arguing generative AI is not designed for language learning and could expose vulnerable students to linguistic biases.
chapters.title: Naomi Sachs testifies on AI exemptions for disabled and ELL students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: Hello, can people hear, is my mic, okay, awesome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Naomi Sachs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: I'm a fairly recent public school graduate and I'm just graduating from university now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: And I would like to speak a little bit on the AI Moratorium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: And first of all, I thank you guys, obviously, for all your work in supporting the AI Moratorium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: And I do think that a lot of great work has been done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: I did want to speak a little bit on the exemptions for students with disabilities and also for English language learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: In particular for generative AI, I am concerned that we are, generative AI, as was mentioned earlier by Joann Simons, the right tools for the right job, generative AI is like,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: made for chatting can create languages, but it's not necessarily made designed for language learning and it's definitely not designed necessarily with the intention of like teaching children a language and I do fear that by allowing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: Obviously, it says when necessary in the guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: It's not really clear what necessary entails, but I do fear that we are perhaps

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: like just throwing like more vulnerable students to the winds of AI, to the throes of AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: And these students are going to be more susceptible to picking up like certain linguistic biases from generative AI if they are exposed to it, especially if they are learning it as a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: second language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: I don't believe that there is any need to, I don't believe that there's ever a necessary scenario for generative AI to be used to teach students English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: I believe that, you know, we've already, obviously,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: Humans are imperfect, but we have systems for teaching languages, and we don't need generative AI systems to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: And further, for disabled students, like generative AI, I know Sanchez already mentioned that there are already safeguards, but I really don't think that generative AI, unless there is evidence that it can be used,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: productively should ever really be exposed to disabled students because the further because the harms of AI will further affect them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naomi Sachs
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony and congratulations on graduating.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Our next panel is Molly Senak, Iman Gad.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Tanisha Grant.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Tanisha Grant.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And Jean Moore, uh, Ilan?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You can start.

chapters.summary: Molly Sunak of the Center for Independence of the Disabled New York testifies that the blanket exemption for students with disabilities treats them as immune to screen time risks, calling for assistive technology to be at the center of policy conversations rather than simply exempted.
chapters.title: Molly Sunak of CIDNY testifies on assistive technology and disability exemptions

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: My name is Molly Sunak.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: I am testifying today on behalf of the Center for Independence of the Disabled New York.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: I am their education and employment community organizer.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: Advancements in digital technology have provided critical access for people with disabilities to spaces that were previously far less accessible.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: However, the recently released guidance on AI and screen time clearly acknowledges the risks associated with unlimited access to technology in a learning environment.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: Students with disabilities, however, are among those seemingly categorically excluded from the protections the guidance seeks to provide.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: There is no guidance on the use of AI and screens when it is being used as assistive technology, except to say that it is exempt from the guidance.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: And while the idea of regarding assistive technology as an exception to these rules might seem like a service to our students with disabilities, it instead treats these students as

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: as if they are immune to the risks posed to students without disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: The guidance in its current form provides students with disabilities with fewer protections from the risks of screen time NAI under the guise of providing them with more exemptions from the restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: This is a reflection of a phenomenon that is unfortunately all too common when providing accommodations for people with disabilities, even when the intentions are ultimately good.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: Many people approach accessibility as if there was a switch that could be flipped to make everything accessible for everyone and think the issue merely lies in finding the right switch.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: However, it is never that simple, especially for young students who are still in the earlier stages of learning about their needs.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: Banning all assistive technology regardless of the benefits and allowing all assistive technology regardless of the risks are ultimately two sides of the same coin.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Molly Sunak
utterances.text: I have a lot more detail in my written testimony, but I would just like to stress that assistive technology needs to be at the center of these conversations, not just included.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony and the very important perspective that you offered.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We appreciate it.

chapters.summary: Iman Gad of Girls for Gender Equity urges prioritizing student privacy and safety over tech companies, raises concerns about heightened surveillance disproportionately affecting Black and Brown students, and shares youth demands for data privacy education and consentful tech.
chapters.title: Iman Gad of Girls for Gender Equity testifies on AI surveillance and youth voices

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon, Chair Dinowitz, Chair Krishnan, and members of the Joint Committee.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: My name is Iman, and I'm the Policy Advocacy Manager at Girls for Gender Equity.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: As the Council assesses screen time and the use of digital devices within New York City public schools, we are here today to urge the City to prioritize the education, privacy, and safety of our students over tech profiteering companies by implementing

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: processes that interrogate the impact of technology on students and supporting young people through proven safety infrastructures, such as tech literacy, restorative justice, mental health access, and immigrant protections.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: At a time when technology and AI are moving at an unprecedented pace, assessing the impact and implications of tech in schools is essential to its proper integration.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: School is a place where young people should be free to feel safe, try new things, and learn, but instead the interests of tech companies have bombarded our students with technology tools that have breached their privacy,

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: made their devices more addictive, and taken away the connection and critical thinking skills that are paramount to their education.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: The expansion of AI systems in educational settings also increases the potential for heightened monitoring and surveillance of students, disproportionately affecting black and brown students who are already subject to greater scrutiny in school environments.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: Further, we are particularly concerned with how the surveillance and collection of data can threaten the safety of our immigrant students being targeted by ICE.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: As the DOE looks to implement new tech policies in schools, we call for the inclusion of youth voices to these conversations and decisions.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: Last November, the Alliance on Gender Equity, our youth-led organizing base, held a youth town hall to inform our School Girls Demand campaign.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: A campaign with the purpose of uplifting the voices of young people and empowering them to ask city officials for what they need.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: AI and technology were hot topics in that room of 70 students from schools across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: Students expressed...

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: Expressed grievances that included the need, the needs for best practices for utilizing AI in learning environments, the racial disparities in AI access,

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: education, climate conscious ways to use AI, the desire to learn about data privacy, their digital footprint, and methods to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: As our youth participants reflected on their time and programs, I'll leave you with this quote that they had.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: I feel like another way that I can achieve social justice is telling my friends and family about consentful tech.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: I feel like that's very important to me now that AI is taking over, making sure that we're using apps and devices that ask for consent before they just take the information that we're giving to them.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: I'll submit the rest in my written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Iman Gad
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Tanisha Grant, a mother and grandmother of autistic children, raises concerns about Black and Brown students lacking basic technology access, the environmental dangers of AI data centers, and the need to focus on literacy before introducing AI.
chapters.title: Tanisha Grant testifies on digital equity, literacy, and environmental dangers of AI

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Christman and Chair Denowitz.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: My name is Tanisha Grant.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: I am a mother of three, a grandmother of four.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: All four of my grandchildren are autistic, and I am also the executive director of an organization that you might know called Parents Support and Parents New York.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: Over these last six years, Parents Support in Parents New York has worked diligently to raise money and to use parts of any grants that we receive to provide digital equity.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: We're talking about students using AI, but we're not recognizing that there are still black and brown students that do not have access to technology at all.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: And I'm very shocked to not hear these things come up in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: I'm also shocked to be the first black mother, black organizer to sit at this table and talk about my black children and grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: I'm also an organizer who fought for culturally responsive education and curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: And it's not culturally responsive to talk about black and brown children and not have organizers and black community leaders at the table when we know that black students are disenfranchised in every way.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: Like I said, we believe in digital equity.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: Digital equity is different than AI access.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: While all of our students should have access to digital equity, I also have not heard anyone talk about the environmental dangers of data centers, of AI.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: When I think about all of this, I think about Terminator.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: And a lot of people, you know, we talk about movies all the time, but a lot of fictional movies turn into our very real reality.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: So I agree with AIM, PSPNY will do everything that we can to stand with you all on the facts that, you know,

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: Before we had technology, before we had Brown versus Board, black children had a literacy rate of up to 90%.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: We're not talking about literacy.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: We're not talking about teaching our children to read.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: We're not fixing the problems that we already have before we go on to something that can destroy our children's cognitive thinking, that can...

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: could destroy our environment.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: I need my great-grandchildren to have water to drink and to wash their bodies with and to grow food.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: So I'll leave y'all with all of that and say that I'm looking forward to continuing this fight and the Department of Education explanation on all of this is inadequate.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: At best.

utterances.speaker: Tanesha Grant
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony, all three of you.

chapters.summary: Alma Addy, a high school senior, testifies about the lack of transparency regarding how AI tools track student data, the need for student input in policy development, and concerns about mandated AI tools with negative effects on learning.
chapters.title: Student Alma Addy testifies on AI data privacy concerns and student transparency

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Our next panel is, oh, back to our student panel now.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We have Alma Adi.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Sika Agbokov.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And Ariana Ahmed Misha.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Hello, committee members.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: My name is Alma Addy, and I am a high school senior at Hunter College High School.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I am also here representing New York Civil Liberties Union as part of their Teen Activist Project.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I'm here due to my concern as a student regarding AI and data privacy.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: The current AI policy does not address how AI usage will affect student data sharing and how schools can track students.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: And we as students need more transparency about how our data would be used with hypothetical AI tools, and that must be reflected in the policy.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: With the new policy, there is no section that addresses a key fact about AI.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: At the end of the day, these AI companies are private businesses that collect data.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: National regulations on AI data collection have not been fully developed.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: And there is minimal transparency about what happens to student data when using AI tools, both on a national level, but also what data schools track.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: This is a

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: massive issue for student safety and student privacy.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Although the policy mentions a screening process to check AI tools before being brought to classrooms, the current technology that students use already tracks us.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Most students, me included, do not understand how this tracking works, and that is terrifying, and we don't know how AI will contribute to that.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Ultimately, uncertainty is why I am here.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I attend a school where I have a choice to opt out of AI products.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: But I know that in recent years, my school has forced us to use emails to access school computers.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I don't know what happens when I put my email into these computers, so I opt to use a personal computer.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Well, what happens when my friends at other schools are told to use AI for certain assignments?

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: What happens when a classroom mandates a tool that has proven negative effects?

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Effects on classroom learning and on development.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: This is happening in schools today and students don't know how to seek relief.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I'm worried about the current surveillance of students through technology.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Student input is key when developing this policy, but so is the input of data privacy experts and we must develop a policy that protects students, protects our classrooms, and pushes back on technology surveillance in school.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sika Abuku, a high school student, testifies about AI being used by teachers for grading and lesson planning with errors, persistent student access to AI tools like Gemini despite filters, and concerns about student data being used to train AI models.
chapters.title: Student Sika Abuku testifies on AI exposure and data collection in schools

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Good afternoon, council members.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: My name is Sika Abuku.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: I'm a high school student and member of the NYCLU Teen Activist Project.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: With the new adoption of AI within schools, many things have changed, not just in New York City, but within our state, country, and world.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: I go to Edward R.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Murrow High School, located in Brooklyn, and for me, it impacts my friends, classmates, and even teachers.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: When AI is used by teachers for grading students'work or checking if students use AI, it impacts students'privacy, confidentiality, and education.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: There are multiple AI companies, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc., where students are being exposed and exploited for private data collection.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: This threat becomes bigger when it's integrated within our education.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: From being a part of our online classroom to being attached to our internet searches, even teachers use AI within lesson planning and can present multiple mistakes.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: I have witnessed this personally in school.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: I've seen in my geometry class, for example, many instances in which AI was used to create diagrams and lesson plans and have given the wrong answer.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: This puts schools, teachers, and students'education at risk.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that schools like mine have put in measures to limit AI use, such as web filters to ban AI in schools, but usage is still persistent.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: And I still...

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: have access to Gemini even in class.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Schools have also limited the internet access with the statewide ban across New York State, and it has changed the way students are able to access information.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Now, when we get to the access in internet, with Chromebooks and computers and Google Classroom, we are still exposed.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Our data goes to these companies and is being used to track behavior, interest, and train more AI models.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: This is a growing problem for students and deserves more care and consideration in terms of the impact within internet access, privacy, and the future education of New York City students.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Perfectly timed.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That was amazing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A plus.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You must have practiced.

chapters.summary: Arun Ahmed Misha, a high school junior, testifies about the lack of student consent in AI pilot programs, the fear of losing human connections with teachers and creative aptitude, and the need for student and parent awareness of AI policies.
chapters.title: Student Arun Ahmed Misha testifies on AI concerns and lack of student consent

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: Hello, Chair Dynowitz, Chair Krishna, and everyone present in this room.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: My name is Arun Ahmed Misha.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: I'm a high school junior and a member of the Teen Activist Project at New York Civil Liberties Union.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: After the first AI guidance came out, I gave countless testimonies in different PEP meetings in the city council here and also helped organize meetings to talk about and educate students about artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: I remember how excited I was waking up in the morning seeing that Mayor Mamdani banned artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: See the vaguely interpreted post?

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: Super excited me instantly reposted that on my social media, only to find out that that was not for us high schoolers.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: It almost felt like we were not important enough to be protected.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: When I read the details, I see that as students, we do not have the chance to consent to the decision.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: made for us.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: If my principal signs up to be a pilot school where products will be tested on us, I do not get to consent and I do not get to refuse to participate.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: Most students do not even know how this policy even works and this policy was even announced.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: It seems like the city is busy in implementing a system that will require high school students to lose human connections with our teachers, to lose their creative aptitude, and to make it seem normal that everything we do in school should be monitored and fed into the artificial intelligence system.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: While the Dewey says that AI will not replace teacher, the people who sells this product says the complete opposite.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: The possibility of losing the teacher whom I think to be taught

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: whom I think to be the torchbearer of my life, the possibility of losing the creativity, which I think made human history incredible, the possibility of students losing attention abilities, which I think

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: harm us all, just by a single policy is the terror that concerns me and thousands of other students.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: When a student reads the news and sees technology companies says that AI is a risk to humanity, what is the role of schools to teach us how to understand it?

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: Our ability to think and ability to have the human connection must remain the future of education.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks students about their access to Gemini on school accounts, what balance they think is appropriate for AI in schools, and what they need from DOE to feel safe in pilot programs. Students emphasize the need for transparency, parental consent, and AI literacy.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions students on AI access and appropriate balance in schools

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I have a question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: First of all, you access Gemini today on your student account?

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Yeah, in the library.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I just want to share for the public that we've heard mixed, or I've heard mixed,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: mixed things about what students have access to on their own accounts.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I myself went to a school yesterday and had access to Gemini and it also popped up on the Google search.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So thank you for sharing that, that it's not just me, that students who have come here still have access to that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to ask a question though, you know, we hear a lot of

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: like the tech companies and even the DOE say, we recognize the concerns around AI, but we also recognize that companies

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: now in many cases require the use of AI, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That is, let's call it a reality of business these days.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What do you all think is the right balance, if any, of including AI in schools at all or recognizing its use in post-high school, post-college?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you think at all, and in what situations there would or would not be a place for it?

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Oh, great.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Honestly, for me, I'm not sure what the best balance is to strike between AI education in schools and full AI bans.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I do know that AI literacy is an extremely important thing, both for the workplace, but also so that we understand how to use those tools responsibly.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: But at the end of the day, this policy is still very vague, and we don't know how AI could be implemented in schools.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: The policy itself says it's school and course dependent.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: So we don't know to what extent we're going to have to use AI or to what extent AI will be integrated into all aspects of learning.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: So it's important to have AI literacy, but the idea of AI being ingrained into every aspect of our education is worrying.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: And also adding on to that, to be really very honest, this entire artificial intelligence or people were exposed to this AI thing only some years ago.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: I would say even two years ago, people barely knew about AI, but so early, such a, such a, such a,

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: I would say recently known stuff coming into the educational system or everything that is surrounded by us is really very scary.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: And also the students whom I talk to most of the time, most of the students don't even know that this even exists and this should be in the work.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: And if this comes up, that's going to be really very hazardous for every single student.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: And the word hazardous is going to be used here because that's going to impact in many ways.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: many different ways in the case of their thinking, creative thinking, in the case of also what they're going to do in the future, and every other thing we could possibly think.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: And also environment, which is also getting highly at risk due to all these policies.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And if there was, I mean, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Yeah, I was going to add on and say, like, I also don't think there's, like, a perfect balance because I feel like in certain subjects, like when I mentioned my geometry class, AI was used to, like, perform diagrams, and they would, like, give you the answer choice, and it was wrong.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: But for many other instances where it was used, like, it was right.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: I think it would be easier for teachers to use it, but then again, it's still going to be integrated into children and, like, I don't know, teenagers.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: And we're learning, like, the basics right now.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Like, we're not in college.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: We're not in university.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: So this is, like, our basics of learning.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: And I feel like the more we integrate it into our lives, the more it becomes more personal for us.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: It's not just at school, but at home.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: And I think it also, like, should be applied to, like, what if, like, students are using it for emotional support?

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Because, like, of course, like, you know, AI can be used to, like, I don't know, support students.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: But it can also, like, have, like, deep emotional connections where students are forming, I don't know, relationships with AI.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: And then when that happens, if, like, a student is struggling with their mental health, then, like, at what point is it to say, like, this is, like, a road?

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: robot and like at what point is like their mental health like at risk when chatting with robots that are just using their information to help the next robot yeah um you guys have given a number of reasons

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: i think i with which i agree with about the harms of ai uh you have the doe here and you're in a public

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: setting.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Alma, you mentioned like, you know, schools could be signing up for this and you wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And then, oh, okay, you're scheduled for this course.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to ask each of you, it's the same question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If your school signs up for it, right, and you are placed in this class, what is one most important thing that you need from the DOE

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: in order to feel comfortable or safe or educated in a school that engaged in this pilot?

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I think for me, first of all, I'm going to say context.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: My school is under the CUNY system.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I go to Hunter College High School, so this isn't the same thing for me specifically.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Heard good things about CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I love CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: I love it so much.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: But if I had to take a class that integrated AI, I'd want to be able to check the DOE website and know this AI tool is being used and this was the exact process that it was screened.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: This is where my data is going.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: This is what schools are tracking.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: And this is what these AI companies are keeping track of.

utterances.speaker: Alma Addy
utterances.text: Beyond that, I don't feel comfortable using these AI tools.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: And hopefully that never happens.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: That's the first ever thing.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: But before that, actually our parents should have the consent.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: My parents or any other parents, they barely knows about this entire policy, how that works, how this is working.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: Even there's this matter that is going on.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: The more mature population are also having a hard time identifying what's the difference between AI and the real pictures and different other things.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: But the fact that these kind of things are going to be implemented in educational system, there should be a necessity to ask our parents because it's also important that our parents'voices are being heard.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: Our voices are also necessary to be heard because at the end of the day, these decisions are going to be made for us and we are going to be experiencing them.

utterances.speaker: Arun Ahmed Misha
utterances.text: So it's really very important that our parents and we also know that what is actually going on and we are aware of all the situations.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: Yeah, I absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: I think like my parents or like parents in general, they don't understand the full extent of AI.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: I think because like, I don't know, younger people are more exposed to the internet or use it more.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: I feel like they don't get like to what extent like it would be implemented into our classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: So like if my school like signed us up for like a, I don't know, an AI talk course or whatever, I would feel like kind of like exposed in a way because when I'm taking tests, like when I'm like getting my grades, like, you know, AI is going to track that.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: And then what if an AI company that my school signed up with uses it for another AI company?

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: It's just like, I don't know, supporting capitalism in a way.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: It's kind of like using information, like student private information, like the grades that you get to like, I don't know, like be put into other places that go to the higher ups, you know?

utterances.speaker: Sika Abuku
utterances.text: So I think just getting parents more involved in like how their children are being exposed to AI.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No, I want to thank this panel, and I know the deal we heard exactly what you said.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it's certainly aligned with what these committees are interested in, which is accountability and transparency and, of course, parental involvement and empowerment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I just want to add, too, thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Your testimony today, your answers to the questions just show how critically you're thinking about these issues and gives me a lot of hope that we can solve these problems with you all on the front lines doing the work and leading the way.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Great job today, too.

chapters.summary: Hilary Kong, a parent, describes her daughter using an AI reading tutor in first grade, digital math games and art benchmarks on devices, and the lack of meaningful parent engagement in technology policy decisions at her school.
chapters.title: Hilary Kong testifies on AI tutors, digital benchmarks, and lack of parent voice

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Our next panel is Hilary Kong, Celeste Elias, Ethan Sachs, and Adriana Alicia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Hillary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: I'm a parent of a five and an eight year old, and the examples I'm giving today is from a school that my children no longer go to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: My daughter read with an AI tutor in first grade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Our admin explained that Amira was DOE vetted and approved, and my daughter was put to use it because she finished her reading curriculum early.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: A few weeks later, a flyer for a digital math game came home in my child's backpack.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: It says, research shows that love of math and test scores increase with more time spent on this app.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Digital art apparently is also one of the DOE benchmarks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Art, math, reading are all ending

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: up on a device.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Who created these benchmarks?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Who from the DOE does this research?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Just saying research shows tells us nothing about who funded and completed the research, what was studied, the effect size, what we should or could interpret from this research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: I've also learned of an over-prioritization on scores and testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Students are reading less books.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: These online tests are designed to have students read short excerpts, and we wonder why our kids don't have the stamina to read full books anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Tests on a screen forces a child's brain to handle two things at once, figuring out the test questions and navigating the computer program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Young children should focus on the material, the work, the learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: We need to bring back tests on paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Lastly, there was no place for conversations over technology policies to happen at our school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: When parents asked questions, we were told that we don't trust our teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: We were invited to join a working group that happened monthly and painfully in the evenings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Many parents thought it was a way to drown out the voices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: A smaller steering committee also formed that strategically excluded

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: those who had a strong or educated opinion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: I urge our city to make good choices about who we trust to make decisions about the safety and the future of our children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Who forms the technology coalition?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Do they have a material stake in the outcome?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Because the parents, educators, and students here advocating

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Our stakes are ethical, mental, and environmental.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Celeste Elias, a kindergarten parent, describes being unable to refuse iPads or iReady assessments despite privacy lawsuits, receiving no response from administrators, and discovering her child was given access to scary TikToks on a teacher's personal phone in pre-K.
chapters.title: Celeste Elias testifies on inability to refuse iPads and iReady assessments

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Celeste.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I'm a kindergarten parent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I emailed the school at the start of the summer about my objections to one-to-one iPads and hours-long iReady assessments, of which are exempt from the current screen time bans for lower elementary grades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: IReady is currently being sued for deceptive marketing and data privacy violations, but I was still told I couldn't refuse an iPad or iReady assessments, nor could I request a paper alternative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: The principal explained iPads are only used for a short time, but refusing one is impossible to integrate it into daily curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: She didn't see the contradiction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: The school and district did not provide anything in writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I emailed Paulo Perdomo a face on August 6th and 27th requesting support and to see written policies governing parent refusal of assessments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I received no response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I sent a letter of religious exemption for all devices and assessments to the superintendent and principal on August 28th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I received no response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: The new policies do not address the DOE's failure to protect student data privacy as exposed in the state's audit and the power school data breaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: Nor does it clear up parental rights to choose when children are introduced to devices or the internet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: In pre-K, a teacher gave my child her personal phone to play games at nap time and access social media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: He said he was watching scary TikToks about skinwalkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: She admitted to giving him her personal phone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I did not feel my concerns were taken seriously by the school admin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I emailed the superintendent and again received no response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: A mother spoke at a pep meeting stating sexual content and a website to make weapons were fully accessible on her child's school device.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: She received no resolution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: So why should I trust the district or city to protect my child when he's again given a device against my wishes?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I know firsthand what a complete failure devices are because I was issued an iPad as a student.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: We consistently got around safety restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: Utah State Audit found 52% of school apps violated data privacy agreements, and 36% of those shared student data with ad companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: Is this data harvesting of our kids lawful and ethical?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: The only ethical and democratic solution is for schools to implement opt-in policies and obtain informed revocable parental consent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: There is no reason to give children access to the internet or a device outside of a tech class other than to let companies profit off and test products on our children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Celeste Elias
utterances.text: I did not consent for my child to be part of an ed tech experiment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hilary Kong
utterances.text: Can you hear me okay?

chapters.summary: Ethan Sachs, a comic book writer and NYC public school parent, describes how AI could replace the kind of hands-on journalism project that sparked his career, warning that artificial intelligence is counterfeit and the urgency to adopt it comes from companies seeking profit.
chapters.title: Ethan Sachs testifies on AI threatening intellectual curiosity and creative learning

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: Well, first of all, thank you for taking the time today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: Humans listening to humans is essential for democracy and for a healthy society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: And the rise of some of these technologies is probably one of the reasons why we're where we are as a larger society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: My name is Ethan Sachs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: I'm a former journalist turned comic book writer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: And more to the point, I'm an alum of the New York public school system and the father of a much, much, much more recent graduate of the New York public school system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: Much of the course of my professional life was sparked by several teachers who instilled in me a love of writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: And as a student in high school, because I think high schools are very susceptible even after this ban,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: I worked, I had a high school journalism class that was incredibly influential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: I worked with a group on a project to make a newspaper, and my contribution was an article on safety at rock concerts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: I was really, I had more hair back then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
