utterances.text: And I got to go to clubs like CBGB's, may it rest in peace, and the garden, Madison Square Garden, and talk to heads of security and really get this sort of backstage tour of what it was like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: And I discovered the power of reporting and doing all this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: Nowadays, that kind of project could be given to this type of technology that would,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: basically put in a prompt and it would do all its work for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: And then what, where does that intellectual curiosity go?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: It's just snuffed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: And so I worry about future generations having access to the kind of thing that changed my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: You know, I think artificial intelligence is the perfect name.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: It's spurious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: It's inauthentic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: It's counterfeit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: And I think what's most...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: What's most artificial is the sense of urgency at adopting this technology, and that comes from the companies themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: And they've shown that it's not about societal benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: Certainly, you can see that in the environmental consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: It's about money, and so it's up to us to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: To not make those decisions based on money.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You should be a proud parent, too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Sachs
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Our next panel is Biada Safari, Kate Mulvaney, Greg Pack, and Crystal Clevin.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And if there's anyone here who wants to testify who has not been called yet, please let the sergeant at arms know.

chapters.summary: Crystal Cleven, a physician scientist and parent, describes the 'screen inferiority effect' showing screens lead to poorer reading comprehension, shares research on preschoolers read to by screens showing ADHD-like EEG findings, and reports parents saying children already watched YouTube in school this week.
chapters.title: Crystal Cleven testifies on screen inferiority effect and smart screen concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Crystal Cleven and I'm a mother of two young kids in the New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: While touring 4K programs, I had a vision of kids sitting in a circle being read to by a teacher with a real book.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: Instead, I repeatedly saw these kids staring up at a smart screen, a robotic voice emanating from the screen reading to kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: While these normally curious and eager three to four year olds were not engaged with the text, the teacher, or each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: I'm a physician scientist, so naturally I dug into the data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: There are extensive high quality studies that demonstrate something called the screen inferiority effect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: Which is the phenomenon that learning on screens leads to poorer reading comprehension, language acquisition, and shallower processing of information than when you do it on paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: One study of preschoolers showed children who were read to by a screen performed significantly worse

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: on attention tests and had EEG findings similar to those with ADHD compared to those who are read to by an adult with a book.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: Yet our youngest kids have some of their first and only book exposures delivered by a screen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: By age five, there is a one million word exposure gap between children who are read to daily and those who are not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: New York City public schools should be racing to close that gap using real books.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: Even screen-based brain breaks or movement breaks used heavily in schools are simply a short form overstimulating videos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: Several studies have shown they worsen attention, self-control, and negatively impact memory and decision making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: We've been in school for four days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: I've had dozens of parents tell me their children, young children, have already watched YouTube in school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: The current non-educational videos, to be clear, the current guidelines are not strong enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: They do not talk about smart screens at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: And we are asking elective officials at the city and state level to implement stronger

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: laws, and enforceable guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Crystal Cleven
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And we'll add two more people to the panel, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Alina Lewis and Jean-Marc Apelon.

chapters.summary: Kate Mulvaney, a parent, demonstrates that YouTube is still accessible on her son's school-issued iPad, describes searching for explicit and violent content that was not blocked, and criticizes the extensive exemptions in the new DOE guidance.
chapters.title: Kate Mulvaney testifies on accessing inappropriate content on school-issued iPad

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Kate Mulvaney and I have a second grader in a DOE school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: And first, I literally access YouTube on my son's school-issued device this afternoon, and anyone who's interested can take a look, I have it right here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Earlier this year, my first, then first grader, told me that he watched Lego Batman in class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Surprised, I asked him how he did so, and he told me he did it on a school-issued iPad, and oh, by the way, he also read about kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: This was around the time of the incident with Savannah Guthrie's mother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: This started my inquiry into what is going on with this device that he was issued in kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: To start, I privately searched, which in and of itself should not be an option for school-aged children on school-issued devices, for some basic terms such as, excuse me, sex, porn, AR-15, beheading, and boobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: And I got the following, some of which I've submitted images of online as part of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: How to Have Sex Like a Porn Star, a Masterclass with Sylvia Sage, Top 5 Most Popular Porn Stars of the 80s, Lots of Stuff About Overcoming Your Porn Addiction, Swingers, a short film, Boy Love, a short film,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: How an AR-15 Works, Lots of Photos and Information About Breast Implants, and Punishment Around the World.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Additionally, I was also able to access the Anarchist Cookbook, which teaches a person how to make various types of bombs, mace, and Molotov cocktails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Even aside from the content, there is simply too much screen use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: If it isn't devices being used to read to our children, videos incorporated into the curriculum to teach them math, and YouTube videos, interviews shown of celebrities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: discussing things like perseverance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: It is smart boards in places like the gymnasium, movies being shown during indoor recess, and Danny Go brain breaks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: When I lamented to my son that he watched a video in math class, he said, but mama, how are the teachers going to know how to teach us if they don't watch the video?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: I'm not sure the new DOE guidance will make that much of a difference when the majority of screen use is exempted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Not only is it built into instruction, it's baked into both city assessments and state tests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Even test prep relies on interfacing with screens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: The issue of one-to-one devices and screen time is not only for those in second grade and below.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: It is a problem for all students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: None of them should be accessing this content or spending this much time in front of any type of screen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony and these shocking examples, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: They really, I think, highlight the holes in the policy and the holes in the oversight from DOE.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So we appreciate that very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kate Mulvaney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Greg Pak, a comic book writer and organizer, criticizes AI pilot programs for using chatbots to give writing feedback, questions whether pilots use databases from major AI corporations, and argues every student should be required to opt in rather than being enrolled automatically.
chapters.title: Greg Pak testifies on AI pilot loopholes and need for opt-in consent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Greg Pak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: I'm a comic book writer, and I organize with Comics Action and the AIM Moratorium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: And I hate consumer-facing AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: So I very much appreciate both of the chairs for asking pointed questions about the pilot programs in particular that the DOE is opening up for high school students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: I've got some other questions, which I would hope you would continue to ask them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: There's a huge loophole with these.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Supposedly, teachers are not supposed to use AI for assessment, but these pilot programs, or grading, but these pilot programs absolutely seem to be using AI for feedback.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: I took a look at the BRISC pilot program online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: And I saw promotional videos which showed kids tapping into computers, talking to chatbots, which were touted as giving them immediate feedback on their writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: I'm a writer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: I think that's one of the worst things I can imagine, to have a chatbot trying to tell me how to write while I'm writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Writing is about process, about thinking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: A chatbot that writes horribly, because we've all seen AI writing, we know it's garbage, shouldn't be used for those kinds of purposes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Ask about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Ask about if the databases of these chatbots are fueled by open AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Do they push, do they use the same databases that are clogged with racism and sexism and all the bad things?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Are they using those from the major AI corporations?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: We don't know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Are they pushing teachers to use AI from chat GPT and all those kinds of things?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: We've seen that some of the brisk supposedly touts its integration with chat GPT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Can kids opt out more to the point every kid should be required to opt into these programs?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: That's the consent you were talking about, Chair Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: I totally agree with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Then regarding the AI literacy programs, who's developing these AI literacy programs?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Every AI literacy program I've seen has been influenced by industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: AI literacy should include AI quitteracy, which is information on how every kid, every person can opt out of AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Teach kids how to not use AI-inflected search.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Teach kids not how to de-

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Remove AI from their devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: Kids should not be guinea pigs used by the industry to test their products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: 50,000 kids in New York City could be signed up for these programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: We know how bad AI is for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: They should not be used as guinea pigs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Pak
utterances.text: And thank you.

chapters.summary: Beata Safari of the NYC Bar Association's Technology Committee raises questions about who tracks cumulative screen time across multiple teachers, the gap between school and home screen time limits, and whether remote learning requirements conflict with banning home devices.
chapters.title: Beata Safari of NYC Bar Association testifies on screen time tracking and homework gaps

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: Good afternoon, chairs and members of the committees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: My name is Beata Safari, and I'm secretary of the New York City Bar Association's Technology, Cyber, and Privacy Law Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: We are grateful that the city is taking a careful approach to AI and technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: As the proud daughter of a public high school music teacher, I particularly appreciate this opportunity to speak with you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: One-to-one screen time is defined as the cumulative amount of time a student directly interacts with a computer or a tablet, presumably during the regular instructional school day, regardless of the subject or the teacher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: Since there's no guidance on what subject matter or teacher should be assigning the screen time, it appears that schools are tasked with establishing a method for monitoring and doling out the cumulative student exposure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: Since these screen times are recommended, or somewhat required, according to the testimony today, are teachers being given relative autonomy to decide when to offer that time in the classroom?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: According to reporting from the Daily News earlier this week, Chancellor Kamar Samuels told reporters that these daily limits should be a, quote,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: guide post.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: The idea is, what's the spirit of reducing screen time?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: End quote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: Chancellor Samuel's point doesn't directly answer the question about who should be responsible for tracking the time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: Additionally, while teachers may still be following the spirit of the policy even if they go over or under on certain days, even if students are limited in screen time at school, there is no such prohibition on the amount of screen time students are permitted at home,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: as First Deputy Chancellor has testified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: So this is another gap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: The policy directly regulates only school-controlled screen time, but not screen-based homework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: For grades 3 through 8, that's potentially significant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: A school could conceivably comply with the in-school recommendation while assigning substantial digital homework every night, which would be contrary to the heart of the guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: Chairs, you mentioned wanting to ban one-to-one devices at home as well for K-5.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: How is this possible if remote learning is required?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: So I think you should also be thinking about and discussing whether you should only have snow days and do away with weather-related remote working and homework as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beata Safari
utterances.text: Thanks so much.

chapters.summary: Jean-Marc Apollon of the NYC Bar Association argues a complete ban on AI for grading may create 'shadow AI' problems, and recommends a limited pilot program where AI recommends and teachers decide, with careful measurement of results and bias.
chapters.title: Jean-Marc Apollon of NYC Bar Association testifies on AI-assisted grading pilot proposal

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Good afternoon, chairs and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: My name is Jean-Marc Apollon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: I'm the co-chair of the New York City Bar Association's Technology, Cyber, and Privacy Law Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: We appreciate that New York City Public Schools is taking a careful approach to artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: AI present real concerns, including bias, inaccurate information, and student privacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: But we believe the current complete ban recommended by the guidance on artificial intelligence and screen time on teachers using AI for grading goes too far.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: On one hand, a complete ban can create a different problem, shadow AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: AI is becoming part of everyday life and work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: If teachers find these tools useful but are told they cannot use them, some may turn to their own personal and unapproved AI systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: That could mean student work or personal information being entered into systems that the city has not reviewed and cannot oversee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: On the other hand, we do not want the opposite extreme either.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Teachers should not remove themselves from the process and let AI grade students or run the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Teachers know their students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: They understand context that an AI system may not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: They should remain responsible for every final grading decision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: NIDR Extreme is the solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: The goal should not be to introduce AI simply because the technology exists, and the goal should not be to prohibit AI simply because the technology presents risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: The goal should be better education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: That is why we recommend a limited pilot program for AI-assisted grading.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: The basic rules should be simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: AI recommends, teachers decide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Start small, select a limited number of schools and teachers, use only AI tools that have been reviewed and approved by the city, then measure the results.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Did teachers save time?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Did students receive better feedback?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Were grades more consistent?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Did the technology treat different groups of students differently?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: How often did teachers disagree with AI?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: And most importantly, did it improve the educational process?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: New York City has an opportunity to show that protecting students and embracing innovation are not opposing goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: We can protect student privacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: We can address bias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: We can keep teachers in control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: And we can still explore whether new technology can improve education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: We should not make decisions based on fear of AI or excitement about AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: We should test it, measure it, and build the policy based on what the evidence tells us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: also reflects both of the co-chairs' opinion of having evidence-based policies and not just emotional or reactive policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean-Marc Apollon
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Alina Lewis, a former DOE teacher and assistant principal, criticizes Amira and iReady as hoaxes on NYC public schools, argues literacy is socially embedded, and refuses to accept that public school students are denied real learning while private school students get play and no screens.
chapters.title: Alina Lewis testifies on ed tech as a hoax and need for real learning

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: Hi, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: My name is Alina Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: I'm a public school parent, New York City public school alum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: I was a DOE high school history teacher and assistant principal in the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: I teach teachers at CUNY in the teacher prep program, and I'm an ed researcher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: Thank you so much for holding these hearings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: And this policy, I am encouraged by the fact that it has opened a very necessary conversation about big tech, ed tech, and our public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: I've seen the shift toward commercial products and large ed tech contrasts in the last 10 to 15 years, and how gradually screen time and the use of all these products and scripted curriculum has increased.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: I'm glad you mentioned evidence-based practices because all the research shows that screens are bad for kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: Research also shows that play, recess, and opportunities for authentic learning experience are effective and good for kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: In other school contexts, educators have been guided by this research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: And in fact, of course, in the most sought after private schools where all the Silicon Valley execs and their kids, they have play and recess and no screens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: But in New York City public schools,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: things look different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: We have a Mira, a bot that reads to kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: Literacy is fundamentally a socially embedded act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: How have we come to this idea that it is good and that is helpful and good to have a bot read to kids?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: We have our kids wasting colossal amounts of time on iReady, which is the biggest hoax that has been played on the New York City public schools in a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: And of course, we have our kids reading snippets of books instead of real books on screens for HMH.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: I refuse to accept the fact that New York City public school students are going to be denied real learning opportunities while the kids of the big tech companies and the tech execs get to play and explore and inquire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Lewis
utterances.text: And thank you for listening.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I agree with you more.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you to this entire panel for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Despen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And while we're transitioning, I do want to plug that the City Council allocates millions of dollars each year to a program called Cities First Readers, which in reference to something we heard more than once,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: it empowers parents and children as young as zero, zero to five, I think, to engage in community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And where they do reading and literacy work, not just for the kids, but with the family, recognizing that literacy and reading

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: is a social, is something that's social and part of our community, not just something that's read to you by a computer.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now we're moving to online testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We have several witnesses online.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: First up is Deepthi Sharma, followed by Kayla Spence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Deepthi Sharma, a parent and tech entrepreneur, testifies about the contradiction of schools promoting reading while assigning screen-based homework, uncurated YouTube access on school devices, and urges treating screen time as a question of use rather than just policy.
chapters.title: Deepthi Sharma testifies on contradictions in screen time policy and uncurated access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: Good afternoon, almost good evening now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: Chairman Dinowitz and Krishnan, thank you for hosting this and members of the committees on education and oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: My name is Deepthi Sharma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: I'm a Queens native, daughter of immigrants, mother of two sons, raising them in New York City public schools in third and fifth grade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: I'm also a serial entrepreneur of two tech companies, a board member at Brooklyn Tech, my alma mater, and I teach entrepreneurship at Barnard College.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: But today I'm here as a parent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: I don't think we've been asking the right question about screening time in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: We spent a lot of energy on access and who has it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: And I know we've been harping on what happened in 2020.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: Right now, my sons can turn on YouTube and end up anywhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: I think we've been hearing it all afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: It's not curated, it's not tracked, and no one is accountable for what it leads to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: I've heard all the things that my kids have been watching, and it's extremely disheartening and inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: It's not just at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: In their after-school programs, kids are handed devices and left on them with no real structure around what they're watching or why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: What frustrates me the most is the contradiction, the same system that tells parents to get their kids reading.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: More is, you know, the one that is putting them on and in front of screens for them to complete homework, to do remote assignments, to fill instructional time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: Their assessments and testing is also all done primarily on screens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: And earlier this year, when my son was supposed to be taking his test, they were all delayed and canceled because of the technology they were supposed to be using.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: But real learning doesn't really happen by staring at a screen alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: I think we all know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: It happens when kids are talking to each other, opening an actual book, going to the library, researching something because they're curious about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: We're quietly replacing that kind of learning with passive screen time and it's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: you know, being called instruction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: So my ask to this committee is to simply just stop treating screen time as a policy, but as a question, you know, of like, what is it actually doing to our kids and start treating it as a question of use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: That means really- Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: Time has expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: Content kids can actually watch on school issued and school facilitated devices and not just open access to YouTube and all the games that exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: My kids actually have a running document with their friends where they share.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: Got about five seconds left.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: And it means protecting them from screen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deepthi Sharma
utterances.text: So thank you for holding this hearing and for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thanks so much, Deepthi.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Next, we have Kayla Spence.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Kayla Spence of CEC District 30 calls for mandates rather than recommendations, criticizes the policy's many carve-outs, questions parent representation in the technology coalition, and urges buying books and hiring librarians instead of ed tech.
chapters.title: Kayla Spence of CEC District 30 testifies on need for mandates not recommendations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Hi, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: My name is Kayla Spence, and I am a parent and a member of Community Education Council for District 30.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: I have to ask, what is the spirit of this policy?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Because if we say that there's a limit, and then there's carve-outs for assessments and homework, screeners, instructional programs, and we go on and on, what's the point of a limit?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: At what point does the exception become the rule?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: CECs like mine across New York City have called for a mandate, not recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: We want clear protections and meaningful limits that every child can count on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Instead, this guidance was released just days before school started without a clear implementation plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Principals, teachers, superintendents, and families have more questions than answers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: What counts towards a limit?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: What doesn't?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Who's enforcing it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: What happens when a school doesn't follow it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: And more importantly, where are parents in this process?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: If New York City Public Schools is building a coalition around technology and screen time, CECs and parent leaders need to be meaningfully represented at the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: How many parents are in this coalition?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: How many classroom teachers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: How were they selected?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: These decisions affect our children every day, and parents should not be brought in after the fact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: As a parent, I also want to know what programs and platforms my child's using, why they're using them, and how long they're using them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: If there is a reasonable on-screen time alternative, why can't I opt out of a routine one-to-one device use?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: The amount of money being spent on educational technology, products, platforms, and device is mind-boggling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Who's asking for all of this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: When I was a kid, I had books.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: We wrote on paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: We covered our textbooks with brown paper bags.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: We went outside for recess and we played.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: We learned from our teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Why can't my kid be a kid?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: I'm not anti-technology, but technology should be a tool and not the default.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: We have limited education dollars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Buy books.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Hire librarians.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Invest in teachers and classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Our children deserve clear protections, not vague recommendations and endless exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Please give us a policy that can be enforced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Please include parents in the process.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kayla Spence
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Next up is Larissa May.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Larissa May, founder of Half the Story, argues bans are a starting line but not the full answer, describes a five-part framework for student digital wellness including phone-free spaces, digital wellness curriculum, student role in policy design, and bringing back pencil and paper.
chapters.title: Larissa May of Half the Story testifies on digital wellness framework for students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Thank you, committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: My name is Larissa May.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: 12 years ago, I founded Half the Story, which is the first youth-led nonprofit with the mission of empowering young people to build healthier relationships with technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Today, I'm here representing the one million students, and I'm happy there were some teens here today, in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: As many mentioned today, there are so many young people that are not represented in this room that are going to be left behind at this defining moment for children, technology, and humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Digital wellness is not a trend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: It's a public health issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: As AI accelerates, protecting kids can't just mean limiting screens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: We also have to protect the things that help them flourish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Last year, as the phone-free school policies were put forth, and this year with the recent AI ban, I'm seeing a gap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Bans are the starting line, but they aren't the full answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: If we take something away without giving kids something meaningful to move forward, we don't create flourishing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Last year, we worked with Governor Hochul to create a teen tech council across the state where we trained teen leaders to lead digital wellness efforts in their school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: We as an organization also raised $300,000 to bring these youth leaders funding to create innovations that would transform human connection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: A student, Jack, transformed the study hall into a phone-free craft space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Caden in the Bronx created a digital wellness day to reteach his peers about what it means to be a human in Connect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: I believe that New York City needs a five-part framework for young people to flourish, to pair phone-free policies with spaces for kids to relearn how to be human, to teach digital wellness in every classroom,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: to give students a real role in policy design, and to partner with admin and leaders so that they can empower their peers in the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: And lastly, to bring back the pencil and paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Digital wellness is wellness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Larissa May
utterances.text: Technology is the human consciousness.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Kelly Clancy, a parent and PhD who has served on institutional review boards, argues no IRB would approve the AI pilots as designed because minors cannot meaningfully consent or withdraw, and no demonstrated benefit to children has been articulated.
chapters.title: Kelly Clancy testifies on IRB concerns with AI pilot ethics and consent

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Now we have Kelly Clancy.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: Thanks for having me today and staying so late.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: My name is Kelly Clancy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: I have three kids in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: I'm on CEC for District 20, part of the AIM Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: And I've been thinking about what I could say that's different from what all of my friends and colleagues have said tonight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: One thing I'll just tell you is my son can access ChatGPT on his school-issued account right now, so all of the blocking's not going great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: The other thing I just wanted to talk about is I have a PhD in political science.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: I've sat on institutional review boards that have reviewed research for ethics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: And I wanted to tell you that I don't think that there is an IRB in the United States that would approve the pilots as they're being designed right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kelly Clancy
utterances.text: And I have a huge concern about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So when IRBs consider research designs, one of the things that they consider is whether a vulnerable population is affected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So whether or not you can meaningfully say no, whether or not you can meaningfully give your consent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Minors are part of that group, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And all of these kids are being opted into something without their consent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so they're not given the right to meaningfully withdraw consent in a way that would be consistent with what an IRB would approve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I have a huge concern about the fact that all of these 50,000 kids, and what we've seen across New York City already, is that AI is deployed in places where there are vulnerable populations, will not be able to meaningfully give informed consent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The other thing that has to be true before research is approved is that there has to be a meaningful benefit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And when I was listening very carefully to Lara Lai talk about how we chose these programs, one thing that no one said was they were chosen because they might have a benefit to kids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our kids are going to help them improve their product and improve the fact that they make money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But no one said that these programs have ever been shown to be better for kids than a human teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so at that point, no IRB in the country would ever approve something that had clear, demonstrable harm to kids and their learning effects and also had no benefit that was being articulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so until there's a world where kids can meaningfully opt into these programs, not to be soon enrolled, this should not be something that is allowed in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Kelly.

chapters.summary: Olympia Kazi, a parent and organizer of a District 6 screen break, calls for a complete screen ban from 8th grade and below, screen-free days for older students, and criticizes DOE representatives for lacking sense of what happens in actual classrooms.
chapters.title: Olympia Kazi testifies on need for complete screen ban and screen-free days

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Final witness on Zoom is Olympia Kazi.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Maybe you can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: You saved the best for last, right, guys?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: I want to thank you for this hearing and for all your advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: My name is Olympia Kazi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: I'm the parent of a fourth and a sixth grader, and I am the organizer of the screen break that took place last year at District 6.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: Listening today to the testimonies, we see that everybody, including DOE, agrees that we have a problem, that it is worsening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: And yet, they're doing nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: Like everybody else said, the emperor is naked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: These screen limits are going to limit nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: They're not going to be implementable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: How are they going to be implementable when they have multiple teachers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: What if the previous person saw a little bit of a video?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: Are they going to be timing this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: This is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: So what I believe we should be doing is we need to have a complete ban from 8 through 5.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: And from May to 12, we should take a page from the pilot that is run for the second year in North Carolina at Granville's County and have entire days blocked out as screen-free days, tech-free days, Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, etc., depending on the age and the appropriateness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: We need to rethink, obviously, all the testing and all the screeners because they're really meaningless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: Let's be honest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: Talk to the real teachers to understand that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: What's striking most, though, today, guys, is that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: DOE doesn't seem to have, the reps had no sense of what is happening in the actual classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: So during screen break that we engaged 38 schools, over 10,000 students in District 6, we saw exactly what was playing out in the classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: We saw, for example, that some younger teachers didn't know how to go screen free in order to educate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: We saw that expeditionary learning didn't allow to go screen free, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: And now we even have mandatory IR ready for math in many cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: I would ask the O.E.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: At a minimum to call Superintendent Martinez, who works for them, and ask him what happened in the schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: Because, or the, I mean, I don't tell them to call me because after what I said today, maybe they don't want to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: But they should talk with their employee because there is some knowledge they should be using.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: Thank you again for everything that you're doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: Excellent questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olympia Kazi
utterances.text: And, you know, thank you for your focus.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We appreciate it very much.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz reads the names of witnesses who registered but did not appear, thanks all participants and council staff, and officially closes the hearing.
chapters.title: Dinowitz reads names of registered but absent witnesses and closes hearing

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That concludes our hearing for today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're going to read the names of some people who register, but do not appear to be here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Jennifer Weber.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Adriana Alicia, Alexis Kalyanides, Lisa Walker, Kyle Ems, Jansen Ogilvie, Nadia Saeed, Brian Romero, Kenny Lai, Matthew Gable, Chowdhury Hassan Mahmood,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Mariela Benavides.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: With that, I think we can close out today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Everyone who's here, Councilmember Wong, all of our teams from the council that are here, thank you for an excellent hearing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This hearing is now closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Good job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I give the last word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, co-chair.

summary: Joint oversight hearing of the Committee on Oversight and Investigations and the Committee on Education examining screen time and digital device use in NYC public schools, featuring testimony from DOE officials, state legislators, educators, parents, and students.

DOE First Deputy Chancellor Danielle Giunta presented the new AI and screen time policy: no individual device use for grades 2K-2, recommended 30-minute limits for grades 3-5, 45 minutes for grades 6-8, and a moratorium on student-facing generative AI through grade 8.

Council members pressed DOE on mandates vs. recommendations, YouTube blocking, data privacy audits, vendor accountability, gamified apps, and parental consent, while public testimony overwhelmingly called for stronger mandates, paper-based alternatives, and evidence-based ed tech evaluation.
title: Committee on Oversight and Investigations
topic: Oversight – Examining Screen Time and the Use of Digital Devices in New York City Public Schools
